title: The times are changing: A primer on novel clinical trial designs and endpoints in critical care research
abstract: Critical care medicine has been a rapidly evolving area of clinical practice since its inception.1 This rapid evolution, supported by scientific and technological advancements, has been further propelled by evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs).2 The RCT has been the gold-standard approach for establishing cause and effect.2 This study design provides the most effective control of confounding by baseline variables, thus addressing the most important threat to establishing cause-and-effect relationships between an intervention and outcome of interest. Overall familiarity of the research community, ease of interpretation, and ability to provide a high-quality answer to a specific research question have facilitated increasing use of RCTs in critical care research. As the number of critical care RCTs has increased over time, several challenges have been identified.2,3 First, substantial heterogeneity of disease and severity of illness presents a unique challenge for trial enrollment, outcome evaluation, and bedside applicability. Second, rapidly obtaining informed consent and deploying an intervention is very different, and often more difficult, within critical care medicine as compared to other practice areas. Third, poor prognosis in many critically ill conditions, such as sepsis, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), and cardiac arrest, presents greater potential for futility.4-6 Furthermore, selecting an optimal trial outcome can be difficult as clinical practicality and applicability must be considered alongside what is important to the patient. Lastly, the standard approach to trial design often creates a rigid and inflexible infrastructure, furthering research inefficiency. Collectively, these factors have contributed to numerous RCTs across a spectrum of critically ill populations and interventions producing neutral results, leading to calls for novel RCT methodology.2,7-13 Furthermore, single-center RCTs producing positive results are frequently overturned by subsequent larger, multicenter RCTs.14 This primer for the clinical pharmacist will discuss innovative clinical trial designs and novel trial endpoints within critical care research. Within each section, emerging approaches aimed at overcoming the challenges and limitations of traditional methodologies will be discussed. Furthermore, practical examples and available resources will be highlighted to assist clinical pharmacists in understanding, interpreting, and applying these methodologies in their clinical practice and/or research. Although growing rapidly, critical care medicine as a specialty remains on the younger end of the spectrum when compared to other fields of medicine and, as such, remains behind in terms of designing and conducting resource-efficient clinical trials. Notable challenges in critical care research and how each contributes to decreased trial efficiency and applicability are summarized in Table 1. In the following section, we provide an overview of alternative study designs that can be utilized to overcome the limitations of traditional RCTs along with examples of their application. Notable Limitations of Study Designs of Traditional RCTs2 Abbreviation: RCT, randomized controlled trial. Issues with applicability and feasibility in RCTs arise when trial protocols are overly restrictive and do not reflect true clinical practice.2,15 This complicates not only trial enrollment and proceedings but also application of trial protocols or results to the “gray areas” of practice at the bedside. Therefore, pragmatic trial designs are of interest within critical are research.16 Trial pragmatism (ie, the degree to which trial enrollment and intervention delivery reflect real-world practice) exists as a continuum rather than a dichotomy, and the PRagmatic-Explanatory Continuum Indicator Summary-2 (PRECIS-2) is a validated tool developed to help evaluate this continuum.17 The PRECIS-2 utilizes 9 domains to assist trialists in evaluating the impact their design decisions will have on applicability. Pragmatic trial designs can be used to better align clinical research and clinical practice, improving efficiency and applicability. Trial embedment is one approach to enhancing pragmatism. In these designs, recruitment, enrollment, randomization, interventions, data extraction, and/or documentation are integrated into existing clinical practice.18,19 For example, a study on stress ulcer prophylaxis utilized a registry-embedded component to improve ascertainments.20 In a trial examining the effect of procalcitonin monitoring on antibiotic use, guidelines were embedded as a decision support tool within the electronic heath record, which increased protocol compliance and presented a change easily translatable to clinical practice.21 Another approach to pragmatism is the cluster RCT, which can be a parallel or stepped-wedge design depending on whether crossover of clusters is utilized (Figure 1).22 Cluster RCTs have been used to study fluid balance control in critically ill patients.23 Additional examples utilizing parallel, stepped-wedge, and other pragmatic designs have been produced by Vanderbilt University Medical Center and the Pragmatic Critical Care Research Group.24 Together, they have enrolled more than 40,000 patients across 15 trials focusing on airway management, fluid management, and antibiotic selection.25-28 Cluster RCTs provide a more efficient design when interventions are best applied to patient groups (eg, patients within an intensive care unit [ICU], healthcare institution, or health system) rather than at the individual patient level. They can reduce crossover between intervention and control groups, enhance external validity, and facilitate evaluation of interventions targeting modification of healthcare environments or behaviors.29,30 Depiction of parallel and stepped-wedge cluster randomized controlled trial (RCT) study designs. Parallel cluster RCTs (top panel) are randomized at the center (eg, ICU, clinic, hospital) level rather than the individual level. Centers (clusters) are randomized to control (shaded blue) or treatment (shaded gray) for the duration of the study (in parallel). Data are collected continuously throughout the study on all clusters. Data from the treatment and control groups are compared in statistical analysis. Stepped-wedge cluster RCTs (bottom panel) are randomized at the center (eg, ICU, clinic, hospital) level rather than the individual level. The study begins with all centers (clusters) exposed to control (shaded blue). Clusters are the randomized to cross over to treatment exposure (shaded gray) at regular intervals (steps). This occurs until all participants have crossed over and experienced the treatment. Data are collected continuously throughout the study on all clusters during both control and treatment time periods. Data from the treatment and control groups are compared in statistical analysis. In contrast to parallel cluster RCTs, wherein clusters are randomized to treatment or control at baseline and only a subset of enrolled clusters receive treatment, stepped-wedge cluster RCTs involve all clusters receiving treatment, with the chronological sequence of treatment allocation across clusters being randomly allocated. Stepped-wedge designs may be better suited to examine complex interventions in a more timely and accurate manner due to the gradual (ie, stepwise) participant recruitment into the intervention.22 This can be especially helpful in critical care medicine when research to inform clinical practice is needed but logistical or operational barriers exist. A drawback of stepped-wedge versus parallel cluster RCTs is greater vulnerability to confounding from changes in practice over time.31 With either cluster RCT design, clustering must be clearly justifiable before conducting a trial with this design.29,30 Additionally, the statistical analysis must account for correlation of outcome risk among patients within the same clusters compared to those from other clusters. Oversimplification of trial interventions (ie, investigating only one or two of many possible alternative interventions) is especially common in critical care research.2 Consider acute ischemic stroke, which can be managed with fibrinolytics, antiplatelets, statins, and/or procedural interventions at varying doses, time points, or durations. Multiple RCTs looking at these interventions individually could be (and have been) conducted. However, a multifactorial design, or the study of multiple interventions within the same trial, can be a more efficient way to investigate several of these interventions at once (Figure 2).19 Examples of multifactorial designs include the FACTT trial in ARDS (conservative vs liberal fluids and pulmonary artery catheter vs central venous catheter) and the VANISH trial in septic shock (vasopressin vs norepinephrine and hydrocortisone vs placebo).32,33 Both studies compared multiple combinations of multiple types of interventions, decreasing the need to repeat individual RCTs. Additionally, there was an increased likelihood trial participations would receive at least some type of active therapy, as opposed to only placebo, due to combinations of interventions. One challenge with multifactorial designs is potentially complex trial protocols, depending on the number of interventions under investigation. Additionally, a common concern with multifactorial designs is potential interactions between multiple interventions, which could make interpretation and application of results challenging.19 Depiction of a multifactorial randomized controlled trial (RCT) study design. Patients enrolled are randomized to a treatment regimen. Each treatment regimen is a combination of different interventions of interest (Treatments 1-3 and Treatments A and B). The multifactorial design allows for each combination of interventions to be studied. Following randomization, patients are exposed to their assigned treatment regimen and data are collected. Data from each of the treatment regimen groups are compared in statistical analysis. The need to answer multiple questions has always existed in critical care research; however, the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic further emphasized the timeliness with which researchers needed to do so and led to the growing use of adaptive trials (Figure 3).34,35 Adaptative in this context refers to changing of a component of trial design after the trial has started (eg, refining sample sizes, abandoning ineffective treatment arms, adjusting patient populations for inclusion, or changing randomization ratios).2,35 A common feature of adaptive trials is response-adaptive randomization, which involves adjusting randomization ratios based on accumulating trial data. This cyclic process continues until a predefined success or futility threshold is met and the study concludes. Bayesian statistical methods are used in adaptive designs because of their ability to handle continuous assessment of accumulating evidence in addition to what is known prior to trial commencement.2,36 The utility of Bayesian analysis has also been demonstrated in post hoc analyses of RCTs originally reporting neutral findings whereby the application of a Bayesian approach suggested a signal of benefit.37 Further discussion on Byesian analysis has been published elsewhere and is beyond the scope of this primer.37,38 Depiction of an adaptive randomized controlled trial (RCT) study design. Patients enrolled are randomized to treatment and control groups, as they typically would be in a traditional RCT. Data are collected on each group over a period of time. During a preplanned interim analysis, accumulated trial data is analyzed and used to modify aspects of the ongoing trial, which in this example is randomization ratio. Preplanned thresholds for trial success and/or futility can also be assessed at an interim analysis to determine if the trial should proceed. Trial modifications are made if needed, and patients enrolled will continue with their assigned treatment. This can occur over repeated interim analyses until trial completion. Data are collected continuously throughout the trial and compared in statistical analysis. Platform trials are an extension of adaptive trials and are another way to investigate multiple treatments in a specific condition.39 Platforms are broad categories or domains of interventions aimed at treating a specific condition, with each platform composed of specific therapeutic agents or combinations thereof. Platform trials can be classified as open or closed.39 Closed platforms consist of a set number of interventions and have a definite stopping point. Alternatively, open platforms begin with a set number of interventions but have the ability to add or drop interventions or platforms based on adaptive rules. This creates a perpetual study design that can be continued as new hypotheses are developed or interventions are identified.40 To date, few critical care trials have used adaptive platform designs; however, with methodological and technological improvements, they are gaining traction in both adult and pediatric populations.41,42 One well-known example is the REMAP-CAP study.43 Although initially designed to study treatments for the adaptive platform was to to interventions for The ongoing REMAP-CAP study platforms for and with the ability to add platforms as new are the platform trial was during the pandemic and facilitated and of multiple clinical trials to potential effective trials have led to the of other adaptive platform trials the of within critical care research that are or will be within the platform trials have often in of specific study due to futility thresholds being of futility can treatment and Furthermore, of randomization ratios can potentially the sample needed to statistical improving trial include the ability to patient the ability to modify treatments or treatment groups over time, and the potential for in trial However, challenges also complex trial protocols and infrastructure, statistical and substantial and resources which use of adaptive platform trials. improving the design and efficiency in critical care research will in of such evidence must be into clinical practice to impact patient The in of is and the need for than focusing on the effect of a clinical these trials investigate interventions to improve of in clinical care and examine the between and the of the are few published critical however, there is an ongoing trial investigating of care and within the With growing for the of and its application to trials will a in critical care research to the bedside. title: A metabolomic recurrence score for risk-stratification of elderly patients (pts) with early colorectal cancer (eCRC)
abstract: Abstract Background Adjuvant treatment decisions for pts with eCRC are currently based on suboptimal risk stratification factors, especially for elderly pts. Metabolomics measures multiple cancer-related metabolites with potential to identify new biomarkers in this setting. We have shown that serum metabolomics can discriminate pts with eCRC from pts with metastatic CRC (mCRC). We hypothesized that a metabolomic score derived from pts with mCRC may identify pts with eCRC with an increased risk of relapse. This hypothesis was tested in a cohort of elderly pts with eCRC. Methods Serum samples from 103 pts aged ≥70 were collected from four clinical trials with 5 years follow up. These samples were derived from 55 pts with eCRC, and 48 with mCRC. Samples were retrospectively analyzed via proton nuclear magnetic resonance (1H NMR), to assess their metabolomic fingerprints. A Random Forest (RF) classification model was built using a training set of 30 eCRC pts free from relapse at 5 years and all mCRC pts (N = 48). This model was then applied to a validation set constituted by the remaining eCRC pts (10 relapse-free and 15 relapsed). A risk-of-recurrence score was built on the basis of the likelihood of the sample being misclassified as metastatic. Results In the eCRC group, 44% (n = 24) received adjuvant chemotherapy, and 27% (n = 15) experienced relapse. In the training set, the RF model discriminated eCRC from mCRC with an accuracy of 74.4%. The RF risk of recurrence score correlated with relapse, with an AUC of 0.754 in ROC analysis. In the training set, by maximizing specificity and sensitivity, a threshold for the RF score was set at 0.55. In the validation set, using this threshold, an AUC of 0.727 in ROC analysis, and a prediction accuracy of 76% (73.3% sensitivity, 80% specificity) were obtained in predicting relapse. Conclusions Serum metabolomics performed on post-operative samples of elderly pts with eCRC identifies pts with higher risk of relapse with good accuracy. This may represent a tool to refine risk stratification in this population, to maximize the benefit from adjuvant chemotherapy. Based on these results, a prospective trial is ongoing (LIquid BIopsy and METabolomics in CRC - LIBIMET). Legal entity responsible for the study The authors. title: Proteomic Identification of Plasma Proteins Associated with Future Dementia Development
abstract: Dementia is a progressive decline of cognitive abilities, severe enough to affect daily life activities and independent function. Dementia is most common in older individuals: about one-third of adults 85 years or older may exhibit Alzheimer disease (AD) related dementia, but it is not a normal part of aging (1). Various neurodegenerative disorders contribute to the development of dementia through progressive and irreversible loss of neurons and brain function. AD accounts for 60%–80% of dementia cases (1). Amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles are key pathological features of AD. Amyloid beta 42 and p-tau are known biomarkers for the presence of AD pathology and therapeutic targets (2). However, these AD biomarkers do not appear to be well suited on their own for determining the risk of developing AD dementia before amyloid pathology or related cognitive symptoms appear. Furthermore, therapies targeting these pathologies have shown modest but not complete clinical improvement of cognitive symptoms. While our knowledge regarding biomarkers for AD and other dementias has increased dramatically in recent years, a better understanding of biological pathways that may lead to development of dementia, and the identification of potential associated biomarkers, may enable the selective application of preventive measures including therapeutic interventions and lifestyle changes. Current known risks for dementia include, but are not limited to, nonmodifiable factors such as age and genetics. For example, the risk of AD dementia and vascular dementia increases with age; while the most significant genetic risk factor for sporadic AD is the presence of the apolipoprotein E gene APOE4 (3). The reason APOE4 increases AD risk is not well understood and inheriting APOE4 does not ensure on its own that the individual will develop AD. Modifiable risk factors of dementia include smoking, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease (4). AD is characterized by a long asymptomatic preclinical phase in which the individuals appear to be cognitively normal (CN) but have evidence of amyloid pathology (2). However, many CN individuals presenting with amyloid pathological changes never develop AD dementia using current cognitive assessments. This further highlights the need to identify new biomarkers and therapeutic targets for long-term dementia risk stratification and disease progression. One way to achieve this is by employing proteomic methods to retrospectively identify proteins that are differentially expressed in individuals who developed dementia versus those who do not. While proteomic studies have been undertaken to identify potentially clinically relevant proteins, most previous studies have focused on identifying risk factors in individuals in a time frame relatively close to disease onset. Walker et al. undertook a multifaceted approach to identify relative plasma protein abundance associated with the development of dementia in individuals 45 to 65 years of age, often decades prior to the development of dementia related symptoms (5). In a primary proteomic discovery analysis, 1784 individuals who developed dementia over the course of a 25-year follow-up period were retrospectively identified out of 10 981 participants in the Atherosclerosis Risk in Community study cohort. This provided a large cohort for SomaLogic’s SomaScan v.4 proteomic analysis utilizing 5284 nucleic acid-based protein binding aptamers to query the association of the abundance of 4877 plasma proteins with long-term neurocognitive outcomes. However, some potential drawbacks of aptamer-based biomarker discovery include overrepresentation of secreted proteins, cross-reactivity with nonintended target proteins, and target protein affinity variations related to protein complexing or single nucleotide polymorphisms. Using this initial proteomic analysis, a total of 32 proteins were associated with future development of dementia (Table 1). After adjusting for known risk factors (APOE4 status, cardiovascular disease, and kidney dysfunction), 26 proteins were found to be associated with the development of dementia within 25 years. Seven proteins were found to be associated with the development of dementia within 15 years as determined by an internal replication study on the original study cohort. Only one protein, Growth/Differentiation Factor-15 (GDF-15), was found to be associated with dementia risk in both the 25-year and 15-year groups. Further work was then performed to better elucidate the potential clinical relevance of the 32 proteins identified by the initial proteomic analysis. Two independent secondary study external replication cohorts were used to attempt to reproduce the association of the discovered proteins with dementia development and to evaluate their association with known CSF biomarkers of AD pathology, neurodegeneration, and neuroinflammation. Fifteen of the 32 originally identified proteins were associated with the development of dementia in at least one of the 2 replication cohorts via SomaScan abundance assessment of 4877 proteins. To assess for potential differential protein expression in brain tissue of AD patients, some (but not all) protein expression patterns in post mortem brain tissues versus control brain tissues were examined in 2 patient cohorts. Eight unique proteins, denoted as + in Table 1, were identified to be differentially expressed in AD patient brain tissue as compared to control brain tissue in at least one cohort. Additional studies were conducted to evaluate the expression of the identified proteins in brain tissue, to assess the biological pathways and protein networks linked with the identified proteins, and Mendelian randomization analysis and genome-wide association studies to assess association with AD, and plasma protein abundance. While these various studies did not uniformly indicate association of all proteins with dementia, several proteins were associated with CSF markers of AD (amyloid beta and p-tau) and/or associated with non-AD specific markers of neurodegeneration (including total-tau and neurofilament light chain). Four of the identified proteins are prioritized AD therapeutic targets; 8 proteins are targets of non-AD existing drugs; and 3 of the proteins have been genetically linked to AD (Table 1). The protein that exhibited the strongest association with 25-year dementia risk was GDF-15, but this immune and stress response protein does not appear to be linked to an AD specific role and was not associated with CSF amyloid and/or p-tau concentrations. This extensive analysis identified 4 potentially overlapping functional pathways, previously known to be associated with long-term development of dementia: proteostasis, immunity, synaptic function, and extracellular matrix organization (ECMO). Fifteen of the 32 originally identified proteins were classified as “prioritized midlife biomarkers of dementia risk and AD” and placed into one of the 4 functional pathways by the authors (see Table 1). While the degree of risk associated with these proteins and associated pathways for the development of dementia is not currently fully understood, these results may spur further investigation into mechanisms that lead to dementia development. For example, the authors suggest a causal relationship for dementia development for the immune-related proteins serpin family A member 3 (SERPINA3) and epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), as well as an association of alteration of the extracellular matrix organization related metalloproteinase proteins such as MMP12 and MMP19, with long-term AD risk. Two synaptic proteins appeared to function as midlife markers of AD-related dementia (cerebellin 4 precursor (CBLN4) and glutamate ionotropic receptor delta type subunit 2 (GRID2)). The proteostasis-related proteins such as the heat shock protein heat shock protein family A (Hsp 70) member 1B (HSPA1B), and the chaperone proteins DNAJ Heat Shock Protein Family DNJB9/DNAJB12, were associated with long-term AD dementia risk and the authors suggest that up-regulation of these proteostasis proteins may occur in response to the presence of protein misfolding before the development of dementia. Using a subset of 13 of these proteins, the authors developed a predictive model for the development of future all-cause dementia. This model only achieved a ROC curve (AUC) of 0.66. This predictive model significantly underperformed when compared to a predictive model that included a combination of known risk factors (such as age, APOE4 status, cardiovascular risk factors) with an AUC of 0.77 in the patient cohort. Combining both predictive models did not improve the performance of either model alone. This data indicates that while the identified proteins may be altered in individuals developing dementia later in life; at present they do not represent strong long-term prognostic biomarkers. Furthermore, the remaining challenges in the predictive power of the long-term markers is evident in comparison to the clinical performance of emerging CSF and circulating biomarkers for the evaluation of the presence of amyloid-related pathology, which often exhibit AUCs >0.90 (2). The impressive amount of evidence generated by Walker et al. will require future effort to fully understand and confirm the relevance of their findings to dementia risk and AD pathogenesis, as many of these proteins have some function unrelated to neurological-specific processes. It should be noted that dementia in the original proteomic cohort was not specific to AD and may have been related to other types of dementia or mixed dementias. Furthermore, SomaScan aptamer technology does not detect all potential proteins within the proteome, and indeed, a newer version of SomaScan (not utilized in this study) has expanded the number of protein abundance targets to 7288. However, it is comforting that proteomic analysis did identify multiple proteins previously identified of pathological/therapeutic interest in AD. While this study yielded novel information regarding biological pathways that may lead to dementia development, it remains to be determined as to how these proteins and pathways might lead to the development of dementia much later in life. Further examination of these proteins and pathways may eventually (but not immediately) translate into advances in targeted early intervention. title: Ageing is associated with increased variability of cellular reprogramming and wound healing
abstract: Commentary on ‘Heterogeneity in old fibroblasts is linked to variability in reprogramming and wound healing’, by S. Mahmoudi et al., Nature, 2019.1 Understanding the determinants of ageing and senescence of cells as part of functional tissues has many implications in translational medicine and is highly relevant for improving treatments of degenerative cardiovascular diseases. The development of methods to create induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) revolutionized the perspectives in regenerative medicine. In 2006, Takahashi and Yamanaka2 first created protocols for establishing iPSCs from murine and later from human tissues. iPSCs are derived through reprogramming of somatic cells by introduction of transcription factors Oct3/4, Sox2, c-Myc, and Klf4.2 Today iPSCs are used to create models for studying cardiovascular diseases, drug effects and for developmental research. During the last years, reprogramming strategies were developed to generate human iPSCs from various tissues such as keratinocytes, blood cells, extramedullary tissue as well as fibroblasts, and to differentiate iPSCs into several types of cells including cardiomyocytes (Figure 1A).3–5 However, the success in creating iPSCs largely differs between tissues, indicating that the cellular origin may determine the reprogramming efficiency. Today, differentiating iPSCs to cardiac cells represents a promising approach in curing degenerative cardiovascular diseases as myocardial infarction or cardiomyopathies. Determinants of reprogramming to iPSCs. (A) By introduction of Oct3/4, Sox2, c-Myc, and Klf4, a variety of cells can be transformed to iPSCs that can be differentiated to cell types of several organs. Cardiomyocytes generated from iPSCs are used to create models of cardiovascular diseases, applications in regenerative medicine as contractible cardiomyocyte patches, engineered heart muscles (EHMs) or biological pacemakers consisting of artificial sinus node cells, and drug testing. (B) The study by Mahmoudi et al. showed that during ageing of mice the variability of reprogramming efficiency and wound healing dynamics, expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines as well as the fraction of activated fibroblasts are increased. In old mice, the efficiency of reprogramming fibroblasts to iPSCs correlated with the ratio of IL-6 to TNF expression levels and the fraction of activated fibroblasts. Reprogramming efficiency was positively correlated with proliferation and negatively correlated with senescence markers. Recently, Mahmoudi et al.1 analysed the influence of ageing on properties of fibroblasts and their ability for reprogramming to iPSCs. Interestingly, cytokine profiles of old mice (28–29 months) showed increased levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines as interleukin (IL)-6 and tumor necrosis factor (TNF), anti-inflammatory cytokines as IL-4, chemokines and growth factors as CSF1 in comparison to young mice (3 months). A similar dependency of cytokine expression patterns on age was observed in lung fibroblasts and human primary fibroblasts. A central finding of the study was that on average the reprogramming efficiency did not largely differ between fibroblast cultures from young or old mice, whereas, the variability in reprogramming efficiency significantly increased with age. Subsequently, differences between fibroblast cultures from older mice that showed high or low reprogramming efficiency were investigated based on a multi-omics approach including transcriptomic, epigenomic, and metabolomic analyses. Interestingly, pathways related to secreted factors, extracellular matrix and contractility were transcriptionally enriched in fibroblast cultures from old mice. Further analyses of transcriptional differences associated with reprogramming efficiency in fibroblast cultures of old mice showed that cellular processes as fibroblast activation or DNA replication were significantly enriched in cultures with high reprogramming efficiency. Thereby, an interesting link could be created between transcriptional programmes involved in wound healing and the observed ability for reprogramming to iPSCs. In wounds, fibroblasts become activated to myofibroblasts that proliferate, produce extracellular matrix (ECM) and essentially contribute to tissue repair.6 Based on multi-omics analyses and validating knockdown experiments, the transcription factor EBF2 could be identified as driver of the gene expression signature associated with fibroblast activation in older mice. Using single-cell sequencing, the authors investigated age-dependent cellular heterogeneity in tissues of skin wounds in mice. Thereby, it could be observed that the proportion of activated fibroblasts was positively correlated with reprogramming efficiency. By immunostaining and fluorescence assisted cell sorting, wound fibroblasts, preselected based on expression of PDGFRα, were further characterized to analyse determinants of reprogramming efficiency, proliferation and senescence. It was observed that activated fibroblasts were indeed proliferating and did not express markers of cellular senescence. Additional experiments showed positive correlation of reprogramming efficiency with proliferation and negative correlation with a senescence marker. Old fibroblast cultures contained higher fractions of cells expressing the marker gene THY1 that correlated with the gene expression signature of activated fibroblasts. Interestingly, however, THY1 expression was negatively correlated with reprogramming efficiency. Conditioned medium from activated fibroblasts, enhanced reprogramming of activated as well as non-activated fibroblasts. The authors concluded that activated fibroblasts show opposing intrinsic and extrinsic effects on reprogramming efficiency and that fractions of activated and non-activated fibroblast types underly the variability in reprogramming. To investigate the influence from extrinsic factors as secreted cytokines or growth factors, media from fibroblast groups with ‘good’ and ‘bad’ reprogramming efficiency were collected. Incubating ‘bad’ cultures with conditioned medium from ‘good’ cultures resulted in a significant increase in reprogramming efficiency indicating that differences between fibroblast cultures could, at least in part, be attributed to extrinsic factors. More specifically, roles of the cytokines IL-6, TNF and IL-1b on the variability of reprogramming efficiencies were studied. Essentially, IL-6 was associated with increased, whereas, TNF and IL-1b were associated with decreased reprogramming efficiency. Interestingly, only TNF had an impact on the observed variability of reprogramming efficiencies of fibroblast cultures from older mice. The authors concluded that fractions of activated fibroblasts and their secretion of cytokines as IL-6 and TNF could be responsible variability in reprogramming between fibroblast cultures. Next, the authors investigated fibroblasts from mice showing slow or fast wound healing trajectories. Similar to observations regarding the efficiency for reprogramming to iPSCs, the wound healing time did, on average, not substantially differ between young and old mice, whereas, the variability in wound healing times was strongly increased in old mice. Single-cell RNA sequencing of all cells from wounds of old mice with either slow- or fast-healing wounds interestingly showed that fibroblasts were more abundant in wounds of slow-healing old mice, whereas immune cells were more abundant in wounds of fast-healing old mice. Three subpopulations of wound fibroblasts were identified, a first subpopulation with similar abundance in slow- and fast healing mice, a second subpopulation over-represented in fast-healing, and a third subpopulation over-represented in slow-healing mice. The second subpopulation showed increased expression of TNF, which led the authors to conclude that TNF secretion is associated with fast healing and bad reprogramming efficiency. Collectively, the study by Mahmoudi et al. indicates that ageing is associated with increased variability of cellular reprogramming in vitro and wound healing in vivo. The observation of different types of activated fibroblasts might in future stimulate re-defining subgroups of wound fibroblasts that have distinct roles in wound healing dynamics. The study characterized various aspects of interrelations between reprogramming of fibroblasts to iPSCs, ageing, wound healing, fibroblast activation, proliferation and senescence. Therefore, it can serve as a valuable basis for future applications of iPSCs as well as research in wound healing and may stimulate advances in regenerative medicine. In cardiovascular medicine, transcriptional heterogeneity of fibroblasts is associated with several pathologies of the ageing heart, including heart failure and atrial fibrillation. Recently, a functional diversification of fibroblasts in the ageing heart was observed.7 In this area of translational research, several techniques using iPSC-derived myocardial patches or biological pace makers were developed (Figure 1A).8,9 Furthermore, several types of heart cells can be derived from iPSCs to study effects of cardiological drugs as ion channel inhibitors or investigate pathomechanisms of genetic disorders.10 An important question is whether it will be possible to regenerate destructed myocardium or increase myocardial contractility using stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes. Thereby, novel options for heart failure treatment might be developed. Knowledge about functional states of fibroblasts and implications of the properties of fibroblasts for deriving pluripotent stem cells will be essential for this area of innovative therapeutic approaches in cardiology. In this context, the study by Mahmoudi et al. contributes to understanding the determinants of reprogramming efficiency. This will be essential for improving protocols and culturing conditions that maximize the yield in generated iPSCs for future applications in personalized regenerative medicine. title: Finding the culprit for the failure of the immune clock as time goes by
abstract: Over the last years, it became clear that circadian rhythms can have major influences on the immune system.1 Circadian rhythms refer to endogenous 24-h cycles that are driven by internal molecular clocks. The importance of this rhythmicity is highlighted by the estimation that at least 10–20% of all mammalian genes are controlled in a circadian manner.1 It is well known that leucocyte trafficking from the bone marrow to the circulation is controlled in a circadian manner, which is regulated by key clock genes like Bmal1 and Arntl.2,3 Disruption of this circadian rhythmicity increases the occurrence of disease-causing inflammation and aggravates various pathologies, both acute ones like bacterial infections and myocardial infarctions and chronic ones like atherosclerosis.1,4 A recent study by Blacher et al.5 in Nature Immunology highlighted the interesting notion that the circadian gene regulation is disrupted upon ageing. Ageing as well as the disruption of circadian rhythmicity are both associated with an increased incidence of various pathologies including cardiovascular diseases.6 One of the main underlying mechanisms for this increased age-related risk is a dysregulation of the immune function, resulting in increased inflammation.7 In their study, Blacher et al. isolated blood monocytes and bone marrow macrophages from young (2-month-old) and aged (20-month-old) mice every 4 h over a 24 h period to investigate the circadian rhythmicity in these cells. Consistent with previously published results,2 young Ly6Chigh monocytes showed a clear circadian trafficking from the bone marrow to the circulation. Interestingly, however, this circadian rhythm is lost upon ageing, as the amount of circulating cells in aged mice hardly changed during the day. Ageing also affected the functionality of the cells, as aged mice demonstrated a reduced survival upon exposure with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) compared with young mice. Even more interesting, LPS injection at ZT12 (lights off) in young mice resulted in an increased mortality compared with mice injected at ZT0 (lights on), a differential circadian-regulated effect that could not be observed in aged mice. In line with this, the phagocytosis of Escherichia coli particles by macrophages also showed a clear rhythmicity in cells from young mice, while this was not the case in cells from aged mice, again clearly demonstrating that the diurnal rhythmicity is lost with ageing. To further elucidate the underlying molecular basis by which this myeloid circadian rhythmicity is lost with ageing, they performed unbiased transcriptomics, again with 4 h intervals, comparing peritoneal macrophages from young and aged mice. Macrophages from young mice showed 680 genes that undergo rhythmic transcription, while aged macrophages only showed 53 rhythmic genes, clearly highlighting that circadian transcription is significantly disrupted in macrophages upon ageing. In line with the abrogated rhythmic phagocytosis upon ageing, it could be shown that phagocytosis-related genes (CLEAR network) are indeed strongly reduced in aged macrophages and they have lost their rhythmicity. Although core clock genes play a key role in regulating this rhythmicity, the expression of these genes was interestingly not altered upon ageing and can therefore not explain these observations. Other underlying mechanisms were therefore investigated. Although chromatin accessibility could not explain the loss of rhythmicity upon ageing, differential binding of transcription factors could be observed. To identify relevant transcription factors, three criteria were used: the differential chromatin access between young and aged macrophages, the differential binding to genes that show distinct oscillatory patterns upon ageing and the loss of rhythmic expression of the transcription factor upon ageing.5 Based on these three criteria, only one transcription factor could be identified, being Kruppel-like factor 4 (KLF4). Using an ex vivo approach, knockdown of KLF4 disrupted the bacterial phagocytosis and the diurnal rhythm of this phagocytic activity. Furthermore, using the UK BioBank, the authors observed that carriers of a KLF4 variant (rs2236599) have a striking increased risk of developing an E. coli infection and an enhanced infection-related mortality, while overall mortality is unchanged. In this specific biobank, age seems to play an important role as carriers of the KLF4 variant have a reduced age-associated risk for an E. coli infection. All in all, KLF4 seems to be a key regulating factor of the observed age-related circadian effects on macrophages. While this study elucidated the genetic regulatory pathways underlying the effect of ageing on circadian rhythmicity, additional mechanisms that result in a diminished KLF4 activity should be further explored in the future. Besides affecting macrophages, KLF4 can also influence non-immune processes, as it has also been identified as a key transcriptional regulator of mitochondrial homeostasis, including in the heart.8 Interestingly, mitochondrial function has also been described to be dysregulated upon ageing and this may accelerate the development of atherogenesis.9 Therefore, it would be interesting to investigate whether KLF4 is also a key regulator behind the age-related accelerated atherosclerosis and whether circadian effects may play a role in this. In line with this, loss of KLF4 or its family members (e.g. KLF2, KLF5, KLF15) in endothelial cells or smooth muscle cells results in vascular dysfunction and promotes atherosclerosis development.10 Since the exact effects of these KLFs on age-related circadian rhythms in vascular cells and vascular function remain elusive, these are interesting focus points for future research. Although Blacher et al. already initiated translation of their observations to humans in the setting of antimicrobial immunity, it would be highly interesting to further validate their findings using different cohorts of patients with various confounding factors including cardiac or vascular pathologies. This study also highlights the need to take into account the circadian rhythm in clinical studies that involve the isolation of cells such as peripheral blood mononuclear cells, as the time of day at which cells are collected may have an impact on the cells behaviour and thereby confound the outcome of the study. Similarly, therapies targeting macrophages and especially therapies that rely on phagocytosis by macrophages, should be performed in a timely fashion, keeping the circadian rhythm in mind to ensure optimal targeting. Taken together, the study by Blacher et al. provides crucial initial data showing an important interaction between ageing, circadian rhythmicity, and KLF4 in macrophages (Figure 1). This study opens the door to further investigate these interactions in other immune cells and in non-immune cells like the vascular cells. Future research should aim to elucidate potential targets that can be used to stimulate the circadian rhythmicity upon ageing, as this may contribute to an adequate immune response throughout the course of life. Ageing disrupts circadian gene regulation in a KLF4-dependent manner. Upon ageing the circadian rhythmicity of gene expression regulation is lost. This loss of circadian rhythmicity goes hand in hand with immune dysfunction and inadequate immune responses. Although more underlying mechanisms are likely and still need further exploration, KLF4 seems to be at least one of the key regulators. Figure has been created with BioRender.com. Biography: Dr Sandrine Lecour is a Full Professor at the University of Cape Town, Deputy Director of the Cape Heart Institute, University of Cape Town and leader of the Cardioprotection Group. Her research group focuses on the delineation of novel cardioprotective signalling pathways, including high density lipoproteins, sphingolipids, and melatonin. Over the past few years, part of her research has focused on the delineation of the Survivor Activating Factor Enhancement (SAFE) pathway, which is triggered by the immune system. She has published over 100 papers in peer-reviewed journals (H index = 45). She is on the Editorial Board of many peer-reviewed journals, including Journal of Molecular and Cellular in Cardiology and Basic Research in Cardiology. Prof Sandrine Lecour is a Fellow of the European Society of Cardiology and she has been a Committee Member of the European Society of Cardiology Working Group on Cellular Biology of the Heart (2011–21). She is currently the Treasurer at International Society for Heart Research, European section. As the co-founder and the President of the South African Society for Cardiovascular Research (SASCAR) (2009–16), she constantly strives to promote the research and training of students in the cardiovascular field in South Africa. Biography: Dr Emiel van der Vorst obtained his PhD in Cardiovascular Biology and Medicine from the Cardiovascular Research Institute Maastricht (CARIM), The Netherlands in 2015, by studying the effects of high-density lipoproteins on inflammation. For his postdoctoral period he investigated the role of chemokines and chemokine-receptors in atherosclerosis at the Institute for Cardiovascular Prevention (IPEK) in Munich, Germany, resulting in several high-impact publications. Since 2019, he is working as group leader at the Institute for Molecular Cardiovascular Research (IMCAR) in Aachen, Germany, as well as at CARIM and IPEK. Currently his research is focusing on elucidating various mechanisms by which the lipid metabolism interacts with the immune system in the context of cardiovascular disease, especially atherosclerosis. His work is funded by various prestigious (inter)national personal grants and he is member of the editorial boards of several cardiovascular focused journals. title: Identifying needs and opportunities for advancing translational research in cardiovascular disease
abstract: In Western Europe, as in the USA, mortality of cardiovascular disease (CVD) has declined significantly in the last 30 years. Life expectancy for patients with coronary heart disease in the USA increased on average by 3 years between 1970 and 2000.1 Several epidemiological analyses support this positive evolution. An analysis of the underlying causes identifies improvements in quality of care and treatment as a major cause, accounting from 50 up to 75% of the success depending on the study samples, the remainder being accounted for by changes in lifestyle and prevention.2 Research and development in several areas of CVD have contributed to this success. In acute coronary events, the identification and development of efficient and safe thrombolytic agents followed by percutaneous coronary intervention with stent implantation were milestones in the reduction of acute mortality and salvage of myocardium.3–5 Statins have brought a major advance in preventing the progression of atherosclerotic disease and have been recognized for their wide mode of action.6 In heart failure (HF), beta-blockers and ACE-inhibitors have increased life expectancy by a leap.7 Some of these improvements have been the result of a classic bench-to-bedside development of a targeted treatment, such as the statins, others have known a more serendipitous development, such as beta-blockers. In other areas, progress in terms of treatment has been less spectacular and fraught with difficulties. Development of antiarrhythmic agents received a large boost from basic insights into cardiac ion channel structure and function, but translation into pharmacology unveiled unexpected pro-arrhythmia risks of some of the highly specific ion channel blockers in class III.8 Automatic defibrillators have taken an important role in the treatment of life-threatening arrhythmias and save lives, but are not without burden and come at a high cost.9 This latter example is but one highlight of the more sobering and darker side of this medical success story: the improved survival and quality of life of patients with CVD comes at a high economic cost. In the US hospitalizations for CVD have tripled and the cost of care is estimated at 386 billion USD per annum (AMA, Kaiser Family Foundation). Within the EU, the annual cost for healthcare systems for CVD was just under €110 billion in 2006 (British Heart Foundation statistics at www.heartstats.org). Interventions, device therapy, and imaging take up a large share of the cost. Ageing of the population, without further improvement in care and prevention, will lead to a high increase in prevalence of CVD. This is already noticeable in the statistics of the last 10 years, showing a decrease in mortality but an increase in prevalence.10 In addition, in countries with less access to medical care, the incidence of CVD is rising and is expected to continue to increase dramatically.11,12 The WHO has estimated that rising life expectancy coupled with adverse trends in major cardiovascular risk factors including obesity and type II diabetes could lead to a doubling in the absolute incidence of CVD by 2050. There is thus a clear need for continued investment into improving our approach to CVD and thus into cardiovascular research. In addition to the remaining need, the major progress that has been made constitutes a strong incentive for priority funding of cardiovascular research in order to build on this success. Addressing the economic need to contain cost, as well as the necessity to provide better care for a growing patient population, a new paradigm is put forward focusing on promoting health and intervening at the early onset of CVD.13,14 This requires that we (i) improve our physiological and molecular understanding of mechanisms of health and disease so we can implement earlier preventive interventions and better-targeted diagnosis and therapy, (ii) that we develop personalized preventive and therapeutic regimens, and (iii) that we streamline the processes involved in translating knowledge into practice to accelerate implementation of new knowledge. The concept of translational research can be interpreted and defined in many ways by scientists. A consensus view is that the end-target of translational research is the patient, with the goal to improve care. The classic or traditional one-dimensional track of translational research is a sequence of events: discovery of a new mechanism and potential therapeutic target in an experimental or basic research setting, with a drug or device being developed, the approach being validated in the clinical setting and eventually being introduced into clinical practice. This concept is still valid, but in recent years it has come under increasing pressure. The drug development and validation in clinical trials come at a huge cost, largely carried by industry, and in a number of cases, the expected clinical benefits have been disappointing. For example, the development of the CETP inhibitor, torcetrapib, was halted in 2006 when phase III studies showed excessive mortality in the treatment group receiving a combination of atorvastatin and the study drug.15 Therefore, the willingness of industry to take risks has decreased. In this ‘traditional’ approach, the principal actors partake in sequence: basic, industry, and clinical researchers. More recent models of translational research give up on this traditional sequence and can start, for example, from clinical data, feeding into experimental or basic research for further mechanistic insight, or from clinical observations on unexpected drug effects, feeding into new applications (‘reverse’ translational research), with many variations in iterative interactions between the different stages, as illustrated in Figure 1. In the traditional process of translation, basic research is the first step to identify new mechanisms of disease and potential targets for therapy that are elaborated in a proof-of-concept and eventually validated in a clinical trial. In reverse translation, this process starts with a clinical observation that is tested in basic experimental research and a proof-of-concept, with re-iterative steps validating new concepts. Such approaches have been quite successful, as can be illustrated by the example of post-conditioning as a mechanism of cardiac protection. title: Transgenerational epigenetic inheritance: from biology to society—Summary Latsis Symposium Aug 28–30, 2017, Zürich, Switzerland
abstract: In biology, inheritance is a process that ensures the transfer of features and traits from parent to offspring. The most classic view of parental inheritance is that it is genetic and is embedded in genes contained in the genome in germ cells. However, genetic inheritance is now known to contribute to only a part of what an individual can transmit to its progeny. Thus, further to innate traits that each individual receives from its parents, acquired traits, which are traits acquired upon exposure to environmental factors or personal experiences, can also be inherited. This form of inheritance is not encoded in the sequence of genes but is mediated by mechanisms and processes elicited by the environment that modify the activity of the genome persistently across generations. Because it is not encoded in DNA sequences, it is called epigenetic or non-genetic. These mechanisms establish a link between the genome and the environment. They relate to the extremely important question of nature versus nurture namely, how much our own make-up is genetically or epigenetically determined, a question that remains unresolved. In August 2017, an international symposium was organized in Zürich, Switzerland to address the question of epigenetic inheritance. The Latsis symposium 2017 on “Transgenerational epigenetic inheritance: from biology to society” held at the ETH Zürich gathered international leaders in the field and focused on major questions and current challenges raised by the concept of epigenetic inheritance. The symposium was one of the first fully dedicated to the theme of epigenetic inheritance and covered scientific aspects from invertebrates to humans, and from behavior to metabolism in humans and animal models, mental health and epidemiology, bioinformatics and ethics. The symposium lasted 2.5 days and was attended by about 150 people from different countries. The program was structured in sessions of 3–3 h 30 min each (total of five sessions) including invited talks and short oral presentations. This summary provides an overview of the speakers’ presentations and focuses on four major topics: (i) evidence and challenges for epigenetic inheritance in humans, (ii) new insight and major questions raised by work in animal models, (iii) methodologies in epigenetics and (iv) evolution, societal impact and broader considerations. The first session focused on clinical epigenetics, and was started by Marcus Pembrey (University College London) with a review of his long-standing work in epigenetic epidemiology, in particular related to food deprivation and smoking. He presented new DNA methylation (DNAme) results shedding light on possible mechanisms of transmission. His talk touched a number of issues critical to the field, from the identification of exposure-sensitive developmental periods to the interpretation of underlying gene and phenotypic differences between the first generations, and the discrepancy between symptoms transmission and changes in DNAme. Markus Pembrey presented recent work on the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC), showing that autism risk is higher in granddaughters if the maternal grandmother has smoked during pregnancy. Autism is one of many devastating neuropsychiatric disorders in which exposure of past generations is likely to play an important role in disease etiology. This is a vivid example demonstrating the importance of research in the field of epigenetic inheritance and the high stakes regarding implications for patients and families. Another question addressed by Pembrey was that of the sensitive period during which the germline is particularly responsive to environmental factors. He reviewed the seminal work he did with Lars Olov Bygren on the impact of food availability on health and mortality of grandoffspring in the Överkalix cohort where the concept of sensitive period and transgenerational programming was first introduced. He pointed out that the effects of scarce food supply is difficult to disentangle from the effects of stress resulting from unfavorable living conditions and famine. This work highlights that early life experiences of parents and ancestors contribute to population developmental variation beyond that due to social transmission. Adelheid Soubry (University Leuven) then discussed different studies on the impact of paternal diet and exposure to chemicals on sperm and offspring. She presented an update on several large human cohort studies and new work on the impact of organophosphate (OP) flame retardants. Measuring OP levels in men and correlating it to DNAme in sperm revealed OP-related changes in DNAme at imprinted genes. An interesting finding was that “cocktail exposure” to several OPs was associated with increased DNAme aberrancies in sperm. This highlights a particular sensitivity of imprinted genes to pre-conception environmental exposure, and a non-additive effect of combining multiple exposures, suggesting that broad DNAme measurements should be more systematically considered in such studies. But DNAme is variable in sperm and some maternally derived DNAme loci are less methylated than expected, suggesting that great care is needed in comparative studies. Her ongoing research highlights an exciting new approach in human studies that includes analysis of sperm samples used for IVF and subsequent analysis of fertilized embryos (those not used for implantation). This resembles attempts made in mice and holds promise to unravel mechanistic links between sperm and embryo, a key challenge in basic research. Pursuing the theme of epigenetic changes induced by chemicals, Marisa Bartolemei (University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia) presented her work on bisphenol A (BPA) exposure during pregnancy, showing that bile acids and tryptophan metabolism underlie metabolic disease induced in mother and male pups. New results show that these effects can be passed to descendants through the matriline, affecting male offspring. Beyond metabolism, skeletal health also seems to be affected by BPA treatment, which fits with the fact that ovarian hormones play a key role in bone health and points to research needs on the broad effects of chemicals and endocrine disruptors. But although compounds such as BPA, dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (DDT) or vinclozolin have long been at the center of studies on epigenetic inheritance, it is still unclear how they, or any environmental factors for that matter, can influence the germline. One possibility is that chemicals can interfere with endogenous factors that can bind directly to receptors expressed in/on germ cells. Indeed, Marine Baptissart (North Carolina State University, Raleigh) presented interesting work from her doctoral studies in the lab of David Volle, showing that a diet fortified with bile acids impacts sperm cells through the G protein-coupled bile acid receptor Tgr5, which is expressed in the germ cell lineage. Her latest data suggest that this effect can be transmitted and impacts DNA condensation due to altered histone/protamine transition, and DNAme in sperm, suggesting that a bile acid receptor in the germline could mediate epigenetic inheritance. To testify the importance of research in the field of epigenetic inheritance in human, Jill Escher (San Jose, CA), a philanthropist and mother of two children with non-verbal autism, presented a moving and personal account linking the tragic story of her family and many other families, with environmental risk factors. Ms Escher urged scientists to study the potential effects of environmental exposure on germ cells in utero and the neurodevelopmental outcomes, and presented the activities of her foundation, the Escher Fund for Autism, in support of such research. Moshe Szyf (McGill University, Montreal) discussed his work on how social stimuli, e.g. licking in rodents, rearing conditions or social rank in primates, and stress affect the epigenome in T cells and germ cells, and stress response in the offspring. He discussed the results of a prospective longitudinal study following the impact of an ice storm in Quebec in 1998, which left millions of Canadians without heat and at winter temperatures. Immune system changes and DNAme levels in T cells of teenage offspring were associated with mother’s exposure to the event during pregnancy. Noting that sperm contains glucocorticoid receptors (GR), he hypothesized that GR may be a link between germ cells and the metabolic and psychological uptake of stressful environments, and provided preliminary evidence for this. Other forms of population trauma and their consequences over generations were discussed by Rachel Yehuda (Mount Sinai Hospital, New York). She described the long-term consequences (up to over 50 years) of traumatically stressful experiences such as the Holocaust and 9/11, on survivors and their offspring, and the development of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and mood or affective disorders. She highlighted sex- and age-specific effects on cortisol levels and sensitivity, associated with changes in the methylation of key genes in related pathways, such as FKBP5, that can be opposite in exposed parents and offspring. In the search for resilience mechanisms, she proposed to “harness epigenetics for positive resilience building.” Of all environmental exposures that affect individuals and their offspring, diet is probably one of the most critical and much work has been done on its impact across generations in animals. Building on the notion in humans that the risk for obesity/diabetes can be transmitted, Josep Jimenez-Chillarón (Hospital Sant Joan de Deu, Barcelona) described a mouse model of adiposity based on increased milk intake during postnatal development achieved by reducing litter size. This manipulation leads to metabolic symptoms such as liver-mediated increase in adiposity and altered glucose tolerance, which persist for at least two generations, and are associated with changes in DNAme in sperm of exposed males and liver of the offspring. The metabolic phenotypes appear complex and differ across generations, consistent with the notion of differences between direct and transmitted effects (see below). An enrichment in tRNA fragments (tRFs) was also observed in the testes of exposed males, in line with previous findings that tRFs in sperm are altered by a nutritional insult. In search for underlying mechanisms, Vardhman Rakyan (Blizard Institute, London) presented results on the effects of protein restriction in mice in utero, showing a decrease in offspring weight specifically when switching from protein restriction to normal diet after weaning. This suggested here too that the effect results from a mismatch between early and late environment. This was associated with differential methylation and copy number alteration of a DNA locus with a specific genetic variant (A instead of C). Notably, the relative number of A variants determined the degree of DNAme upon exposure to protein restriction, suggesting an important mechanism for genotype–environment interaction. Considering the long-term consequences of environmental factors on a much larger time scale, Carlos Guerrero-Bosagna (Linköping University) exploited different breeds of domesticated chicken and their only living ancestor, the red jungle fowl, to analyze DNAme. Such analyzes revealed the possibility to accurately reconstruct chicken phylogeny. Preliminary results suggest that, likely through mechanisms of deamination, DNAme may impact the genome by leading to single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) or copy number variation (CNV). Interestingly, the probability of DNAme correlated with phylogenetic distance, and although the exact causal link is not yet established, these results suggest that environmentally-induced epimutations may drive genomic evolution, a concept he and Michael Skinner already proposed in Darwin finches. Dating back to the pioneering work of Michael Skinner indeed, endocrine disruptors and chemicals/pollutants have been another key focus of the field of epigenetic inheritance. At the symposium, Skinner gave a broad overview of almost two decades of research from his lab, detailing, cataloging and comparing the transgenerational impact of various compounds on physiological and cellular functions. His latest work comprehensively assessed changes in different epigenetic factors after exposure to the insecticide DDT. He showed that not only DNAme in differentially methylated regions (DMRs), but also short and long non-coding RNAs, and histone retention are altered in sperm after DDT exposure, and are passed to the following generation in a complex pattern, with little direct overlap between individual changes across generations. As one of the main contributors to the field who had long emphasized the important role of DNAme, he summarized the current state of research as follows: “All epigenetic processes are involved in epigenetic inheritance. We need to stop arguing which ones are or aren’t involved, they all seem to have different functions.” His systematic cross-generational analyzes brought new understanding that beyond epigenetic changes that are directly induced in germ cells of exposed individuals, other changes can emerge in the second or third generation, that do not necessarily match with those in the first generation. This points to a form of epigenetic dynamics across generations. Searching for direct overlap between changes in F1 and F3 might therefore not be that useful and informative. Regarding the mechanisms underlying epigenetic inheritance, a clear trend in the field is the focus on sperm RNAs as vectors of information transmission from father to offspring. Several speakers presented new data highlighting the involvement of RNA in epigenetic inheritance. Minoo Rassoulzadegan (University of Nice), who has pioneered the field of RNA-mediated epigenetic inheritance, introduced a new concept involving heritable RNAs. She showed how paternal telomere size, usually associated with lifespan, can be inherited. New data from her group suggest that telomeric repeat-containing RNAs (TERRAs), that bind to telomeres and regulate their length, are transmitted from sperm to oocyte upon fertilization. Indeed, telomere size is paternally inherited and associated with paternal lifespan, making these RNAs strong candidates for this transmission. Using a model of postnatal traumatic stress, Katharina Gapp (Sanger Institute, Cambridge) from the lab of Eric Miska then presented work on the causal involvement of sperm RNAs in epigenetic inheritance. She discussed new results highlighting that short and long non-coding RNAs must be considered together to understand their role in information transfer from sperm to oocyte/offspring. She showed that injection of long RNAs from the sperm of males exposed to traumatic stress in postnatal life into wild-type zygotes can recapitulate some of the phenotypes observed in directly exposed males, but short RNAs cannot or produce different effects, suggesting that long RNAs are also involved in transmission. A following talk on the same mouse model addressed the question of the potential vectors that alter the epigenome in germ cells. Before any substance can reach the germline and modify its epigenome, it needs to get to the testis and/or epididymis. This transport may occur through the bloodstream. Gretchen van Steenwyk from the lab of Isabelle Mansuy (University/ETH Zürich) showed that blood-borne factors are causally linked to the inheritance of phenotypes induced by postnatal trauma. Blood therefore appears as an important biological fluid, and highly relevant for translational approaches since it is easily accessible in humans. Further to humans and mice, several other animal models also provided mechanistic insight into epigenetic inheritance. Abhay Sharma (Delhi University) reported the transgenerational impact of high sugar diet on body weight and chromatin remodeling in Drosophila. Notably, an opposite phenotype is observed in F1 and F2, and the number and identity of affected genes are also different between females and males. A switching experimental design highlighted that it is not so much the diet itself, but rather the mismatch between parental and offspring diet that causes metabolic alterations.
