title: New light shed on the treatment of heart failure and on novel therapeutic targets
abstract: For the podcast associated with this article, please visit https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/pages/Podcasts. This Focus Issue on heart failure and valvular heart disease contains the Fast Track Clinical Research article ‘Ferric carboxymaltose and exercise capacity in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and iron deficiency: the FAIR-HFpEF trial’ by Stephan von Haehling from the Georg- August University in Goettingen, Germany, and colleagues.1 The authors note that iron deficiency plays an important role in several cardiovascular diseases.2–5 Yet the evidence is lacking that correcting iron deficiency (ID) has clinically important benefits for patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). FAIR-HFpEF was a multicentre, randomized, double-blind trial designed to compare intravenous ferric carboxymaltose (FCM) with placebo (saline) in 200 patients with symptomatic HFpEF and ID (serum ferritin <100 ng/mL or ferritin 100–299 ng/mL with transferrin saturation <20%). The primary endpoint was change in 6-min walking test distance (6MWTD) from baseline to week 24. Secondary endpoints included changes in New York Heart Association class, patient global assessment, and health-related quality of life (QoL). The trial was stopped because of slow recruitment after 39 patients had been included (median age 80 years, 62% women). The change in 6MWTD from baseline to week 24 was greater for those assigned to FCM compared with placebo (least square mean difference 49 m; P = .029). Changes in secondary endpoints were not significantly different between groups. The total number of adverse events (76 vs. 114) and serious adverse events (5 vs. 19; rate ratio 0.27; P = .043) was lower with FCM than placebo. The authors conclude that in patients with HFpEF and markers of ID, intravenous FCM improves 6MWTD and is associated with fewer serious adverse events. However, the trial lacks sufficient power to identify or refute effects on symptoms or QoL. The contribution is accompanied by an Editorial by Veraprapas Kittipibul and Robert Mentz from the Duke Clinical Research Institute, Durham, NC (USA).6 The authors note that the present modest-sized study does not allow for definitive conclusions and, while the results are promising, they should be interpreted with caution. Future randomized controlled trials should not only confirm this positive signal of i.v. iron therapy on exercise capacity but also reassess its benefits on health-related QoL and clinical endpoints, including mortality and hospitalization. A randomized controlled trial evaluating the impact of ferric derisomaltose on cardiopulmonary exercise performance (i.e. peak VO2), rather than 6MWTD, and the KCCQ score in HFpEF is underway (IRONMET-HFpEF). This is an exciting time for the field of HFpEF, with a series of recent discoveries of effective treatments (e.g. SGLT2 inhibitors and potentially GLP1-RAs) following decades of neutral or borderline results. We are hopeful that this favourable journey will continue and that i.v. iron therapy will eventually be added to the list of successes in HFpEF therapy. Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) has become the first choice to treat older patients with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis (AS).7–14 In a Fast Track Clinical Research article entitled ‘Transcatheter aortic valve implantation in low-risk tricuspid or bicuspid aortic stenosis: the NOTION-2 trial’, Troels Højsgaard Jørgensen from the Rigshospitalet in Denmark, and colleagues aimed to compare TAVI with surgery in low-risk patients ≤75 years of age, including both tricuspid and bicuspid AS.15 The Nordic Aortic Valve Intervention (NOTION)-2 trial enrolled and 1:1 randomized low-risk patients aged ≤75 years with severe symptomatic AS to TAVI or surgery. The primary endpoint was a composite of all-cause mortality, stroke, or rehospitalization (related to the procedure, valve, or HF) at 12 months. A total of 370 patients were enrolled with a mean age of 71 years and a median Society of Thoracic Surgeons risk score of 1.1%. A total of 100 patients had bicuspid AS. The 1-year incidence of the primary endpoint was 10.2% in the TAVI group and 7.1% in the surgery group (absolute risk difference 3.1%; hazard ratio [HR] 1.4; 95% CI, 0.7–2.9; P = .3). Patients with TAVI, when compared to surgery, had lower risk of major bleeding and new-onset atrial fibrillation and higher risk of non-disabling stroke, permanent pacemaker implantation, and moderate or greater paravalvular regurgitation. The risk of the primary composite endpoint was 8.7% and 8.3% in patients with tricuspid AS (HR 1.0) and 14.3% and 3.9% in patients with bicuspid AS (HR 3.8) treated with TAVI or surgery, respectively (P for interaction = .1). The authors conclude that among low-risk patients aged ≤75 years with severe symptomatic AS, the rate of the composite of death, stroke, or rehospitalization at 1 year is similar between TAVI and surgery. Transcatheter aortic valve implantation outcomes in young bicuspid AS patients warrant caution and should be further investigated. The contribution is accompanied by an Editorial by Niklas Schofer and Stefan Blankenberg from the University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf in Hamburg, Germany.16 The authors highlight that given the current evidence the choice of treatment modality for younger patients with AS should be based on individual risk–benefit assessment taking into consideration patients’ life expectancy, anatomy, and medical treatment. The present trial cautiously looks to the future to pave the way towards TAVI as the first treatment choice even in younger patients below 75 years of age. Without any doubt, persuasive 10-year results are needed to establish the foundation for the ultimate step in this direction. The trial further raises concerns for TAVI treatment in bicuspid AS patients and informs the community about potential pitfalls in future trial designs targeting the treatment of bicuspid AS patients. Finally, an ageing society, which will increasingly face non-communicable diseases such as AS, needs to invest in independent medical strategy trials to determine the best medical approach. In a Fast Track Clinical Research article entitled ‘Sex-related differences in severe native valvular heart disease: the ESC-EORP Valvular Heart Disease II survey’, Julia Mascherbauer from the University Hospital St Pölten in Austria, and colleagues assess sex differences in disease characteristics and treatment of patients with severe native valvular heart disease (VHD) included in the VHD II EURObservational Research Programme.17 A total of 5219 patients were enrolled in 208 European and North African centres and followed for 6 months (41% AS, 5.3% aortic regurgitation [AR], 4.5% mitral stenosis [MS], 21% mitral regurgitation [MR], 2.7% isolated right-sided VHD, 25% multiple left-sided VHD). Indications for intervention were considered concordant if corresponding to class I recommendations specified in the 2012 ESC or 2014 AHA/ACC VHD guidelines. Overall, women were older, more symptomatic, and presented with a higher EuroSCORE II. Bicuspid aortic valve and AR were more prevalent among men while mitral disease, concomitant tricuspid regurgitation (TR), and AS above age 65 were more prevalent among women. On multivariable regression analysis, concordance with recommended treatment was significantly poorer in women with MS and primary MR (both P < .001). Age, patient refusal, and decline of symptoms after conservative treatment were reported significantly more often as reasons to withhold the intervention in females. Concomitant tricuspid intervention was performed at a similar rate in both sexes although prevalence of significant TR was considerably higher in women. In-hospital and 6-month survival did not differ between sexes (Figure 1). (A) Valvular heart disease (VHD) subtypes stratified by sex; (B) forest plots displaying women’s odds ratios for ‘Intervention scheduled or performed’ and (C) ‘Transcatheter intervention’ in patients with concordant VHD, adjusted for the EuroSCORE II; (D) reasons to withhold interventions despite guideline recommendation; (E) Kaplan–Meier curves for overall survival at 6 months, stratified by sex. CAD, coronary artery disease; MR, mitral regurgitation.17 Mascherbauer et al. conclude that VHD subtype varies between sexes. They also note that concordance with recommended intervention for MS and primary MR is significantly lower for women, and that survival of men and women is similar at 6 months. The contribution is accompanied by an Editorial by Patrizio Lancellotti from the University of Liège Hospital in Belgium, Yun Yun Go from the National Heart Centre Singapore, and Mani A Vannan from the Piedmont Heart Institute in Atlanta, GA (USA).18 The authors note that three decades after Dr Bernadine Healy first described the Yentl syndrome the cardiology community has made progress in diagnosing and managing ischaemic heart disease in women. However, gender data gaps still exist in many areas of cardiology, including VHD, HF, arrhythmias, and cardiometabolic disease; thus, closing the gender gaps in cardiovascular research remains work in progress. Ultimately, we strive for equitable healthcare, where sex or gender equality is an important but not the sole determinant. The holy grail should be the representation of women (and men) of different races, ethnicities, and socioeconomic backgrounds in cardiovascular research to help us better understand health behaviours and needs at the intersections of these identity dimensions. Many patients are prescribed loop diuretics without a diagnostic record of HF. In a Clinical Research article entitled ‘Loop diuretic therapy with or without heart failure: impact on prognosis’, Jocelyn Friday from the University of Glasgow in the United Kingdom, and colleagues point out that little is known about their characteristics and prognosis.19 Glasgow regional health records (2009–16) were obtained for adults with cardiovascular disease or taking loop diuretics. Outcomes were investigated using Cox models with HRs adjusted for age, sex, socioeconomic deprivation, and comorbid disease (adjHR). Of about 200 000 patients (median age 65 years; 55% women), 81% neither took loop diuretics nor had a diagnostic record of HF (reference group), 12% were taking loop diuretics but had no HF recorded, 4% had HF recorded and took loop diuretics, and 3% had HF recorded but were not receiving loop diuretics. Compared with the reference group, 5-year mortality was only slightly higher for HF in the absence of loop diuretics (22%; adjHR 1.2), substantially higher for those taking loop diuretics with no record of HF (40%; adjHR 1.8), and highest for HF treated with loop diuretics (52%; adjHR 2.2) (Figure 2). Structured Graphical Abstract.19 The authors conclude that for patients with cardiovascular disease, many are prescribed loop diuretics without a recorded diagnosis of HF. Mortality is more strongly associated with loop diuretic use than with a record of HF. The diagnosis of HF may often be missed, or loop diuretic use is associated with other conditions with a prognosis similar to HF, or inappropriate loop diuretic use increases mortality; all might be true. This manuscript is accompanied by an Editorial by Annika Rosengren from Sahlgrenska University Hospital in Gothenburg, Sweden.20 Rosengren concludes that with higher awareness of HF among clinicians, wider use of natriuretic peptides for diagnostic purposes, and with modern treatment, patients who do not need diuretics are likely to show a slightly different phenotype than in classical HF where congestion is a presenting feature. Importantly, their relatively favourable prognosis should lead to an increased awareness among clinicians about HF as a potential cause of vague and non-specific symptoms of fatigue, deconditioning, and palpitations, prompting a careful evaluation and laboratory tests, in particular in the presence of risk factors for HF such as coronary heart disease, hypertension, diabetes, or obesity. Among patients on loop diuretic treatment lacking a clear indication, their continuing use should be carefully evaluated, which in many cases could mean added diagnostic work-up. Also, because symptoms and signs may be both non-specific and at the same time not sensitive enough, it should be possible to identify as well as define HF at an earlier stage, through a more liberal use of measurements of natriuretic peptides, interpreted in the context of the clinical setting, and followed by cardiac imaging, if needed HF is a leading cause of mortality worldwide and is characterized by significant co-morbidities and dismal prognosis.21–24 Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) aggravate inflammation in various cardiovascular diseases. Their function and mechanism of action in HF pathogenesis remain underexplored. In a Translational Research article entitled ‘Von Willebrand factor exacerbates heart failure through formation of neutrophil extracellular traps’, Ge Mang from The Second Affiliated Hospital of Harbin Medical University in China, and colleagues investigated the involvement of a novel VWF-SLC44A2-NET axis in HF progression.25 NET levels were examined in patients with HF and mouse models of transverse aortic constriction (TAC) HF. PAD4 knockout mice and NET inhibitors (GSK-484, DNase I, NEi) were used to evaluate the role of NETs in HF. RNA sequencing was used to investigate the downstream mechanisms. Recombinant human ADAMTS13 (rhADAMTS13), ADAMTS13, and SLC44A2 knockouts were used to identify novel upstream factors of NETs. Elevated NET levels were observed in patients with HF and TAC mouse models of HF. PAD4 knockout and NET inhibitors improved the cardiac function. Mechanistically, NETs induced mitochondrial dysfunction in cardiomyocytes, inhibiting mitochondrial biogenesis via the NE-TLR4-mediated suppression of PGC-1α. Furthermore, VWF/ADAMTS13 regulated NET formation via SLC44A2. Additionally, sacubitril/valsartan amplified the cardioprotective effects of the VWF-SLC44A2-NET axis blockade. The authors conclude that this study establishes the role of a novel VWF-SLC44A2-NET axis in regulating mitochondrial homeostasis and function, leading to cardiac apoptosis and contributing to HF pathogenesis. Targeting this axis may offer a potential therapeutic approach for HF treatment. The contribution is accompanied by an Editorial by Stefano Ministrini and Amedeo Tirandi from the University of Zurich in Schlieren, Switzerland.26 The authors note that additional research is warranted to confirm these experimental observations, especially regarding the role of Slc44A2 as neutrophils receptor of vWF, the possible pleiotropic effects of sacubitril/valsartan, and the pharmacological relevance of the proposed interaction between sacubitril/valsartan and Slc44A2. Indeed, in these aspects, the authors provided only associative evidence, mainly derived by computational studies. Should these observations be confirmed, they would pave the way to novel treatment for HF based on the modulation of the vWF/ADAMTS13 axis, for instance by administration of recombinant ADAMTS13, as already proposed for myocardial infarction, acute ischaemic stroke, and chronic kidney disease. Valve interstitial cells (VICs) undergo a transition to intermediate state cells before ultimately transforming into the osteogenic cell population, which is a pivotal cellular process in calcific aortic valve disease (CAVD). In a Translational Research article entitled ‘Lumican promotes calcific aortic valve disease through H3 histone lactylation’, Yuming Huang from The First Affiliated Hospital of Nanjing Medical University in China, and colleagues successfully delineated the stages of VIC osteogenic transformation and elucidated a novel key regulatory role of lumican (LUM) in this process.27 Single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) from nine human aortic valves was used to characterize the pathological switch process and identify key regulatory factors. The in vitro, ex vivo, in vivo, and double knockout mice were constructed to further unravel the calcification-promoting effect of LUM. Moreover, the multi-omic approaches were employed to analyse the molecular mechanism of LUM in CAVD. ScRNA-seq successfully delineated the process of VIC pathological transformation and highlighted the significance of LUM as a novel molecule in this process. The pro-calcification role of LUM was confirmed on the in vitro, ex vivo, in vivo level, and ApoE−/−//LUM−/− double knockout mice. The LUM induced osteogenesis in VICs via activation of inflammatory pathways and augmentation of cellular glycolysis, resulting in the accumulation of lactate. Subsequent investigation unveiled a novel LUM driving histone modification, lactylation, which plays a role in facilitating valve calcification. More importantly, this study identified two specific sites of histone lactylation, namely, H3K14la and H3K9la, which were found to facilitate the process of calcification. The confirmation of these modification sites’ association with the expression of calcific genes Runx2 and BMP2 was achieved through ChIP-PCR analysis. The authors conclude that the study presents novel findings, being the first to establish the involvement of LUM in mediating H3 histone lactylation, thus facilitating the development of aortic valve calcification. Consequently, LUM would be a promising therapeutic target for intervention in the treatment of CAVD. title: The growing role of genomics and genetics in the management of cardiovascular diseases
abstract: For the podcast associated with this article, please visit https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/pages/Podcasts. This Focus Issue on genetics starts with a Viewpoint article entitled ‘Education in cardiovascular genomics and genetics: time for action’ by Giuseppe Limongelli from The University of Campania Luigi Vanvitelli in Naples, Italy, and colleagues which address the important topic of education in cardiogenetics and cardiogenomics, an emerging field in cardiology, with progressive and targeted education needs for students, scientists, clinicians, and different healthcare professional figures.1 In December 2024, the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) Council for Cardiogenomics met to discuss the current state of the art in cardiovascular genetic medicine enriched by several recent excellent publications.2–11 The group sought to address a key question in contemporary cardiology: namely, is it time to include education in cardiovascular genetics and genomics in the core training for cardiologists? The answer was an unequivocal yes, given its potential to improve the diagnosis and treatment of cardiovascular disease. However, the challenge lay in determining the most effective means of achieving this goal. Certain genetic forms of dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) entail a higher arrhythmic risk. It is unknown whether DCM patients with high-risk arrhythmic genotypes also develop more advanced heart failure (AHF) complications. In a Fast Track Congress article entitled ‘Arrhythmic genotypes in dilated cardiomyopathy and risk of advanced heart failure’, Nerea Mora-Ayestarán from Puerta de Hierro Majadahonda University Hospital in Madrid, Spain, and colleagues report their study of AHF events in a large multicentre cohort of genotyped patients with DCM receiving contemporary treatment, with a special focus on individuals with variants in high-risk arrhythmic genes.12 Clinical data from 1203 genotyped DCM patients were collected from 19 Spanish centres. Patients were classified into high-risk arrhythmic genotypes (LMNA, FLNC, desmosomal genes, PLN, TMEM43, and RBM20), TTN, other genes, and genotype negative (Gen−). The primary endpoint was a composite of AHF events (ventricular assist device implantation, heart transplant, and AHF-related mortality). The secondary endpoint was a combination of malignant ventricular arrhythmias (MVAs). A DCM-causing variant was identified in a high-risk arrhythmic gene in 16% of patients, 16% had variants in TTN, 11% in other genes, and 57% were Gen−. After a median follow-up of 5.7 years, AHF events occurred in 24.3% of patients in the high-risk arrhythmic group, and in 18.7, 13, and 10.1% of patients with other genotypes, TTN, and Gen−, respectively (hazard ratio 1.85 for high-risk arrhythmic genes compared with other groups). MVA occurred in 29.7% of patients (hazard ratio 2.52 for high-risk genotypes vs other groups). High-risk arrhythmic genotype was the main independent predictor of AHF in multivariate analysis. High-risk arhythmic genotype and late gadolinium enhancement were independent predictors of MVA (Figure 1). 12 The authors conclude that patients with high-risk arrhythmic genotypes also experience more AHF events, supporting a differential therapeutic approach in this group of patients beyond sudden death prevention. The manuscript is accompanied by an Editorial by Jean-Benoît le Polain de Waroux and Maarten De Smet from the St-Jan’s Hospital in Bruges, Belgium.13 The authors underscore that the study of Mora-Ayestarán and co-authors was a Spanish national effort with a, presumably, largely Caucasian population. The question remains of whether these results may be generalized to populations with other genetic backgrounds. This is especially relevant in patients with DCM. As mentioned previously, rare monogenic variants are easy to determine, but for most patients the risk of developing life-threatening arrhythmias or HF is also determined by other genetic and environmental factors. Nevertheless, this research opens the door for the development and implementation of risk scores that, in addition to arrhythmic risk, assess the probability of progression to AHF and provide guidance on when to start specific treatment. In this regard, future studies exploring the impact of intermediate effect and common variants on the DCM phenotype and the development of polygenic risk scores to predict arrhythmic and HF outcomes and treatment efficacy are warranted. Acquired somatic mutations are a hallmark of ageing and are increasingly recognized as contributors to disease susceptibility. Mosaic loss of the Y chromosome (mLOY) in leucocytes represents the most common form of acquired clonal mosaicism in men, and is associated with incident cardiovascular diseases including HF, atrial fibrillation, fatal myocardial infarction in men with coronary artery disease (CAD), or HF-associated death in chronic kidney disease.14,15 While the genetic predisposition to mLOY has been recently investigated, the effects of mLOY on the systemic proteome signature have not been comprehensively characterized. In a Fast Track Congress article entitled ‘Loss of Y chromosome: proteomic signatures in human cardiovascular disease’, Michael Weyrich from Goethe University Frankfurt in Germany, and colleagues examine the association between mLOY and the plasma proteome signature in men enrolled in the UK Biobank.16 mLOY cells revealed concordant up-regulation of the coding genes for 47 of the 173 (=27%) proteins significantly associated with incident HF. The up-regulated genes in peripheral blood mononuclear cells demonstrated signature pathway enrichment related to inflammation and the innate and adaptive immune system concordant with the proteomic plasma signature. Specifically, the up-regulated genes in mLOY cells included those genes coding for the proteins PLAUR, CD300E, LILRA5, TNFRSF10B, and LAMP3, which all were significantly associated with the incidence for and mortality from all four cardiovascular disease conditions, HF, atrial fibrillation, hypertensive heart disease, and aortic aneurysm. The authors conclude that mLOY amplifies pathogenic pathways well established to contribute not only to cardiovascular disease incidence but also to cardiovascular mortality, and may thus offer novel therapeutic targets in men with mLOY. Truncating variants in the titin gene (TTNtv) are the most common genetic cause of DCM but also occur as incidental findings in the general population. In a Clinical Research article entitled ‘Titin-related familial dilated cardiomyopathy: factors associated with disease onset’, Renee Johnson from the Victor Chang Cardiac Research Institute in Darlinghurst, Australia, and colleagues investigate factors associated with the clinical manifestation of TTNtv.17 An international multicentre retrospective observational study was performed in families with TTNtv-related DCM. Shared frailty models were used to estimate associations of variant characteristics with lifetime risk of DCM, and logistic regression to estimate odds ratios (ORs) for individual-level clinical risk factor profiles (cardiac conditions, cardiovascular comorbidities, and lifestyle) and DCM. A total of ∼3000 subjects in 1043 families with TTNtv-related DCM were studied. TTNtv-positive subjects were 21-fold more likely to develop DCM (OR 21.21). Disease onset was earlier in males but was similar for TTNtv of different types and locations. The presence of clinical risk factors was associated with earlier DCM onset (OR 3.41), with a prior history of atrial fibrillation having two-fold increased odds of DCM (OR 2.05). The prevalence of clinical risk factors increased with age; however, the strength of the DCM association was greatest for young-onset ( 500 000 people in the UK Biobank and Vanderbilt’s BioVU, genetically predicted IL-17RA levels reduced the risk of cardiovascular disease exclusively in those with JAK2-CHIP. Further, only JAK2-CHIP carriers with low genetically predicted IL-17RA levels were at heightened risk of cardiovascular disease incidence. Mechanistic studies using atheroprone JAK2-V617F mice suggested that inflammasome activation and plasma membrane rupture mediated by Ninjurin-1 may create a protective feedback mechanism where Th17 cells signal to TREM2 macrophages via IL-17RA, thereby dampening inflammatory responses. The authors conclude that JAK2-CHIP patients treated with IL-17 blockade may experience elevated CVD risk. The issue is also complemented by two Discussion Forum contributions. In the commentary entitled ‘The limitations of biomarkers in addressing bias in alcohol and cardiovascular disease research’, Elizabeth Farkouh, Shantanu Srivatsa, and Michael Farkouh from Mayo Clinic Alix School of Medicine in Rochester, MN, USA, UNC Chapel Hill School of Medicine in NC, USA, and Cedars Sinai Health System in Los Angeles, CA, USA comment on the recently published paper entitled ‘Urinary tartaric acid as a biomarker of wine consumption and cardiovascular risk: the PREDIMED trial’, by Inés Domínguez-López et al., from the University of Barcelona, in Spain.28,29 The editors hope that this issue of the European Heart Journal will be of interest to its readers. title: Leducq-funded network: calcification-omics, molecular elucidation, and therapeutics (COMET)
abstract: Vascular calcification is a highly prevalent and clinically significant pathology affecting both women and men across all ages. It manifests in the intima or media of small and large arteries with genetic, age-associated, and metabolic diseases. Vascular calcification is among the strongest independent predictors of cardiovascular events, including myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, and peripheral arterial disease,1,2 and is often fatal in conditions such as calciphylaxis and rare genetic syndromes such as generalized arterial calcification of infancy.3,4 The global burden of vascular calcification is rising due to ageing populations and the increasing prevalence of diabetes and chronic kidney disease (CKD). However, despite its clinical relevance, no targeted therapies currently exist. Vascular calcification is regulated by both biological and physicochemical processes that drive calcium and phosphate mineral deposition within the extracellular matrix (ECM) of the vessel wall. Calcification can occur throughout the arterial tree, with distinct tissue-specific patterns and anatomical locations of the mineral that influence clinical outcomes. For instance, medial calcification causes arterial stiffening, contributing to pressure overload and organ damage, particularly to the heart and brain.5 In atherosclerotic intimal calcification, small, spotty calcium deposits correlate most strongly with plaque instability and poor prognosis, although both small and large deposits may contribute to plaque progression, erosion, and rupture.6,7 Once thought to be unmodifiable, vascular calcification is now recognized as a potentially reversible process. Mounting evidence suggests that halting or even reversing calcification could meaningfully improve cardiovascular health. Hence, the passion that drives the COMET investigators results from a simple central hypothesis: targeting vascular calcification may significantly reduce cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. Focused research over the last 20 years using in vitro models and animal and human studies has identified vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) as central orchestrators of calcification. Endothelial cells (ECs), inflammatory cells, and adventitial fibroblasts also play important roles. Key mechanisms include the loss of calcification inhibitors (produced by VSMCs or circulating in the serum), osteochondrogenic differentiation of vascular cells, and the nucleation of mineral deposits on extracellular vesicles or the ECM. However, critical knowledge gaps remain, particularly regarding the identity of cell populations and key molecular regulators that drive or prevent calcification across different disease contexts. The heterogeneity of VSMCs and the tissue-specific nature of calcification represent major obstacles. Most existing studies focus narrowly on known transcription factors and signalling pathways, often reinforcing prevailing dogma and overlooking novel regulators. Emerging single-cell and spatial ‘omics’ technologies now offer unbiased, high-resolution insights into VSMC phenotypic plasticity both temporally and spatially. Integrating these multimodal datasets with large-scale human genetics will be essential to uncovering actionable targets and novel biological mechanisms. Equally underexplored is the composition of the mineral and how it is formed and modulated by chemical processes occurring in the ECM microenvironment. Ageing, a major risk factor for vascular calcification, alters ECM structure and function via enzymatic and non-enzymatic modifications, disrupting ECM-cell signalling, cell differentiation, and vascular remodelling.8 However, the causal relationships between specific ECM modifications and underlying cellular changes and calcification remain poorly defined. Recent multi-ancestry genome-wide meta-analyses have uncovered novel loci associated with coronary artery calcification.9,10 Yet, there remains a gap in identifying causal biomarkers to improve patient risk stratification across ancestry and sex. Furthermore, there is an urgent need for novel imaging agents that selectively bind distinct ECM components or mineral phases, enabling earlier and more precise detection. Progress in understanding the genesis and progression of vascular calcification demands an interdisciplinary approach—one that links biological and chemical insights and bridges basic science with clinical translation. The COMET network embodies this vision, bringing together an expert team of cardiologists, nephrologists, biotechnologists, biologists, bioinformaticians, and chemists to develop novel targeted therapies for patients suffering from calcification-related diseases. Led by Drs Rajeev Malhotra (North American co-ordinator; Mass General Brigham, Boston, MA, USA), Catherine M. Shanahan (European co-ordinator; King’s College London, London, UK), Clint L. Miller (University of Virginia, Charlottesville, VA, USA), Yabing Chen (Oregon Health & Sciences University, Portland, OR, USA), Melinda J. Duer (University of Cambridge, Cambridge, UK), Maryam Kavousi (University Medical Center Rotterdam, Rotterdam, The Netherlands), and Rafael Kramann (RWTH Aachen University, Aachen, Germany), COMET is uniquely positioned to tackle this complex pathology. The network is focused on several key priorities, critical to the development of new therapeutics: (i) defining culprit VSMC and EC sub-populations in different disease contexts, (ii) discovering new molecular targets and regulatory pathways, and (iii) understanding how the ageing ECM modulates cell phenotype and nidus formation in different vascular niches. COMET leverages genetic and multi-omic datasets, advanced physicochemical imaging, and in vitro and in vivo models to uncover how molecular, cellular, and matrix-level factors interact to drive the mineralization process (Figure 1). These data will inform both candidate-based and AI-enabled therapeutic strategies, applicable to rare genetic disorders and common cardiovascular diseases in the general population. Overview of workflow in the COMET network to identify causal regulators and modifiers of vascular calcification. The figure was created using BioRender Supported by the Leducq Foundation, COMET is committed to pushing the envelope forward in our understanding of vascular calcification and associated highly morbid and age-accelerated human diseases, such as MI, stroke, CKD, diabetes, and calciphylaxis. We are also strongly committed to training the next generation of scientists. This collaborative network provides a powerful training platform for emerging investigators to develop interdisciplinary expertise and skills required to make meaningful and lasting contributions in the fight against vascular calcification. All authors declare no disclosure of interest for this contribution. The research described in this paper is made possible by a Fondation Leducq Network of Excellence grant (#24CVD02) given to all co-authors, the COMET consortium.

title: The future of heart replacement therapy: four frontiers of transformation
abstract: Heart transplantation has always lived in paradox: it is both the most advanced form of organ replacement and one of the most biologically constrained. For over half a century, we have relied on a miracle of logistics—hearts must be found, matched, and implanted within hours. Immunological barriers must be crossed, complications managed, survival extended. And yet, despite all obstacles, the human heart has been replaced successfully in thousands of patients, giving new life where none seemed possible. But now, the future asks for more than success—it asks for evolution. Around us, four converging revolutions are reshaping what heart replacement therapy could become. Technologies that defy ischaemic time. Machines that mimic or even surpass biology. Bioengineered organs born in labs, not in donors. And intelligent systems that personalize decisions beyond human capacity. This future is not linear. It does not replace one model with another. It is a synthesis: a reimagining of time, material, biology, and cognition. What follows is not a prediction—it is a possibility. And it begins with the most foundational change of all (Figure 1): Once a relentless ticking clock, time has long defined the limitations of heart transplantation. But that era is ending. Advances in preservation now allow us not only to transport hearts across continents but to treat and improve them while they wait. With cold-controlled static systems (e.g. SherpaPak™), hypothermic oxygenated perfusion (HOPE), and normothermic ex vivo perfusion (e.g. OCS™), ischaemia is no longer fate—it’s a manageable risk.1 What’s more, the preservation window has evolved into a therapeutic platform. During ex situ perfusion, donor hearts can be modulated biologically: ischaemia-reperfusion damage can be mitigated, inflammatory cascades attenuated, and even genetic properties altered. Early studies have demonstrated the feasibility of viral inactivation (e.g. HCV), immunomodulatory gene therapy (IL-10), and antigen conversion (ABO) in perfused organs.1,2 Targeted approaches may soon reduce immunogenicity or enhance resilience, allowing broader and safer use of the so-called marginal hearts.1 These advances are not incremental—they are transformative. They redefine what a ‘transplantable’ heart is. And they allow for what once seemed impossible: global organ exchange with safe, extended preservation. The heart no longer races against time. In the near future, it may be the one that sets the pace. The four pillars of the future heart. Heart replacement therapy is undergoing a profound transformation across four converging domains: (1) Time—dynamic preservation platforms extend ischaemic windows and enable therapeutic modulation of donor hearts; (2) Mechanics—next-generation artificial and hybrid hearts integrate biocompatibility, adaptive circulation, and smart sensor technologies; (3) Biology—bioengineered organs via xenotransplantation, decellularization, and 3D printing may offer scalable alternatives to donor shortages; and (4) Intelligence—AI-driven risk prediction, personalization, and nanoparticle-based therapies redefine decision-making and tolerability. These pillars are not replacements of one another, but components of a new integrative paradigm for cardiac replacement—one that reimagines biology, material, time, and cognition While biological hearts remain the gold standard, mechanical alternatives are evolving beyond their role as mere stopgaps. The total artificial heart (TAH) is no longer a futuristic curiosity—it is becoming a viable platform for long-term support and destination therapy. Devices are shrinking, becoming smarter, and integrating seamlessly into patients’ daily lives. Cable-free energy transfer, sensor-guided self-regulation, and remote monitoring are transforming these systems from passive pumps into responsive, intelligent companions.3 The next generation of mechanical hearts won’t just mimic cardiac output—they will adapt in real time. Embedded algorithms can respond to physiologic stress, adjust flow, and even predict complications before they manifest clinically. As bio-compatible surfaces improve, hybrid solutions combining mechanical strength with biologically active interfaces may reduce thrombosis and infection risk.4 Beyond bridging to transplant, mechanical hearts are increasingly used in patients who may never receive a donor organ. In an ageing population with growing contraindications to immunosuppression, this may define a new frontier. Tomorrow’s mechanical heart is a design choice—no longer a compromise. And with each iteration, we move closer to a device that doesn’t just support circulation but participates in the patient’s life with autonomy, safety, and dignity. If mechanics offer precision, biology offers promise. The idea of growing or customizing human-compatible hearts is no longer confined to speculative science. Efforts in xenotransplantation, decellularization, recellularization, and 3D bioprinting are converging towards one goal: replacing the need to wait for a suitable donor by creating one.5 Genetically engineered pig hearts have already been transplanted into humans in pioneering trials. While challenges remain—early graft failure, infection risk, and ethical complexity—these cases demonstrate technical feasibility. Further refining immunogenic profiles through CRISPR-based edits and pathogen elimination may push xenotransplantation from heroic exception to scalable solution.5,6 Parallel efforts are exploring biofabrication. Decellularized human or animal scaffolds seeded with patient-derived cells, or fully printed constructs using hydrogel matrices and vascular bioinks, are inching closer to functional prototypes. These constructs lack native contractility—but with progress in materials and biophysics, it’s no longer if, but when.5,7 Biological design is the most ambitious pillar in the future of heart replacement—less mature than others, but arguably the most transformative. In time, we may shift from ‘matching’ organs to ‘designing’ them—tailored for the recipient’s anatomy, immunology, and destiny. Heart replacement has long relied on urgency, size, and geography. But a new paradigm is emerging—one where data, not distance, drives decisions. Artificial intelligence (AI) is poised to revolutionize every step of the transplant process: from donor selection to recipient matching, from risk prediction to therapy personalization. Machine learning algorithms already assist in assessing donor heart quality beyond traditional metrics.5,8 By integrating imaging, biomarkers, and molecular profiles, AI can better predict graft resilience, even before procurement. Matching tools now incorporate not only weight and blood type, but dynamic estimations of immunological compatibility and post-transplant prognosis.8,9 The next frontier is true individualization. Systems like the iBox or I-Score aim to forecast long-term outcomes based on multi-omic, clinical, and behavioural data.5,9 Digital twins may simulate how a heart performs in a specific patient. This moves us from ‘suitable’ to ‘optimal’.5 Emerging technologies also hint at precision drug delivery: nanoparticles targeting immunosuppressants directly to the graft, reducing systemic toxicity.10 While tolerance induction remains elusive, such approaches may reduce the burden of lifelong immunosuppression. In this data-driven future, the heart transplant becomes not just a procedure—but a calculated, continuously adapting therapy. And AI does not replace physicians—it sharpens their lens on what truly matters: outcomes tailored to the individual. The heart has always symbolized life. In the future of heart replacement, it becomes more: a platform for innovation, integration, and imagination. We no longer ask only how to replace a failing heart—but what else can be transformed along the way: time, matter, identity, and decision. Each of the four pillars—preservation, mechanics, biological creation, and intelligent systems—stands alone. But together, they form the architecture of a new era. One where boundaries dissolve and possibilities multiply. This is not science fiction. It is science becoming future. The heart—still fragile, still human—remains at the centre. But around it, we build a system that thinks and adapts. title: The management of heart failure: a brief look into the future
abstract: Heart failure (HF) is a major cause of death, hospitalization, morbidity, and cost, with a global prevalence of more than 65 million persons. In Western countries, HF is the most common diagnosis for hospitalization in persons ≥ 65 years. With the development of new therapies which extend the survival of patients with HF and with the ageing of the general population, this prevalence is likely to continue to grow. Thus, HF remains a serious worldwide problem. Fortunately, it is being addressed in preclinical and early clinical studies that are reviewed briefly in this article. Genetic studies have shown that DNA is damaged in mice with HF induced by aortic constriction and an insulin-like growth factor binding cytokine is released by senescent vascular endothelial cells. A vaccine-based molecule against this cytokine ameliorated the cardiac dysfunction, raising the possibility in the future that the development of HF might be reduced by a vaccine in patients at high risk.1 Transthyretin amyloidosis is now recognized more frequently than heretofore to be a cause of a cardiomyopathy that is often fatal. In a Phase 1 study using CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, a single infusion of an investigative drug resulted in striking reductions in serum transthyretin amyloid, suggesting that this serious myopathy may be controlled2; a Phase 3 trial is currently underway. The expression of another gene (BINi) is often reduced in patients with HF, and a trial in patients with chronic HF administered this gene using an adeno-associated viral vector is likely. The circulating messenger (m) RNAs of other genes has been combined to create genetic risk scores which are likely to be of benefit in patient management.3 Although the genetics of HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) are still obscure, the combination of five mRNAs may identify patients at high risk of developing this condition has been described. This could alter clinical management and improve clinical outcome. Metabolomic profiling: It has been observed that the proteome is a strong predictor of mortality in patients with HF, regardless of left ventricular ejection fraction.4 Increased plasma ketone concentrations are associated with enhanced cardiac output and reduced pulmonary arterial wedge pressure. The mechanism of these important actions may be related to providing additional ‘fuel’ to the failing heart and/or reduction of systemic vascular resistance. Indeed, ketogenesis appears to play an important role in the salutary effects of SGLT2 inhibitors,5–7 and orally administered ketones may prove to be beneficial in the management of patients with HF. With new assays, thousands of plasma proteins can now be measured accurately and rapidly. Using machine learning, a small fraction of these are predictors of early mortality which will personalize the care and outcome of patients with HF. Obesity is a chronic disorder that increases the likelihood of the development of HFpEF. Approximately one-third of patients hospitalized for HFpEF in the USA present with central obesity. It is likely that oral glucagon-like protein agonists (GLP-1), probably combined with other potent anti-obesity medications, will play an important role in the prevention and management of HFpEF. Cell therapy for HF has undergone multiple preclinical and early Phases 1 and 2 trials; the former have shown that the injected cells have only a brief life in the myocardium and that any benefit observed may be of pleiotropic origin.8 Among the various cell types that have been studied, autologous pluripotent stem cells and bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stromal cells appear to be the most promising. Although a single delivery of these cells may provide modest benefit, preclinical studies have demonstrated that deliveries repeated at intervals enhanced this benefit. This observation may not be practical clinically if the cell delivery must be made into the heart.8 It has also been suggested that intact cells may not be necessary to get these effects. Cell products such as specific mRNAs and microRNAs may be angiogenic and/or anti-apoptotic. If that proves to be the case, it could have a profoundly beneficial effect in the future management of HF. Devices: Cardiology became a distinct specialty at the end of the 19th and the beginning of the 20th centuries by the development of three non-invasive devices: the measurement of arterial pressure, electrocardiography, and cardiac size (by roentgenography). Subsequently, cardiac catheterization, pacemakers, prosthetic heart valves, and heart-lung machines are among the devices that have greatly enhanced the specialty. Attention is now focused on the development of new devices designed to augment the action of drugs in the prevention and the reduction of the severity of HF. They fall into two categories—implanted and wearable.9 Three implanted devices have been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for the management of chronic HF. The CardioMEMS system of implantable monitors provides continuous pulmonary artery pressure remotely. This can guide pharmacologic therapy and thereby enhance survival and HF hospitalization in patients with HF and reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF).10 Cardiac contractility modulators (CCM) consist of an implanted power source that delivers non-excitatory biphasic electrical impulses to the inter-ventricular septum during the brief refractory period following ventricular contraction,11 These stimuli enhance myocardial contractility by increasing intracellular calcium concentration and/or modifying myocardial gene expression and thereby improve HF patients’ functional capacity and maximal O2 consumption (VO2) and the quality of life in patients with HFrEF. The third approved device in chronic HF is barostimulation in which electrical stimulation of the carotid sinuses increases parasympathetic activation and reduces sympathetic activation, thereby also enhancing ventricular function.12 Intermittent occlusion of the superior vena cava by a balloon mounted on a catheter may be of benefit in patients with acutely decompensated HF.13 Stimulation of the vagus and phrenic nerves and/or of the diaphragm is currently being studied and may prove to be effective in patients with advanced HFrEF. In preclinical studies, a novel transaortic pulsatile pump placed in the descending aorta has undergone encouraging results to unload ventricular function in pigs in cardiogenic shock. While these devices may be effective, they occasionally cause infection or malfunction and are quite costly. However, it is likely that their continued improvement will reduce the threshold for their application in patients with HFrEF, whose symptoms cannot be controlled by medical therapy. It is likely that non-invasive monitoring and telehealth will play increasingly important roles in patients with HF, especially in rural areas. In addition to the information provided by electrocardiography and remote measurement of arterial oxygen saturation, of physical activity (and plasma concentration of glucose in patients with T2D) will be employed more frequently and will be helpful in the determination of the need for adjustment of therapy, of personal visit to a health care facility, or of hospitalization.14 Two additional approaches could have enormously salutary effects in reducing the frequency and severity of HF. The first, for asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic persons, consists simply of much stricter application of established guidelines for primordial and primary care.15 The second, for patients with advanced HF and a serious prognosis, is xenotransplantation of a genetically modified porcine heart, since availability of human donor hearts is inadequate. This approach requires further efforts designed for inhibiting rejection. Between these two ends of the spectrum of HF, the many advances summarized above are likely to improve the future management of patients with this important condition. title: Atherothrombosis: its mechanisms and novel targets
abstract: For the podcast associated with this article, please visit https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/pages/Podcasts. This Focus Issue on Vascular biology and medicine and mental health starts with a State of the Art Review article entitled ‘Smooth muscle cells in atherosclerosis: essential but overlooked translational perspectives’ by Pascal Azar from the University of Geneva, Switzerland, and colleagues which provides a comprehensive overview of current insights into smooth muscle cell phenotypic diversity, function, and spatial localization within stable and unstable plaques, focusing on their relevance to human pathology.1 Smooth muscle cells have been identified as the most abundant cell type present in the atherosclerotic plaque, the culprit underlying most cardiovascular diseases and their fatal outcomes. Despite their crucial role in plaque formation and progression,2–6 smooth muscle cells do not receive as much attention as inflammatory or endothelial cells. The purpose of this review is to examine the roles of smooth muscle cells in the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis and their potential as therapeutic targets. The review also addresses the contribution of clonal expansion of smooth muscle cells in plaque progression, evaluates emerging diagnostic tools which may reflect smooth muscle cell physiology, and highlights strategies to modulate smooth muscle cell behaviour for improved cardiovascular outcomes. Special attention is given to the clinical translation of these therapies, considering the challenges and opportunities in leveraging smooth muscle cells as therapeutic targets. Vascular and valvular calcification play an important role in several cardiovascular diseases.7–15 In particular, medial arterial calcification (MAC) characterizes human arterial ageing, potentially remaining clinically silent for decades. However, in susceptible individuals and patients with diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease, it becomes a critical risk factor for cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, and it is a significant risk factor for chronic limb-threatening ischaemia and limb amputation. In a State of the Art Review article entitled ‘Medial arterial calcification in ageing and disease: current evidence and knowledge gaps’, Peter Lanzer from the Goitzsche Clinic in Bitterfeld, Germany, and colleagues highlight the clinical manifestations of MAC, the contemporary understanding of MAC pathogenesis, and future perspectives for novel strategies for MAC prevention, diagnostics, and therapy.16 A key biological feature of MAC pathogenesis is the phenotype switching of vascular smooth muscle cells, ultimately responsible for the deposition of hydroxyapatite crystals and the progressive medial layer destruction associated with intimal thickening. The signalling pathways targeting the vascular smooth muscle cells in ageing and disease are partly shared. Due to the MAC-related arterial wall stiffening and intimal thickening, MAC fundamentally alters central and peripheral haemodynamics. Yet, a comprehensive understanding of MAC’s impact on haemodynamics is lacking. Ankle–brachial index, ultrasound, and X-ray radiography can detect only advanced MAC in the clinical setting. Due to its slow progression, MAC provides many early detection, prevention, and timely intervention targets. However, no effective pharmacological treatment is currently available to alter its course, and revascularizations remain the only treatment option in symptomatic patients. To prevent, reverse, or delay MAC, further research is needed to reveal the complete picture of molecular pathogenesis and the haemodynamic impact of MAC vasculopathy (Figure 1). Medial arterial calcification (MAC) is a degenerative process associated with vascular ageing, which is notably accelerated by diseases such as diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease (left panel). The molecular signalling pathways involved in ageing and disease are partly shared16 Platelets play a key role in atherothrombosis.17–21 In particular, reticulated platelets (RPs), hyper-reactive and RNA rich, are associated with increased risk of cardiovascular events and suboptimal response to antiplatelet therapy in coronary artery disease (CAD). However, the underlying mechanisms remain poorly defined. In a Fast Track Congress article entitled ‘Reticulated platelets in coronary artery disease: a multidimensional approach unveils prothrombotic signalling and novel therapeutic targets’, Kilian Kirmes from the Technical University of Munich, Germany, and colleagues aim to characterize the molecular and functional phenotype of RPs in CAD and assess their potential as therapeutic targets.22 Reticulated platelets and mature platelets (MPs) were isolated from CAD patients based on RNA content and CD41 expression. Paired RP vs MP comparisons were conducted within each donor. Transcriptomic profiling (RNA-seq) was integrated with high-dimensional proteomics (mass cytometry) and validated in independent cohorts. Functional studies, including flow cytometry-based platelet–platelet binding, in vitro thrombosis, platelet spreading, and intracellular phospho-protein profiling, assessed the impact of phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3 K) and glycoprotein VI (GPVI) pathways. Results were curated in Platlas, an open-access interactive web resource. Among 95 CAD patients, RPs exhibited elevated activation marker expression and enrichment of prothrombotic pathways compared with MPs. RNA-seq revealed up-regulation of GP6, TBXA2R, and VWF transcripts, novel GPVI splicing, and RP-specific non-coding RNAs including novel circular RNAs (circRNAs). Proteomic and functional assays confirmed heightened PI3 K and GPVI signalling, with increased phosphorylation of AKT, PI3 K, and SYK, and elevated reactive oxygen species production. RPs showed increased aggregation and spreading, and greater recruitment in thrombus formation, which were significantly reduced by PI3 K (LY294002) and GPVI (glenzocimab) inhibition. The authors conclude that this study provides the first mechanistic explanation for RP hyper-reactivity, revealing a distinct molecular profile and identifying GPVI and PI3 K inhibition as promising targets for tailored antiplatelet therapy in CAD patients with elevated RPs. The manuscript is accompanied by an Editorial by Huijun Edelyn Park and Scott Cameron from Lerner Research Institute in Cleveland, OH, USA.23 The authors underscore that as platelet biology continues to evolve, integrating platelet heterogeneity into treatment paradigms will be essential. This impressive study lays the groundwork for future investigations that move from mechanistic insight to therapeutic intervention, while highlighting the need for biomarker-driven patient selection in the quest to reduce thrombotic events without increasing bleeding risk. The integration of transcriptomic, proteomic, and functional data in low-yield platelet subpopulations such as RPs demonstrates the feasibility and the challenge of mechanistically grounded platelet phenotyping in cardiovascular disease. Risk stratification of patients with acute pulmonary embolism (PE) is critical to provide targeted interventions aimed at improving patients’ outcomes. In a Clinical Research article entitled ‘Acute pulmonary embolism: a multimarker calculator to predict short-term outcomes’, David Jiménez from the Ramón y Cajal Hospital in Madrid, Spain, and colleagues validate a multimarker prognostic calculator and compare its performance with that of the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) model.24 The multimarker calculator estimates absolute risk of key outcomes for an individual patient, based on the individual variables of the simplified Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index, natriuretic peptide levels, troponin levels, and concomitant lower limb deep vein thrombosis. Using data for haemodynamically stable patients with acute PE from the Registro Informatizado de la Enfermedad TromboEmbólica, the study compared the performance of the multimarker calculator and the ESC model using measures of discrimination and calibration. The primary outcome was 30-day all-cause mortality. A total of 60 042 stable patients with PE (mean age: 67 years, 52% female) were included. Compared with the ESC model, the multimarker calculator provided significant C-statistic improvement in the whole cohort (0.79 vs 0.56; P 10% to identify intermediate-high risk PE, the positive predictive value for mortality was 15.7% (vs 5.0% for the ESC model; P < .001) (Figure 2). Structured Graphical Abstract24 The authors conclude that in stable patients with acute PE, the use of a multimarker calculator substantially improves the risk stratification for mortality beyond that of the ESC model. The manuscript is accompanied by an Editorial by Irene Lang from the Medical University of Vienna, Austria.25 The author notes that Jimenez et al. demonstrate that the eStiMaTe calculator has a better discriminatory power to identify the sickest patients within those identified as intermediate-high risk according to the ESC risk model, but we will have to tease out in the future whether those are the patients dying from acute right ventricular failure that may be preventable with short-term mechanical treatments. Future risk scores may have to include dynamic biomarker assessments that directly relate to the temporal deterioration of the right ventricle. One option would be to introduce serial high sensitivity troponin measurements performed 1 h after the first to assess the possibility for worsening right ventricular function in the setting of acute PE, or serial serum lactate measurements. Nuclear receptors (NRs) are involved in cardiovascular physiology and pathology. Dax1 is a co-repressor of several protective NRs. However, whether Dax1 influences atherosclerosis remains unclear. In a Translational Science article entitled ‘Nuclear receptor Dax1 promotes atherosclerosis by lipid transport inhibition and autophagy suppression in macrophages’, Feifei Li from Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, China, and colleagues aim to explore the role of Dax1 in atherogenesis and find a pharmacological approach targeting Dax1 to prevent atherosclerosis.26 Dax1 levels were examined in human atherosclerotic arteries. Atherosclerosis animal models were established in mice with macrophage-specific Dax1 knockdown following administration of AAV8-PCSK9 (adeno-associated virus 8-proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9) and double knockout of macrophage Dax1 and ApoE. Transcriptomic and proteomic analyses were employed to decipher the underlying mechanisms. 2′-Deoxycytidine, an inhibitor of Dax1, was used to verify the effects of Dax1 in macrophages and in mice with atherosclerosis. Dax1 mRNA content was up-regulated in NRs in human atherosclerotic arteries compared with non-atherosclerotic arteries. The elevation of Dax1 was prominent in the macrophages of atherosclerotic arteries. Macrophage-specific Dax1 knockout mice had less atherosclerosis than controls. Mechanistically, Dax1 inhibited liver X receptor alpha (LXRα), and interacted directly with transcription factor EB (TFEB) to suppress autophagy, resulting in lipid accumulation and inflammation in macrophages. Additionally, 2′-deoxycytidine decreased Dax1 levels, enhanced autophagy, reduced lipid accumulation, and inhibited atherosclerosis in mice. The authors conclude that this study demonstrates that Dax1 levels are increased in atherosclerotic plaques. Dax1 promotes atherosclerosis by interacting with TFEB to suppress autophagy and inhibiting LXRα for lipid transport in macrophage, indicating that Dax1 is a potential target for atherosclerosis. The manuscript is accompanied by an Editorial by Martina Lorey and Katariina Öörni from the University of Helsinki in Finland.27 They note that in this study targeting Dax1 influences both LXRα and TFEB activity, and thus has the potential for a double atheroprotective effect. In fact, due to the beneficial effects of LXRα, its agonists have been tested for treatment of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. However, the clinical application of LXRα agonists faces challenges, including induction of hypertriglyceridaemia and increased liver fat. Similarly, TFEB is a regulator of various metabolic processes, which is something to bear in mind when altering its expression. More promiscuous ligands always have more potential for off-target effects, which should be carefully considered in follow-up studies due to the vastly higher expression of Dax1 in endocrine tissues. Li et al. did not observe that administration of 2'-deoxycytidine would lead to substantial changes in steroid hormone levels in mice. In the case of atherosclerosis, the target cell—the macrophage—has a low expression of Dax1. Therefore, it seems especially prudent to have a targeted approach, for example by employing nanoparticles carrying ligands for macrophage-specific receptors to transport the drug. In a Translational Science article entitled ‘Deletion of METTL14, a key methylation regulator, attenuates vascular ageing’, Xin Liu from The Second Affiliated Hospital in China, and colleagues aim to investigate the role of METTL14 in inflammation in the pathogenesis of vascular ageing.28 The natural ageing mouse model, the D-galactose-induced ageing mouse model, and endothelial cell-specific METTL14 knockout mice were generated. The roles of METTL14 in vascular ageing were investigated in human, mice, and various endothelial cells. Up-regulation of METTL14 was observed in the aortic endothelial cells of aged mice, aged humans, and senescent human umbilical vein endothelial cells, human aortic endothelial cells, and mice aortic endothelial cells. Endothelium-specific knockdown or knockout of METTL14 notably inhibited arterial stiffness, arterial remodelling, and endothelial senescence, whereas endothelium-specific overexpression of METTL14 yielded opposing effects. At the cellular level, METTL14 knockdown ameliorated cellular senescence, inflammatory responses, and oxidative stress in senescent endothelial cells. Mechanistically, METTL14 facilitated m6A modification of TLR4 mRNA, thereby enhancing its stability. Knockdown of TLR4 reversed the detrimental effects of METTL14 on vascular ageing. Importantly, vascular ageing, along with related atherosclerosis, positively correlated with blood METTL14 and TLR4 elevations in humans. The authors conclude that this study hints at the role of METTL14/TLR4 signalling in the pathogenesis of vascular ageing, and METTL14 knockdown emerges as a potential therapeutic strategy for mitigating vascular ageing and associated vascular diseases. Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory disorder with high morbidity and mortality rates worldwide. Emerging evidence has reported that Kinesin family member 13B (KIF13B), a crucial motor protein, integrates hepatic lipid metabolism and the inflammatory response to limit liver disease. However, the relationship between KIF13B and atherosclerosis remains unknown. In a Translational Science article entitled ‘The macrophage-derived motor protein KIF13B enhances MERTK-mediated efferocytosis and prevents atherosclerosis in mice’, Yitong Xu from Peking University in China, and colleagues aim to elucidate the specific role of KIF13B in atherosclerosis and its potential therapeutic significance.29 The investigation first assessed the relationship between KIF13B expression and the progression of atherosclerosis in human cohort data and carotid plaques from patients. Subsequently, Kif13b knockout (Kif13b−/−) mice on an Ldlr-deficient background (Ldlr−/−) were generated to obtain double knockouts (Kif13b−/−; Ldlr−/−) as well as myeloid-specific Kif13b knockout mice (Lyz2 Cre;Kif13bf/f) with AAV8-PCSK9. Moreover, Ldlr−/− mice received bone marrow transplants from either Kif13b−/−, Ldlr−/−, or Ldlr−/− mice and were fed a Western diet (WD) for 12 weeks. KIF13B expression was significantly reduced in patients with atherosclerosis and negatively associated with the severity of atherosclerotic progress in WD-fed Ldlr−/− mice. In contrast to Kif13b−/−-Ldlr−/− mice showing a significant increase in plasma total cholesterol and more atherosclerotic lesions compared with the corresponding control mice, depletion of myeloid-derived Kif13b and bone marrow transplantation with macrophages lacking Kif13b did not alter plasma lipid levels but elicited larger atherosclerotic plaques with increased macrophage infiltration and more apoptotic cells. In vitro studies showed that upon oxidized LDL treatment, macrophages with Kif13b deficiency also displayed significantly increased cholesterol accumulation and impaired efferocytosis with reduced MERTK expression. Mechanistic studies revealed that loss of Kif13b decreased the expression of ITCH, leading to accelerated ubiquitination and degradation of MERTK mediated by CBL (Casitas B-lineage Lymphoma; an E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase) in macrophages. Moreover, oral administration of NX-1607, a CBL antagonist, significantly reversed the reduction of the MERTK protein level and defective efferocytosis, ultimately protecting against atherosclerotic development caused by Kif13b deficiency in vivo. The authors conclude that the study reveals that KIF13B is a crucial modulator responsible for maintaining proper macrophage efferocytosis to prevent atherosclerosis development through the KIF13B/ITCH/CBL/MERTK axis, suggesting that KIF13B is a potential therapeutic target for the treatment of atherosclerosis in future clinical trials. The manuscript is accompanied by an Editorial by Kai-Uwe Jarr, Lingfeng Luo, and Nicholas Leeper from Heidelberg University Hospital, Germany, and Stanford University School of Medicine, CA, USA.30 The authors note that this study marks an advance in our understanding of the immunological regulation of atherosclerosis and unveils a promising new therapeutic axis. By identifying KIF13B and CBL as critical regulators of efferocytosis, it shifts the paradigm from broadly suppressing inflammation to activating proresolving mechanisms. This innovative immunotherapeutic approach addresses a major unmet need in cardiovascular medicine.
