title: Introduction
abstract: This issue of Immunological Reviews provides a comprehensive exploration of immune responses, cellular dynamics, and genetic factors influencing neurodegenerative and neuroinflammatory diseases, with an emphasis on Alzheimer's disease (AD) and other neurodegenerative disorders. Across seven chapters, leading researchers delve into various interconnected aspects of neuroimmunology. Topics include the gut microbiome's influence on AD through immune modulation and the role of neuroinflammation in compromising neuronal integrity. The contributions also cover central nervous system (CNS) macrophage functions in maintaining myelin health, the genetic basis and immune characteristics of Aicardi–Goutières Syndrome (AGS), and the centrality of apolipoprotein E (ApoE) in AD pathology. Each chapter brings new insights into how innate and adaptive immune responses influence both the progression and potential treatments of neurodegenerative conditions, focusing on mechanisms from genetic risk factors to environmental influences that shape disease trajectories. What makes this issue especially intriguing is its multidisciplinary approach, merging insights from genetics, immunology, microbiology, and neurobiology to shed light on therapeutic possibilities. The exploration of prenatal influences on microglia, for instance, offers a fresh perspective on early-life risk factors for CNS diseases, while discussions on nucleic acid sensing reveal emerging connections between infection response and neurodegeneration. By presenting both current research and ongoing gaps in knowledge, the issue serves not only as an informative resource for scientists and clinicians but also as a stimulus for further studies aimed at discovering new treatments and interventions. Tastan and Heneka review the complex role of neuroinflammation within the CNS, particularly focusing on how it influences neuronal integrity, structure, and functionality. Neuroinflammation is largely mediated by key CNS cells—such as microglia, astrocytes, pericytes, and infiltrated peripheral immune cells—whose activation contributes to neurodegenerative diseases. Neuroinflammation can be triggered by various factors, including infections, systemic inflammation, blood–brain barrier (BBB) disruption, and traumatic brain injuries. Once activated, these cellular responses lead to a cascade of events, including the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, and other molecules, resulting in a persistent inflammatory response within the CNS. Key mechanisms involved in neuroinflammation include pathogenic infections, systemic inflammation, and the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome—a cellular complex involved in inflammation response. Disruption of the BBB is also a critical factor, as it permits the influx of peripheral immune cells, which exacerbate the inflammatory response within the CNS. Neuroinflammation impairs neuronal integrity through structural damage to synapses and axons, disruptions in calcium signaling, dysfunction in long-term potentiation, and broader alterations in brain networks. These changes not only affect neuronal structure but also significantly impair function, leading to cognitive dysfunction, memory impairment, and sensory disturbances. Additionally, mood disorders, cellular aging, and cellular senescence are associated with chronic neuroinflammation, emphasizing its widespread impact on neuronal functionality. Ultimately, Tastan and Heneka underscore the need to address knowledge gaps regarding neuroinflammation's role in CNS diseases and neuronal health. Future research into how neuroinflammatory pathways impact synaptic structures, neuronal signaling, and CNS network stability is essential for developing therapeutic approaches that may mitigate inflammation-related neurodegeneration and functional impairments. Chandra and Vassar explore the potential role of gut microbiome (GMB)-derived metabolites in AD, highlighting a promising avenue for therapeutic strategies targeting the gut–brain axis. Recent studies have shown that the gut microbiome can significantly influence AD pathogenesis through the production of bioactive metabolites, which affect immune regulation and other physiological processes. This review focuses on key gut-derived metabolites, including short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), bile acids (BAs), trimethylamine-N-oxide (TMAO), and pro-inflammatory byproducts like lipopolysaccharide (LPS), summarizing their respective impacts on AD-related processes and discussing the potential for therapeutic applications. SCFAs are bioactive compounds that have shown promise in preclinical studies as AD therapeutics when administered at optimal doses and timings. BAs, on the other hand, exhibit a more complex relationship with AD, as several BAs have been associated with disease progression, while others, such as tauroursodeoxycholic acid (TUDCA), show protective effects in AD mouse models. TMAO is generally viewed as detrimental, as elevated levels in AD patients correlate with biomarkers of AD pathology and exacerbate disease-related phenotypes in animal models. Similarly, elevated LPS levels in AD patients are associated with heightened neuroinflammation, amyloidosis, tauopathy, and cognitive decline. Therapeutic strategies aimed at reducing LPS or TMAO could therefore offer neuroprotective benefits in AD. Overall, the review emphasizes the need for continued investigation into the gut microbiome's influence on AD, particularly in the context of the gut–brain axis, to facilitate the development of effective GMB-targeted treatments. Modifying levels of these gut-derived metabolites could offer novel, non-invasive therapeutic options that harness the body's existing microbiome to combat neurodegenerative disease. Lin and Holtzmann explore how ApoE influences AD, particularly through its effects on amyloid-β (Aβ) deposition, tau pathology, and the immune system's innate response. The review delves into ApoE's structural characteristics, its role in normal brain physiology, and its involvement in AD, focusing especially on immune regulation by microglia and astrocytes. ApoE, which exists in three primary isoforms—ApoE2, ApoE3, and ApoE4—has been shown to impact AD pathology significantly. The ApoE4 isoform is associated with a higher risk and accelerated progression of AD compared to ApoE2 and ApoE3. ApoE is predominantly produced by astrocytes under normal conditions, but in AD, its production is upregulated in reactive microglia and damaged neurons. ApoE influences lipid transport, neuronal repair, and modulates Aβ aggregation and clearance. Critically, APOE4 accelerates Aβ aggregation and deposition. Removing non-lipidated ApoE bound to Aβ or reducing ApoE expression can decrease amyloid burden in the brain, highlighting potential therapeutic strategies. Apart from Aβ, ApoE also plays a role in tau pathology. Tau proteins, when hyperphosphorylated, form neurofibrillary tangles. Similar to its impact on Aβ, the ApoE4 isoform exacerbates tau pathology and related neurodegeneration, whereas the absence of ApoE or reduction of ApoE levels can alleviate tau-related neurodegeneration. Another significant aspect of AD pathology associated with ApoE is cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA), which involves amyloid deposits in the walls of brain blood vessels, increasing the risk of microhemorrhages and brain edema. ApoE regulates CAA, with ApoE4 exacerbating amyloid deposition in blood vessels. ApoE depletion through gene knockout or immunotherapy can reduce CAA and its associated complications without triggering amyloid-related imaging abnormalities, thus presenting another promising therapeutic avenue. Beyond these pathological roles, ApoE affects the immune response in AD. ApoE is involved in regulating microglia and astrocyte activation. In AD, microglia and astrocytes respond to pathological changes by shifting into reactive states, which can either exacerbate or mitigate AD pathology. ApoE also affects T-cell activity, indicating a broader influence on immune regulation in AD. Ultimately, Lin and Holtzmann emphasize the need for further research into the complex interactions between ApoE isoforms, amyloid and tau pathology, and immune responses. Additionally, it suggests exploring therapeutic strategies targeting ApoE, particularly ApoE4, to modulate AD progression and reduce its pathological burden. Hoffman and Miron examine the roles of different CNS macrophage populations in maintaining the myelin sheath surrounding neuronal axons. Myelin, produced by oligodendrocytes, is essential for efficient nerve impulse conduction and provides metabolic support to neurons. Myelin dysfunction, stemming from developmental issues, neurological diseases, or age-related degeneration, can lead to severe CNS impairments. This review explores the involvement of CNS macrophages—particularly microglia, border-associated macrophages (BAMs), and monocyte-derived macrophages—in the development, maintenance, and regeneration of myelin, along with their contributions to myelin pathology. Microglia have diverse and context-dependent roles. During white matter development, microglia clear out defective oligodendrocyte cells and excess myelin, ensuring proper myelin formation and preventing spontaneous demyelination. In adults, they serve as protective agents by maintaining oligodendrocyte stability and preventing hypermyelination. In cases of white matter damage, however, microglia may adopt a pro-inflammatory profile, contributing to demyelination through the release of inflammatory signals, though they can also assist in remyelination by clearing cellular debris, supporting the recycling of lipids, and releasing growth factors. Aging alters microglial function, often impairing their ability to phagocytize myelin debris and regulate lipid metabolism, which may increase susceptibility to neurodegenerative conditions. BAMs are another group of CNS macrophages that reside along the blood–brain barrier, vasculature, and other border regions within the CNS. These cells contribute indirectly to white matter health by preserving blood–brain barrier integrity and regulating cerebrospinal fluid flow. Their functions vary according to their molecular profiles; some BAM subsets are associated with lipid metabolism and phagocytosis, while others may influence immune responses by recruiting additional immune cells. BAMs that express the AD risk gene variant ApoE4 are associated with reactive oxygen species production and myelin loss, suggesting a potential link to neurodegenerative conditions. Monocyte-derived macrophages, which infiltrate the CNS during a brief postnatal period, are largely absent in healthy adult CNS but become prominent during demyelination and remyelination processes. These cells adopt a pro-inflammatory phenotype when myelin damage occurs, releasing signals that activate microglia and BAMs, and they can contribute to myelin loss through phagocytosis of damaged sheaths. However, during remyelination, monocytes transition to a regenerative state, marked by an anti-inflammatory profile that supports early-stage myelin repair. Together, these findings underscore the diverse and dynamic roles of CNS macrophages in myelin health. Understanding the unique contributions of each macrophage population could provide insights into potential therapeutic avenues for treating myelin-related diseases. Stilman and colleagues explore how nucleic acid-sensing mechanisms traditionally associated with immune defense have roles in the CNS. Typically, these pathways detect pathogen-derived RNA and DNA to initiate immune responses, such as production of type I interferons (IFN-I, i.e., IFN-α and IFN-β), which combat infections. However, recent studies show that nucleic acid-sensing receptors in neurons and glial cells can also recognize self-derived nucleic acids, leading to unintended inflammatory responses that contribute to neurodegenerative diseases. Nucleic acid-sensing receptors function by identifying nucleic acids and initiating defense pathways through signaling proteins such as RIG-I, MDA5, and the cGAS-STING pathway, which are typically associated with pathogen defense but are now known to play roles in brain cells as well. Under normal conditions, neurons and glia utilize these pathways to maintain cellular health and development. For example, they help prevent the spread of infections by responding to RNA or DNA that enter cells abnormally. However, under conditions of cellular stress, self-derived nucleic acids can activate these pathways, leading to inflammation and damage to brain cells. In neurodegenerative diseases, these sensing pathways become dysregulated. Stilman and colleagues provide an overview of how nucleic acid sensing contributes to neurodegeneration, with mechanisms such as the release of mitochondrial DNA from damaged neurons and microglia, which activates the cGAS-STING pathway. This pathway produces inflammatory cytokines that exacerbate neuronal damage, creating a cycle of inflammation and cell death. In AD, amyloid plaques in the brain stimulate microglia to produce IFN-I, leading to chronic inflammation that can worsen disease progression. Another example is the involvement of Let-7 microRNAs, which promote neurodegeneration through mechanisms involving both cell-intrinsic and cell-extrinsic pathways. Apart from their roles in pathology, nucleic acid-sensing receptors also have regulatory roles in neuronal development and function. The review illustrates how specific toll-like receptors (TLRs) in neurons influence the development of neural circuits. For instance, TLR3 and TLR7 limit neurite outgrowth and neuronal morphology, which are critical to forming functional neural networks. Additionally, these receptors play a role in sensory neuron signaling; TLR7 and TLR3 activation in dorsal root ganglion neurons promote action potential firing, which is crucial for sensory processing. During brain development, nucleic acid-sensing pathways help ensure neural circuit integrity by removing damaged neurons. For example, TLR9 sensing DNA damage during development drives microglia to clear damaged neurons, allowing proper formation of sensory networks. Furthermore, nucleic acid sensing appears to support memory formation. In a process known as conditional fear conditioning, neurons in the hippocampus form DNA breaks, which TLR9 recognizes to facilitate synaptic remodeling needed for memory consolidation. Overall, Stilman and colleagues review presents nucleic acid sensing as a double-edged sword in the CNS. While it is crucial for defense and developmental regulation, its aberrant activation can lead to neuroinflammation and degeneration. Future research may help uncover ways to modulate these pathways to protect against neurodegenerative diseases. Hofer and colleagues examine the Aicardi–Goutières Syndrome (AGS), a rare, genetic, autoinflammatory encephalopathy characterized by heightened IFN-I production due to mutations in genes that control antiviral responses and nucleic acid metabolism. AGS typically manifests in infancy or early childhood and progresses with a broad spectrum of neurological, dermatological, and systemic symptoms, including brain inflammation, skin lesions, and liver abnormalities. The root causes of AGS are genetic mutations that lead to the accumulation of nucleic acids or related hybrids in the cytoplasm. This triggers chronic production of IFN-α, setting off inflammatory cascades, and autocrine/paracrine signaling through the IFNAR receptor to induce gene expression changes associated with inflammation. The review covers key genes implicated in AGS, such as TREX1, RNaseH2, SAMHD1, ADAR1, and IFIH1, each of which contributes to abnormal nucleic acid accumulation or IFN-I pathway activation. In TREX1 mutations, cytoplasmic dsDNA accumulation leads to heightened IFN response, while RNaseH2 mutations result in RNA hybrid buildup. Similarly, SAMHD1 mutations allow cytoplasmic RNA hybrid accumulation, while loss of function in ADAR1 leads to the activation of dsRNA sensing pathways, especially through the Z-RNA binding protein ZBP1. Mutations in IFIH1—encoding MDA5—directly activate this IFN-I pathway. These genetic alterations, typically involving activation of cGAS-STING or MDA5-MAVS signaling, culminate in the phosphorylation and activation of TBK1, which drives interferon regulatory factor IRF3 and boosts IFN-α production. The chapter also discusses the clinical heterogeneity of AGS and its systemic impacts, particularly highlighting neurologic, dermatologic, and hepatic complications. A central focus is on preclinical models that replicate aspects of AGS for therapeutic research. Rodent models are extensively used, including mice with mutations in key AGS genes like TREX1, RNaseH2, SAMHD1, ADAR1, and IFIH1, as well as models with IFN-α overexpression. Additionally, non-rodent models and stem cell-derived models contribute to the understanding of AGS by simulating the multisystemic, progressive pathology of the disease. These models have illuminated many of the pathophysiological processes underlying AGS. Finally, the review discusses AGS gene expression data across various primary and stem-cell-derived human cell types, including those relevant to AGS pathology such as neurons and immune cells. These data reveal differential gene expression patterns that may inform cell-specific therapeutic targeting. Overall, Hofer and colleagues underscore the importance of developing comprehensive AGS models to deepen our understanding of autoinflammatory mechanisms and refine potential treatments aimed at mitigating the excessive IFN-I response in AGS. Tagliatti and colleagues delve into the impact of prenatal environmental stressors on microglia. Emerging research indicates that adverse prenatal conditions, such as maternal infections, malnutrition, high-fat diets, and sleep disturbances, significantly increase the likelihood of neurodevelopmental issues in offspring. Tagliatti and colleagues summarize current findings on how these prenatal stressors reprogram microglia, potentially making them more vulnerable to dysregulation later in life, with implications for neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders. One of the primary prenatal stressors affecting microglia is maternal infection, often referred to as maternal immune activation (MIA). MIA models have provided substantial insights into how prenatal infections alter microglia in offspring. Studies show that MIA leads to specific transcriptomic and proteomic changes in microglia, which affect their responsiveness to later stressors. These molecular changes often shift microglia from a resting state to an activated state. This state, when induced early, can make offspring more susceptible to neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism and schizophrenia. Maternal malnutrition, including high-fat diet, represents another significant risk factor for altering microglial development. Nutritional deficiencies during pregnancy can reprogram microglia's responsiveness to inflammation, creating a heightened state of reactivity that persists into adulthood. This altered microglial state has been associated with increased inflammation, impaired synaptic pruning, and altered neurogenesis in animal models, contributing to long-term cognitive and emotional challenges in offspring. Such findings underscore the importance of maternal diet on fetal brain health, suggesting that a balanced nutritional intake during pregnancy can help mitigate these adverse effects. Sleep deprivation during pregnancy is also emerging as a potential stressor that affects microglia. Current findings suggest that sleep deprivation in expectant mothers might serve as a general stressor that activates microglia, but it remains unclear whether this activation follows specific molecular pathways. The implications of maternal sleep loss on offspring brain development are still being explored, particularly concerning whether it induces chronic activation of microglia or temporary changes that resolve over time. Tagliatti and colleagues also highlight the role of sex differences in microglial responses to maternal stressors. Male and female offspring often exhibit different patterns of microglial activation following prenatal stress, possibly due to variations in sex hormones. These differences may influence vulnerability to certain disorders; for instance, males may be more susceptible to conditions like autism spectrum disorder, while females may face higher risks of depression or anxiety. Exploring these sex-based differences could guide future therapeutic approaches to manage or mitigate these risks. Finally, the review of Tagliatti and colleagues calls for further research on the paternal contributions to offspring microglia vulnerability, as recent studies hint at the potential influence of paternal health and lifestyle on offspring neurodevelopment. While maternal factors have traditionally been the focus, the possible paternal impact on microglia maturation and function remains largely uncharted. In summary, the reviews in this issue of Immunological Reviews collectively underscore the intricate interplay between the immune system and neurodegenerative diseases, offering novel insights and highlighting the critical need for further research in neuroimmunology. As we move forward, the potential for new therapeutic interventions targeting immune pathways in neurodegenerative diseases becomes increasingly apparent. title: Cancer and epigenetics – basic research and clinical implications: Joint Meeting of the Fourteenth International Symposium of the Hiroshima Cancer Seminar and the Eighth Meeting of the Tottori Bioscience Promotion Foundation, October 2004
abstract: The Joint Meeting of the Fourteenth International Symposium of the Hiroshima Cancer Seminar (HCS) and the Eighth Meeting of the Tottori Bioscience Promotion (TBP) Foundation was held on 30–31 October 2004 at the International Conference Center, Hiroshima. The symposium consisted of 12 special lectures and 34 free paper presentations for poster session; approximately 250 people were present and actively discussed topics relating to cancer and epigenetics, from basic research to clinical implication. Prior to this symposium, an Open Lecture to the public by HCS was held on 30 October. Kazunori Kodama (Radiation Effects Research Foundation, Hiroshima) spoke about cancer prevention to more than 120 people. To begin the meeting, Eiichi Tahara (Radiation Effects Research Foundation, Hiroshima), Chairman of the HCS Foundation, gave an opening address. Tahara introduced a brief background and the purpose of this series of symposia. Since the establishment of the HCS Foundation in 1992, annual international symposia are organized to create an opportunity for basic scientists and clinical researchers to exchange ideas for cancer research, cancer prevention and cancer therapy. This year, the organizing committee planned to explore the important issue of ‘Cancer and Epigenetics’. The epigenetic mechanism is deeply involved in the pathogenesis of human cancers. CpG island methylator phenotypes (CIMP) might be one of the major pathways responsible for the development of gastrointestinal cancer. Because inactivation of various suppressor genes by promoter methylation or chromatin modification commonly occurs in human cancers, these may provide potential targets for therapeutic intervention. The participants profit by exchanging and learning ideas from informative presentations and discussions, and also contribute to future development in cancer treatment and prevention. Jean-Pierre Issa (University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, USA) delivered a lecture, entitled ‘Bedside epigenetics’, and described the impact of epigenetic process in tumorigenesis and cancer management. Epigenetic changes in cancer consist of primary DNA methylation changes, as well as histone code changes related to DNA methylation or abnormalities in specific histone modifying enzymes. The field is rapidly moving towards clinical applications in patients with cancer, including risk assessment, early detection, prognostication and therapeutic targeting. In colorectal cancer, methylation in normal appearing mucosa appears to increase with age and to be particularly pronounced in patients with advanced preneoplastic and neoplastic lesions. Measurement of methylation in normal appearing mucosa could therefore predict the risk of cancer development, as will be argued for the MGMT gene. In multiple tumor types, a high degree of CIMP appears to be associated with a poor prognosis following standard management. In colorectal cancer, the presence of CIMP in patients who present with stage IV disease is associated with a short survival following 5-fluorouracil based therapy. Drugs that inhibit DNA methylation (5-azacytidine and 5-aza-2’-deoxycytidine, or DAC) are now used in clinical trials for various malignancies. Data suggest that, in myeloid malignancies, the efficacy of DAC is greater at low doses that favor hypomethylation over cytotoxicity, and that responses require the induction of in-vivo hypomethylation. Overall, it seems clear that epigenetic processes will have a significant and varied impact on the management of neoplasia in humans. Mitsuo Oshimura (Tottori University, Yonago) described the epigenetic regulation in imprinted domains in cancer. Genomic imprinting, the phenomenon whereby mono-allelic expression of certain genes occurs depending on their parental origin, plays an important role in mammalian development, growth and cell differentiation. Disturbance of normal imprinting is frequently associated with various types of cancer. LIT1 is an imprinting control center at human chromosome 11p15.5. Several lines of evidence suggested that LIT1 transcript regulates chromatin modifications, resulting in alteration of gene expression in the domain in some, but not all cancer cells. The human paternally expressed gene 3 (PEG3) on chromosome 19q13.4 is one of the candidate tumor suppressor genes for glioma. It has been identified that three expressed sequence tags (EST), H80201, H78825 and AW197312, exhibit paternal allele-specific expression, using human monochromosomal hybrids containing a paternal or maternal origin of PEG3 locus. The EST H80201 was expressed only from the paternal allele in normal lymphoblasts by using a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP). Monoallelic expression of EST H80201 was also detected in non-tumor adult brain tissues of gliomas. These EST were located directly adjacent to PEG3 in a head-to-head orientation. This new transcript, imprinted transcript 1, is located upstream but oriented opposite to PEG3 (ITUP1). Bisulfite sequencing and reverse transcription (RT)-PCR indicated that hypermethylation of the promoter correlated with the absence of these transcripts. ITUP1 and PEG3 may be coordinately regulated, and down-regulation of both genes could be important in the development of glioma. Hidenobu Soejima (Saga University, Saga) presented on the epigenetic regulation of LIT1 imprinting domain and its implication in human diseases. To clarify the chromatin-based imprinting mechanism, the histone modification status at a differentially CpG methylated region of LIT1 (DMR-LIT1) was investigated. Mice harboring targeted deletion of DMR-LIT1 on the paternally inherited chromosome and microcell hybrids harboring targeted deletion of human DMR-LIT1 resulted in the de-repression of imprinted genes including KIP2, indicating that DMR-LIT1 is an imprinting control region for the domain. This region is demethylated in half Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome (BWS) patients and in several tumors. Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assays revealed that in both species, DMR-LIT1 with the CpG-methylated, maternally derived inactive allele showed histone H3 Lys9 (H3K9) methylation, whereas the CpG unmethylated, paternally active allele was acetylated on histone H3/H4 and methylated on H3 Lys4 (H3K4). In the BWS patients with DMR-LIT1 imprinting defect, H3K9 methylation disappeared completely. Furthermore, in esophageal cancer cell lines, expression of imprinted KIP2 gene was statistically correlated with loss of CpG methylation at DMR-LIT1, not with KIP2 promoter methylation itself. Loss of CpG methylation at DMR-LIT1 was also associated with loss of H3K9 methylation. These findings suggest that the histone modification at DMR-LIT1 plays an important role in imprinting control within the imprinting domain, and that loss of histone H3K9 methylation together with CpG demethylation on the maternal allele might lead to the BWS phenotype and might be involved in esophageal cancer. Satoshi Fujii (Hiroshima Red-Cross Hospital, Hiroshima) described the role of histone modification in the imprinted tumor suppressor gene. ARHI is a maternally imprinted tumor suppressor gene whose expression from the paternal allele is markedly down-regulated in breast cancer in addition to loss of heterozygosity. Consistent with imprinting, all three CpG islands of ARHI gene were partially methylated in normal human breast epithelial cells. Reactivation of ARHI expression in breast cancer cell lines by CpG demethylating agents and/or histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitors was related to the methylation status of the CpG islands in the ARHI promoter, especially CpG island II. ChIP assays revealed that treatment with a CpG demethylating agent and/or HDAC inhibitor could increase ARHI expression in breast cancer cells, with a corresponding increase in histone H3K9/18 acetylation and decrease H3K9 methylation. The similar experiments were performed in mouse A9 hybrid cell lines containing only a single maternal (A9–1M) or paternal (A9–1P) allele of human chromosome 1. The histone H3K9/18 acetylation level at ARHI was much higher in A9–1P cells than in A9–1M cells. By contrast, A9–1M cells had much higher H3K9 methylation levels at ARHI than did A9–1P cells. Only treatment with a combination of HDAC inhibitor and a demethylating agent reactivated the imprinted allele. These data suggest that parental allele-specific DNA methylation, histone H3 acetylation and H3K9 methylation are key regulatory mechanisms in ARHI imprinting. Yutaka Kondo (University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, USA) gave a talk on the role of histone modifications in tumor suppressor genes in cancers. The status of histone modification at silenced tumor suppressor gene loci was examined in colorectal cancers. DNA methylation and histone modifications (H3K4 undermethylation, H3K9 underacetylation and H3K9 hypermethylation) were closely correlated at silenced loci in colorectal cancers. Treating cells with inhibitors of HDAC and inhibitors of DNA methylation resulted in large effects on the histone code associated with reactivation of gene expression, suggesting that the sequence of loss of histone acetylation followed by gain of histone methylation on H3K9 is needed for silencing. Next, to evaluate the global distribution of target genes silenced by H3K9 methylation in cancer, a human CpG island microarray was probed with DNA obtained by ChIP using anti H3K9 methylated antibody or anti H3K9 acetylated antibody. Eleven genes, one EST, two unknown fragments and 13 repetitive sequences were identified as targets of H3K9 modification. In addition, a strong correlation was found between the ratio of K9 methylation/acetylation and DNA methylation in those clones. To examine the mechanisms of aberrant histone methylation and which histone methyltransferases may be involved, RNAi-based inhibition of histone methyltransferase, SUV39H1, G9a and EZH2 expression was studied. The preliminary data show that treatment of cancer cells with RNAi to SUV39H1, G9a and EZH2 potentiates gene reactivation, markedly inhibits cell growth and causes profound morphological changes in cancer cells. Mitsuyoshi Nakao (Kumamoto University, Kumamoto) described the role of methylated DNA-binding proteins in transcription and genomic stability. DNA methylation contributes to genome regulation including control of gene expression and chromatin structure. Genome stability is also linked to this epigenetic modification. In the nucleus, the methylated DNA is recognized by methylated DNA-binding domain (MBD) proteins. There are at least five mammalian MBD proteins: MeCP2, MBD1, MBD2, and MBD3 for transcriptional repression, and MBD4 (also known as MED1) for mismatch repair as a thymine glycosylase. Among them, MBD1 acts as a transcriptional regulator through the cooperation of MBD, cysteine-rich CXXC domains, and a C-terminal transcriptional repression domain (TRD). The MBD of MBD1 recruits histone methyltransferase Suv39h1, HDAC1/HDAC2 and HP1 that can bind methyl H3K9. MBD1-containing chromatin-associated factor 1 (MCAF1), also known as the human homolog of murine ATFa-associated modulator (AM), interacts with TRD of MBD1. It is particularly noted that MCAF1/AM converts dimethyl to trimethyl H3K9 by histone methyltransferase SETDB1/ESET. These data indicate that MBD1 may tether Suv39h1-HP1 and SETDB1-MCAF1 complexes to methylated DNA regions, suggesting the presence of pathways from DNA methylation to histone methylation for epigenetic regulation. Furthermore, MBD1 is involved in genome integrity by cooperating with methyl-purine DNA glycosylase, one of the key molecules in the base excision repair. Issay Kitabayashi (National Cancer Center Research Institute, Tokyo) reported the function and regulation of the AML1 transcription factor complex. Specific chromosome translocations are frequently found in human leukemia and often result in the expression of fusion gene products. The genes encoding the AML1/CBF transcription factor complex are the most frequent targets of these translocations. The AML1 complex contains histone acetyltransferases such as p300 and MOZ, promyelocytic leukemia (PML), a corepressor mSIN3A and a protein kinase (AML1K). MOZ and p300/CBP stimulates AML1-dependent transcription. In contrast, a leukemia-associated fusion MOZ-CBP inhibited AML1-mediated transcription and inhibits differentiation of M1 myeloid cells. A specific isoform of PML (PML I) was able to recruit AML1 and coactivator p300 in PML nuclear bodies and enhance the AML1-mediated transcription in the presence of p300. Overexpression of PML I stimulated myeloid cells to differentiate into neutrophils. These results suggest that PML I could act as a mediator for AML1 and its coactivator p300/CBP to assemble into functional complexes, and consequently, activate AML1-dependent transcription and myeloid cell differentiation. AML1K mediated phosphorylation of AML1, p300 and MOZ. AML1K stimulated HAT activity of p300 and transcription activation by GAL4-p300. AML1K strengthened interaction between AML1 and MOZ. The genes encoding AML1 and some of the AML1-interacting proteins are the targets of leukemia-associated chromosome translocations, suggesting that common pathways may be shared by distinct myeloid malignancies and underscores the importance of this complex in hematopoiesis and leukemogenesis. Toshikazu Ushijima (National Cancer Center Research Institute, Tokyo) focused on genome-wide screening techniques for differences in DNA methylation between two genomes. His group previously developed methylation-sensitive-representational difference analysis (MS-RDA). The advantage of MS-RDA is that it focuses on unmethylated and CpG-rich regions of the genome, and thus differential methylation of unique CpG islands can be intensively screened, avoiding interference by repetitive sequences. In an analysis of human stomach cancer, they identified silencing of nine genes, Lysyl oxidase (LOX), H-ras like suppressor (HRASLS), bA305P22.2.3, Filamin-c (FLNc/g-filamin/ABPL), HAND1, a homolog of RIKEN2210016F16, FLJ32130, Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor g angiopoietin-related (PGAR/HFARP/ANGPTL4/ARP4) and Thrombomodulin (TM), as a result of methylation of 5′-CpG islands. Among the nine genes, growth-suppressive activities had been reported for LOX and HRASLS in ras-transformed fibroblasts and for TM in melanoma cells. Tumor-suppressive activities of LOX and HRASLS were examined in gastric cancers by introducing their cDNA into gastric cancer cell lines. Introduction of LOX successfully suppressed cellular growth, colony formation in soft agar, and tumor growth in nude mice, while that of HRASLS did not. These results indicate that LOX is a novel tumor-suppressor gene in human gastric cancers. The power of methylation-based genome-wide screening was impressive. Victor V. Lobanenkov (National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, USA) presented epigenetic regulation of human genome universally involving CTCT/BORIS-binding regions. Many human pathologies including cancer and imprinting disorders may involve common types of epigenetic deregulations non-randomly distributed throughout genomes. It is hypothesized that an ‘epigenetic havoc’ often observed in such pathologies, including LOI in tumors that exhibit regional genome-wide demethylation with a narrower site-specific hypermethylation, might be associated with a common particular malfunction of the DNA-targeting mechanisms necessary for the proper localization and functional reading of epigenetic marks. Such targeting should involve sequence-specific DNA-binding factors, but their identity remained elusive until CTCF-binding regions have emerged as the most likely places of epigenetic modifications in mammals. The duplicated ‘multivalent’ 11 Zn-finger DNA-binding domains (11ZF-DBD), which comprise one-third of the total length in the two paralogous nuclear factors of similar size, CTCF and BORIS, appear to conduct the DNA-targeting part in the molecular orchestra of normal and aberrant epigenetic marking in mammals. Unlike normal somatic cells with CTCF, the vast majority of cancer cells are found to abnormally coexpress CTCF and BORIS together. Several studies of the IGF2/H19 LOI, caused by altering normally mono-allelic CTCF-binding in tumors by aberrant bi-allelic hypo- or hyper-methylation of at least one of several CTCF-sites in the H19 ICR, suggested that CTCF and its targets are taking the central stage in human cancer (epi)genetics. Hidetoshi Tahara (Hiroshima University, Hiroshima) gave a talk on genetic and epigenetic regulation of cell cycle genes in human aging. Cellular senescence causes cells to arrest proliferation, essentially irreversibly, by induction of cyclin dependent kinase inhibitors such as p16INK4a and p21waf1. title: Focus: Plant sciences in Korea
abstract: It sounded fresh and interesting when I was asked by Physiologia Plantarum to organize a ‘country-based’ focus issue. In addition to the journal's self interest, this type of special issue can reveal a country's scientific focus, which might not have been apparent even to the people involved in the research. An analysis of papers that have been published during last ten years in 36 plant-oriented scientific journals reveals a simple country-based sketch of global activity in the plant sciences (Table 1). Countries ranked within the top 10, in terms of the cumulative publication number, are mostly from Northern America, Europe, Japan and Australia. The cumulative number of papers from Asian countries, other than Japan, is much smaller than those from the leading countries but some have shown impressive increases in publication rates during this period. In particular, Korea and China have noticeably increased the number of papers being published annually, and in other parts of the world only Brazil equaled this increased output. Detailed analysis of how these countries have reinforced their scientific capability in plant biology, as well as other fields, is an interesting research topic and with this issue Physiologia Plantarum highlights the recent developments in experimental plant sciences in Korea. In this Focus Issue, we have invited fourteen articles, twelve review and two research articles, all written by Korean corresponding authors affiliated to Korean institutions, and we regret that we were not able to invite many other internationally well known Korean plant scientists to participate in this issue. This Focus Issue is not intended to focus on a specific topic, the aim is to highlight the achievement of Korean plant scientists working in diverse fields, and thus it necessarily contains a wide range of topics. However, for comprehensive understanding of the authors’ fields, the articles here are roughly grouped into five categories; growth and development, hormones and signaling, stress signaling, transport of macromolecules and Brassica genomics. The authors in this issue have worked for many years in their specialties, and this is reflected in the reviews published in this issue. In this section there are five reviews covering the topics of floral, leaf and root epidermal development, and expansin (the cell wall-loosening protein)-mediated plant growth and development. Two reviews by Noh and Noh (2006) and Lee et al. (2006) discuss the regulation of flowering time. The former review focuses on the role of chromatin modifiers and the latter emphasizes the cross-talk between signal integrators and the parallelism between Arabidopsis and rice in floral induction pathways. Multiple genetic pathways are operative to regulate the floral meristem identity genes for flower induction; namely, autonomous, vernalization, photoperiod, GA (gibberellin), and FRI (FRIGIDA) pathways (Boss et al. 2004; Putterill et al. 2004). Noh and Noh (2006) summarize the general role of chromatin remodeling tool kits in FRI, autonomous, vernalization, and photoperiodic pathways. FRI, autonomous, and vernalization pathways all targets FLC (FLOWERING LOCUS C, a floral repressor) transcription; negatively by FRI and positively by other two pathways. The review comprehensively illustrates that different sets of chromatin-remodeling factors, either directly or indirectly regulating histone methylation and acetylation, act on the FLC chromatin. The latest discoveries on the role of chromatin modifiers, such as BRAHMA, EBS, and TFL2, in the photoperiod pathway are introduced. The review by Lee et al. (2006) focuses on FT (FLORAL LOCUS T) as an integrator not only of the photoperiod pathway and the signal from FLC but also of the light-quality pathway and the signal directly (via FCA and FVE) from the autonomous pathway. The review integrates recent results demonstrating that signaling from CO (CONSTANS) to FT and SOC1 is not simply parallel but FT cross-talks to SOC1 to activate its transcription. The review highlights FT as a recently identified ‘mobile floral signal’(Huang et al. 2005), and discusses related topics and questions. Conservation and divergence of floral induction regulation in Arabidopsis and rice are described. The key components and integrators, such as FT, SOC1, and CO (HD3a, OsSOC1, and Hd1, respectively in rice), and the regulatory hierarchy between them in the pathways are well conserved in both species. However, the gear driven by Hd1 (rice CO) operates in reverse relative to the Arabidopsis counterpart so that Hd1 negatively regulates Hd3a (rice FT), consistent with the short-day property of rice floral induction. Another pathway through Ehd1, which positively regulates rice Hd3a and AP1, provides rice with its own floral induction pathway. Leaves, with their amazingly diverse forms, appear mostly as flattened two dimensional shapes. This may represent an adaptation for efficiently harvesting photons. However, plants invest considerable effort to keep this optimized shape. Among the characteristic mechanisms used by plants to achieve this are adaxial-abaxial polarity, proximal-distal polarity, polar expansion, symmetry, and flat morphology of the leaf. How these mechanisms operate together to produce a leaf is summarized by Kim and Cho (2006). The role of miRNAs during early leaf development was described. The review focuses on the polar expansion of the leaf; long and narrow vs. short and wide. Two pairs of genes, ROT3/AN and ROT4/AN3 for cell expansion and division, respectively, are shown to modulate this leaf property. The determination of cell fate is a fundamental process in the development of multicellular organisms, and thus understanding how this is governed has been on of the main challenges for developmental biology. Cells of the Arabidopsis root epidermis have two possible cell fates; hair cell or non-hair cell. The determination of these two fates is innately cell-position dependent and implemented by the interaction between MYB, bHLH, and WD40 proteins, where WEREWOLF (WER) and CAPRICE (CPC) for MYB transcription regulators, GRABRA3 (GL3) and ENHANCER OF GLABRA3 (EGL3) for bHLH transcription regulators, and TRANSPARENT TESTA GLABRA1 (TTG1) for the WD40 protein. The review by Schiefelbein and Lee (2006) provides an update on recent results demonstrating refined genetic interactions between these components and introduces a newly found factor responsible for positional information flow. Schiefelbein and Lee (2006) also focus on newly identified WER-binding cis-elements, the molecular genetic behavior of GL3/EGL3, and the proposed role of leucine-rich receptor like kinase SCRAMBLED (SCM), which could be a putative receptor of the positional cue from underlying root tissues. This review on root epidermal fate determination provides a well-illustrated model of regulatory circuits and flows from perception of the positional cue to cell specification. In this model, SCM perceives the positional signal and determines the positional expression of WER, and the downstream regulatory circuits ultimately control the expression of GLABRA2 (GL2), a repressor of hair morphogenesis. The review suggests several important future directions; for example, characterization of the relay molecules between SCM and WER, regulation of GL2 and GL3 by the MYBs, molecular function of TTG1, downstream molecules for hair morphogenesis and their regulation by GL2. Since the first two expansins, the cell wall-loosening proteins, were discovered in cucumber (McQueen-Mason et al. 1992), the expansin family has increased considerably, with 35 and 58 members found in the Arabidopsis and rice genomes, respectively. As the expansin family contains so many members, it has been divided into several subfamilies depending on amino acid sequence divergence and recently the nomenclature of these subfamilies has been unified; EXPA, EXPB, EXLA, and EXLB (Kende et al. 2004; http://www.bio.psu.edu/expansins/). A review by Choi et al. (2006) in this issue summarizes the evolution, expression, biochemistry, and biological function of this unique wall loosening protein family in different plant species. Among the interesting updates is the biochemical and biophysical properties of vegetative EXPBs, which bind tightly to cellulosic cell walls, in contrast to their soluble sister EXPBs from pollens. This review also refreshes the putative role of expansins in mycorrhizal activity and nodulation. A review on cytokinins by Hwang and Sakakibara (2006) focuses on the metabolism and perception of cytokinins. The metabolism section provides a helpful synthetic illustration of the different cytokinin metabolic pathways in higher plants and Agrobacterium. The difference in eukaryotic and prokaryotic pathways of cytokinin biosynthesis primarily appears to begin from the subtle difference in substrate specificities of isopentenyltransferases (IPTs, the first step catalyst) between the two systems; dimethylallyl diphosphate (DMAPP) in the plant cytosol and hydroxylated DMAPP in bacteria and plastids for the substrate. Seven Arabidopsis IPTs show different subcellular localizations and varying spatio-temporarily expression patterns, indicative of the ubiquitous role of cytokinins. Two AtIPTs are likely to have tRNA-IPT activities that produce cytokinins from tRNA by prenylation but their physiological role remains to be characterized. The review summarizes various ways of regulation of cytokinin metabolic enzymes. Among the major regulatory factors are hormones (auxin, abscisic acid, and cytokinin itself), developmental cues (SHOOT MERISTEMLESS, a KNOX1 protein), and nitrogenous compounds (NO3−, NH4+). The review provides a summary of verified cytokinin receptors and related histidine kinases. Intriguing phenotypic differences are described for the same AHK4/WOL/CRE1 allele. Diverse expression patterns and different molecular functions between the receptors are discussed so as to open new research directions in this field. Interestingly, among the many unpublished data mentioned in this review is the specified role of AHK3 in plant organ longevity. Lesions of AHK3, but not of AHK2 or AHK4, caused early senescence of the leaf, and its overexpression increased leaf longevity (Kim et al. 2006). Choe (2006) summarized recent advances in the research of brassinosteroid (BR) metabolism that is catalyzed mostly by cytochrome P450 monooxygenases. The review presents many parallels between BR biosynthetic pathways from different plant species. The final enzymes (and genes) in BR biosynthesis, from castasterone (CS) to brassinolide (BL), have been recently characterized from Arabidopsis and tomato (Kim et al. 2005; Nomura et al. 2005), and both steroids are also known to be biologically active in rice and pea. In this regard, an interesting interpretation was presented that BL may play a major role in reproductive development while CS is important in vegetative growth. This was inferred from the observations that tomato and Arabidopsis mutants defective in CS-to-BL conversion showed weak vegetative phenotypes. The second half of the review focuses on catabolism or inactivation of BRs. The degradation of these steroid hormones, balanced with their biosynthesis, is proposed as a mechanism to fine tune plant growth and development. Interestingly, it is suggested that agronomically advantageous phenotypes could be obtained through BR-deficiency; for example, short status, better photosynthetic capacity, more erect leaves, etc in cultivated rice. A research article by Joo et al. (2006) illustrates the cross talk between BR, auxin, ethylene, and light signaling networks. Ethylene biosynthetic enzymes, aminocyclopropane carboxylate (ACC) synthases, have long been known to be up-regulated by auxin. This paper provides further evidence that BR up-regulates ethylene production in dark-grown Arabidopsis seedlings, most likely by activating the expression of ACC synthase 4 (ACS4). However, light treatment or auxin-insensitive dominant mutations, such as axr1-3 and axr2-1, abolished the BR-induction of AtACS4, implying cross talk between BR, auxin, and light to regulate the ethylene level and thus to tune the seedling growth in different light conditions. Transport of macromolecules between cells is carried out either apoplastically or symplastically. Two reviews describe apoplastic sucrose transport and symplastic macromolecular transport. Sucrose loading from mesophyll cells to the phloem can be either apoplastic or symplastic. However, sucrose unloading in the developing seed is thought to occur apoplastically. To complete the apoplastic sucrose transport process, a three-protein (or enzyme) system is required; H+/sucrose transporter (SUT), invertase, and monosaccharide transporter (MST). Lim et al. (2006) summarized recent research on these proteins and genes from rice and other cereal caryopses. Functional studies of these genes in rice are expected from J-S Jeon's group as they have generated many T-DNA insertional rice mutants for these genes. There are many cases for non-cell autonomous action by certain genes. A review by Chen and Kim (2006) comprehensively summarizes recent studies on the plasmodesmata (PD) for short-distance and the phloem for long-distance signaling. The PD section in the review focuses on the structure of and the macromolecules transported through the PD. Molecular characteristics of PD components and four major approaches for elucidating the components are summarized; isolation of proteins from PD-enriched cell walls, screening PD- targeting proteins using the transient expression of a green fluorescence protein (GFP)-tagged cDNA library, isolation of trafficking mutants with the use of fluorescence tracer-loading assay, and proteomic technology using PD-enriched cell walls. Transcription factors such as LEAFY, SHORTROOT, and KNOTTED1 (KN1) and other PD-transportable proteins are described together with the mechanism of how they pass through the PD channel. A recent interesting result by J-Y Kim's group is that the homeodomain of KN1 is not only necessary but also sufficient for PD trafficking (Kim et al. 2005). A plethora of proteins and mRNAs have been characterized from the phloem sap that might function as long-distance signaling molecules. For example, the pumpkin phloem sap likely contains up to 1000 proteins. Unlike photoassimilates, which are simply transported by bulk flow through the sieve tube, the entry, translocation, and exit of signaling macromolecules in this system seems to be highly controlled. An example for this is that the root-ward movement of pumpkin CmPP16, an RNA carrier, is selectively controlled by protein-protein interaction. Non-cell autonomous RNAs include mRNAs and small RNA species. SUT1, NACP, STMP, WRKYP, and GAI mRNAs from pumpkin are known to be mobile through the sieve tube system. Interestingly, GAI mRNA movement seems to be controlled by a conserved sequence motif in many plant families. Cataloging small RNAs in the phloem sap by Yoo et al. (2004) revealed that 18∼25 nucleotide-long single stranded RNAs predominate in the sap but it also includes genuine small-interfering RNAs and micro RNAs. These small RNA species have been suggested to function in systemic gene silencing. A live cell is physically an open system, exchanging different forms of energy and materials with its surroundings. However, the energies and materials are not always hospitable; rather they are frequently hostile to the cell. These unfriendly physical stimuli from the environment are called either abiotic or biotic stresses depending on their origin. In this section, I introduce two reviews describing abiotic stresses and one research article for biotic stress. Since the majority of organisms on earth have evolved to use oxygen and transfer electrons for energizing the cell, oxidative stresses are inevitable and cells have developed protective mechanisms from these stresses. Jang et al. (2006) focuses on the intriguing role of eukaryotic peroxiredoxins (Prxs) in protecting against, and signaling oxidative stresses. 2-Cys Prx, as a dimer, catalyzes the degradation reaction from toxic hydrogen peroxide to water; the peroxidase action. On the other hand, heat shock or oxidative stress (or both factors cooperatively) causes an architectural transition of Prx from a dimer to higher molecular weight structures. This structural transition further induces a functional transition of the protein from a peroxidase to a molecular chaperone, which protects biologically important proteins from stressful conditions. Although this detailed mechanism was elucidated in yeast cells (Jang et al. 2005), similarly structured Prxs are found in all eukaryotes including mammals and plants. In plants, Prxs are localized to the chloroplast in which frequent oxidative damage is expected. The review describes how plant Prxs show similar structural and functional transitions during exposure to abiotic stress. Abscisic acid (ABA) is the hallmark plant hormone mediating abiotic stresses. title: Lessons from Lumiracoxib: Are cyclooxygenase‐2 inhibitors less hepatotoxic than non‐selective non‐steroidal anti‐inflammatory drugs?
abstract: In this issue of the journal, Pillans et al. report three women who developed severe hepatotoxicity with lumiracoxib, a recently introduced cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) inhibitor.1 All had histologic evidence of significant hepatocellular necrosis. One of these patients died from acute liver failure while the other needed a liver transplant. A further five cases of liver injury have since been reported to the Australian Therapeutic Goods Administration. Of these cases, two patients have died and two have undergone liver transplantation. Many of the affected individuals were women but this is not unusual in case series of patients with drug induced liver injury (DILI). Drug dose or duration of use was not predictive of liver toxicity. Lumiracoxib is structurally similar to diclofenac (a known cause of DILI) and shares with it the proclivity for forming reactive (hepatotoxic) metabolites and adducts with glutathione. In turn, these can lead to glutathione depletion, covalent binding to proteins and oxidative stress.2,3 Autoantibodies (chiefly antinuclear antibodies) were noted in all three of the reported cases. However, autoantibodies are nonspecific markers of tissue injury and can be present (often transiently) in cases of DILI. The authors' contention that immune mechanisms may be operational is supported by a recent genome wide association study.4 This involved 41 cases of lumiracoxib-induced liver injury and 176 lumiracoxib-exposed controls without liver injury. The main finding of the study was a strong association between lumiracoxib hepatotoxicity with specific human leukocyte antigen (HLA) markers within the major histocompatibility complex class II region. Of the several HLA alleles identified, HLA-DQA1*0102 had the highest sensitivity (73.6%) in identifying cases at risk.4,5 These case reports have persuaded health regulatory authorities to call for withdrawal of lumiracoxib from clinical use. While there is a long history of drug withdrawals from hepatic injury secondary to non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAID), the association of significant hepatotoxicity with the COX-2 subclass of NSAIDs was unforeseen. The report questions the perception that COX-2 inhibitors are less likely to cause hepatic damage than nonselective NSAIDs when in fact it may be that COX-2 inhibitors share the same uncommon but occasionally serious liver injury risk with other NSAIDs. Before turning to the issue of COX-2 inhibitor hepatotoxicity, it is pertinent to review our current understanding of (non-selective) NSAID-related liver injury. NSAIDs are among the mostly widely prescribed drugs and their usage continues to increase commensurate with the aging of the population. Not surprisingly, up to 10% of cases of DILI are attributable to the use of NSAIDs.6 The overall frequency of hospitalization for NSAID-associated hepatic injury is estimated at 3–23/100 000 patient-years.6 However, these figures are probably an underestimate of the risks involved. As is common with data relating to adverse drug reactions, underreporting is common, relying on voluntary reports and subject to other influences such as media coverage and potential litigation. NSAIDs comprise a heterogeneous group of drugs and the risks of liver toxicity could be conceivably greater for some classes than others. This is certainly the case for drugs such as sulindac that have been associated with a much higher frequency of DILI. At one time or another, most NSAIDs have been implicated in causing adverse hepatic drug reactions whose diverse disease phenotype ranges from acute hepatitis, cholestasis (ibuprofen) and cholestatic hepatitis (sulindac), chronic hepatitis (diclofenac), granulomatous hepatitis (phenylbutazone) through to acute liver failure leading to withdrawal from clinical use (bromfenac).7 The emergence of cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) inhibitors offered the prospect of selective COX-2 inhibition to achieve peripheral anti-inflammatory effects without disrupting COX-1, which is necessary in maintaining gastrointestinal mucosal integrity. To an extent, this objective has been achieved with the COX-2 inhibitors although there are lingering concerns about methodological issues in pivotal studies; this has provoked lively debate about how absolute the gastrointestinal protection really is. Toxic effects outside the gastrointestinal tract have also been a concern. Rofecoxib, an early and much publicized member of this class, has been withdrawn due to reports of cardiovascular toxicity while valdecoxib has been implicated in serious allergic skin reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome.8 Against this backdrop of uncertainty, where do COX-2 inhibitors stand with regards to the potential for causing hepatic injury? The cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) inhibitor group include selective (celecoxib, rofecoxib) as well as preferential inhibitors (nimesulide).With respect to nimesulide, there are several case reports documenting a range of hepatic side effects ranging from acute hepatitis, cholestasis through to acute liver failure. This has lead to suspensions or withdrawal from use in Finland, Spain and other European countries. However, these findings have not always been consistent. One Italian population based study also reiterated the association between liver injury and NSAID use but noted that the risk of liver injury with nimesulide was similar to that of other NSAIDs (adjusted rate ratio 1.7/100 000 person years, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.9 to 3.3).9 When selective COX-2 inhibitors are considered, here too, there are well-documented cases of acute hepatitis or cholestatic hepatitis with celecoxib10 and rofecoxib.11 However, when large datasets from clinical trials and meta-analyses involving the use of COX-2 inhibitors in patients with osteoarthritis have been analyzed, there did not appear to be any additional risk of hepatotoxicity with these drugs (Table 1).12 Laine et al. reviewed data compiled from seven population-based studies and over 100 randomized controlled trials involving NSAIDs. They noted an increase in serum aminotransferases with rofecoxib (2%) and lumiracoxib (3%) but did not identify any excess risk of COX-2 inhibitor hepatotoxicity.12 Sulindac and nimesulide were associated with a higher risk of hospitalization from liver injury.12 However, a Taiwanese study evaluating the risk of acute hepatic injury with NSAIDs concluded that the risk of hospitalization with celecoxib (odds ratio [OR] = 1.92, 95% CI = 1.38, 2.69) was similar to that of other non-selective NSAIDS (OR = 2.13, 95% CI = 2.00, 2.28).13 Over 4500 patients with acute hepatitis secondary to NSAIDs were included in this report. Thus the evidence presented so far is conflicting as to whether COX-2 inhibitors differ from non-selective NSAIDS with respect to the likelihood of causing hepatic injury. The few documented case reports with these drugs and occasional case series of patients with severe liver toxicity such as the one reported in this issue suggest that vigilance is necessary. Further, whereas COX-2 inhibitors may be preferred to non-selective NSAIDs in situations where there is a risk of gastrointestinal toxicity such considerations seem less compelling with respect to avoiding hepatic toxicity.

title: Year‐in‐review 2009: Asthma, COPD and airway biology
abstract: In this review, we present important global advances in asthma, COPD and airway biology in 2009, and, in the context of these global advances, we highlight articles published in Respirology. Our aim is to provide a summary and interpretation of new data published in the journal about airway diseases, which will contribute to a better understanding of their pathogenesis, and lead to improved diagnosis, prevention and treatment. John Upham Researchers continue to discover genetic variations that are linked to asthma. Recent highlights have included reported links between asthma and variants in genes that regulate epithelial cell proteins. Variants in the filaggrin gene increase the risk of asthma in people with atopic eczema,1,2 while He and colleagues described a genetic variant in the region of the thymic stromal lymphopoietin gene that is associated with asthma and airway hyperresponsiveness.3 The field of asthma genetics is increasingly moving towards large genome-wide association studies. For a more detailed description of progress in asthma genetics, readers should refer to one of the many recent review articles.4 The pathophysiology of asthma involves a complex interplay between resident structural cells within the airways and infiltrating inflammatory cells of haematopoietic origin. The role of T-helper type 2 (Th2) cells in allergic inflammation in asthma has been established for some time. However, the increasing recognition of asthma as a heterogeneous disease has prompted investigators to reassess T-cell subsets in different types of asthma. Gene expression profiling has shown the existence of at least two asthma subtypes, termed ‘Th2-high’ and ‘Th2-low’ by Woodruff and colleagues.5 In addition, it is now clear that Th17 cells can mediate both neutrophilic airway inflammation and airway hyperresponsiveness in experimental animals and that both these features are steroid-resistant.6 The pattern of cytokines produced during acute asthma exacerbations differs from that seen in stable disease. Calderon and colleagues reported a bias towards interleukin (IL)-13 production by CD4 T-cells during acute exacerbations in children, whereas IFN-γ responses were increased during convalescence.7 Reduced numbers of T regulatory cells has been linked to a number of inflammatory diseases including asthma. Matsumoto and co-workers showed in a mouse model that the frequency of lung T regulatory cells was inversely associated with allergic inflammation and airway hyperresponsiveness, while parallel studies in humans showed relative deficiency of circulating T regulatory cells in asthma.8 Antigen presenting dendritic cells are exquisitely sensitive to environmental stimuli such as inhaled allergens,9,10 are tightly regulated by airway epithelial cells,11 and are thought to have a key role in the initiation and maintenance of asthma. In early childhood, dendritic cells appear to play an important immunoregulatory role, as relative deficiency of plasmactyoid dendritic cells during infancy is linked to more frequent respiratory infections and a greater likelihood of asthma by the age of 5 years.12 The nerve growth factor signalling pathway was shown to be important in a guinea pig model of asthma.13 This pathway is subject to regulation by SH2-Bb, a recently described signalling molecule expressed in alveolar macrophages.13 Airway administration of Aspergillus fumigatus spores can enhance allergic inflammation induced by a second allergen (ovalbumin).14 The key mechanism involves protease-mediated damage to epithelial cells, and this may also lead to airway remodelling.14 The mast cell clearly has a central role in asthma pathogenesis. Elliot and colleagues examined lung tissue from cases of fatal asthma and showed that mast cell degranulation and airway smooth muscle shortening were most marked when death occurred within a few hours of the onset of asthma symptoms, as compared with cases in which the asthma exacerbation developed over a longer period of time.15 Rhinoviruses are important triggers for acute asthma exacerbations in children and adults, and this may be related to impaired immunity in asthma.16 Recent studies have highlighted the complexity of the host immune response to rhinovirus infection in vivo,17 and the extent to which responses vary among the many different rhinovirus strains.18 Interestingly, antiviral immune pathways activated during acute asthma exacerbations in children may also lead to enhanced expression of high-affinity IgE receptor,19 thereby providing a plausible biological mechanism whereby viruses might enhance reactivity to allergens in some people with asthma. These types of studies represent important steps towards developing novel approaches to therapy for asthma exacerbations. Airway wall remodelling in asthma appears to be relatively resistant to current asthma therapies and therefore continues to be an area of great interest to researchers. Kuroishi et al. studied the ability of transforming growth factor beta (TGFβ)-1 to induce epithelial-mesenchymal transition.20 Using primary mouse tracheal epithelial cells, the authors showed that TGFβ-1 was able to induce expression of α-smooth muscle actin and vimentin, and loss of epithelial cell markers. Basal epithelial cells seemed to be most susceptible to epithelial–mesenchymal transition.20 Airway smooth muscle hyperplasia and hypertrophy are thought to represent a key component of airway obstruction and remodelling in asthma. Shin et al. examined the effects of TGFβ on airway smooth muscle cells in vitro.21 TGFβ had no obvious effects on smooth muscle proliferation but was able to induce smooth muscle cells to release vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). State of the art proteomics was used to evaluate the influence of leukotriene (LTE)-4 on human bronchial epithelial cells.22 The key finding was that LTE-4 down regulates glucocorticoid receptor expression, interfering with the therapeutic effects of glucocorticoids in asthma, and potentially contributing to steroid resistance in asthma.22 The effects of simvastatin on small airway remodelling were studied in an animal model of cigarette smoke-induced airway inflammation.23 Simvastatin inhibited airway inflammation and reduced small airway thickening and collagen deposition. These findings may be relevant not only for COPD, but also for asthma, especially for those asthmatics who smoke. While recent studies in humans have suggested that statins do not improve clinical aspects of asthma control in the short term, atorvastatin may reduce numbers of sputum macrophages in asthma,24 so we are likely to see further interest in the anti-inflammatory properties of statins in asthma. Researchers continue to look for improved methods of non-invasive monitoring of inflammation in asthma. The pH of exhaled breath condensate appears to be a rapid and reproducible biomarker of inflammation, and one key study reported recently in Respirology showed that asthmatics who smoke have lower exhaled breath pH than non-smoking asthmatics.25 This appeared to be related to the level of oxidative stress in smokers, as assessed by 8-isoprostane in exhaled breath. Future studies will need to determine whether exhaled breath pH will be useful in monitoring the long-term effects of smoking on asthmatic airway inflammation. New techniques of imaging are increasingly being applied to the evaluation of airway disorders. Magnetic resonance angiography has been used to evaluate lung perfusion in bronchiolitis,26 while a variety of investigators have recently outlined the use of hyperpolarized helium MRI to assess ventilation heterogeneity in asthma.27,28 Investigators are increasingly turning to detailed analysis of inflammatory cells and inflammatory mediators to better define specific asthma phenotypes.5,29–31 Asthma patients with chronic persistent airway obstruction showed prominent expression of IL-12, IL-13 and IFN-γ in bronchial biopsies, whereas a very different pattern of cytokine expression was observed in patients with intermittent obstruction.32 Nadif and co-workers used careful analysis of differential leukocytes in peripheral blood to define patterns of granulocytic inflammation in asthma.30 This approach has considerable appeal for large-scale epidemiological studies in which invasive monitoring is difficult, and may be especially relevant to asthma research in regions of the world with limited access to research funding.
