title: Brain endothelial cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS)–stimulator of interferon genes (STING) signaling pathway in aging and neurodegeneration
abstract: The cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS)–stimulator of interferon genes (STING) signaling pathway has emerged as a key mediator of neuroinflammation. While current studies primarily attribute its effects to neurons and glial cells, emerging research suggests that cGAS-STING signaling may play a critical role in cerebral vasculature, particularly in brain endothelial cells. Therefore, studying the role of inflammation caused by the cGAS–STING pathway in brain endothelial cells could provide a more comprehensive understanding of neuroinflammatory disease and new avenues for therapeutic interventions. Here, we review the multifaceted role of global cGAS–STING signaling in various neurological and neuroinflammatory diseases and the potential contribution of cGAS–STING in brain endothelial cells. The vascular system in the brain creates a unique environment crucial for proper brain functioning (Sweeney et al., 2019). Inflammation in blood vessels compromises both vascular and cerebral function. It is increasingly recognized as a critical factor contributing to the development of various neurological disorders. Recent research has indicated that cGAS–STING signaling, an innate immunity pathway (Paul et al., 2021), may play a central role in vascular inflammation. Neurovascular inflammation in aging and neurodegeneration: Neuroinflammation is a prevalent feature and plays a pivotal role in aging and neurodegenerative disorders (Paul et al., 2021). While neuroglia are increasingly studied in aging and neurodegeneration, less is known about the contribution of the vasculature and brain endothelial cells (BECs), which represent another significant site of inflammation in the central nervous system (CNS). Neurovascular inflammation results in blood–brain barrier (BBB) leakage, dysfunction of the neurovascular unit, and hypoxia. This amplifies the inflammatory response within the CNS, contributing to neuronal dysfunction and damage (Sweeney et al., 2019). As the primary barrier in blood vessels between blood and the surrounding tissues, the endothelial cells (ECs) are a key player in vascular inflammation. BECs have especially great importance as they—together with pericytes and astrocytes—form the multicellular BBB and contribute to the selective permeability of the BBB (Sweeney et al., 2019). By interacting with both immune signaling molecules in the blood and CNS immune cells, BECs act as an important bridge between functions of the innate immune system, making them an interesting target for anti-inflammatory treatment. Endothelial inflammation is a multifaceted process involving various mechanisms. Recent research has indicated that the cGAS-STING pathway may be involved in triggering the inflammatory processes in endothelial cells (Yu et al., 2022). The aim of this perspective is to examine the potential role of BEC cGAS–STING in various neurological and neuroinflammatory diseases. We first review the role of global cGAS–STING signaling in these diseases. We then discuss the current evidence of the cGAS–STING pathway in triggering endothelial inflammation and dysfunction. The cGas–STING pathway overview: cGAS–STING signaling serves as a crucial regulator of inflammatory responses (Paul et al., 2021). This pathway, designed to sense DNA within the cell and trigger an immune response, acts as a surveillance mechanism for damaged and infected cells. DNA triggering this response can originate from diverse sources. Pathogenic sources include double-stranded DNA viruses, retroviruses, some intracellular bacteria, and parasitic protozoans. Moreover, self-DNA—both extracellular and genomic—and mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) can also activate cGAS under specific circumstances (Paul et al., 2021). cGAS recognizes long double-stranded DNA in the cytoplasm and undergoes activation to synthesize 2′,3′-cGAMP (Figure 1). This molecule then binds to STING in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, leading to STING oligomerization and translocation to the Golgi. In the Golgi, STING recruits TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1) to form a signalosome, facilitating TBK1 autophosphorylation. Subsequently, TBK1 phosphorylates STING, providing a docking site for interferon (IFN) regulatory factor 3 (IRF3), which is also phosphorylated by TBK1. Activated IRF3 forms dimers and translocates to the nucleus, stimulating the transcription of type I IFNs and other IFN-stimulated genes. Additionally, the cGAS-STING pathway activates nuclear factor-κB, mitogen-activated protein kinase, and the STING-PERK signalosome within the endoplasmic reticulum, further contributing to the ensuing immune response.Figure 1: Schematic diagram of activation of the cGAS–STING signaling pathway in BECs.During aging and neurogenerative conditions, cytosolic DNA is recognized by cGAS, leading to the synthesis of a 2′,3′-cGAMP. 2′,3′-cGAMP binds to STING in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, causing STING transportation to the proximity of the Golgi, where it recruits TBK-1. TBK1 phosphorylates STING, activating the transcription factors IRF3 and NF-κB. Activated IRF3 and NF-κB then travel to the nucleus to promote the transcription of type I IFNs and NF-κB inflammatory genes. Alternatively, the cGAS-STING pathway can be activated independently of the DNA sensing pathway. Excessive and continuous production and release of IFN and other inflammatory cytokines resulting from activation of the cGAS-STING pathway can lead to BEC inflammation and dysfunction. This dysfunction results in BBB leakage, allowing IFN, other inflammatory cytokines, plasma proteins, and blood immune cells to permeate into the brain parenchyma. Ultimately, this contributes to the escalation of the neuroinflammatory and neurodegenerative process. Created with BioRender.com. BBB: Blood–brain barrier; BEC: brain endothelial cell; cGAS: cyclic GMP–AMP synthase; dsDNA: double-stranded DNA; EC: endothelial cell; IFN: interferon; IRF3: interferon regulatory factor 3; mtDNA: mitochondrial DNA; NF-κB: nuclear factor kappa B; STING: stimulator of interferon genes; TBK1: TANK-binding kinase 1.While the cGAS–STING pathway plays a prominent role in anti-viral, anti-tumor, and inflammatory responses through driving IFN and cytokine production, cGAS and STING also have various functions outside of immunity. cGAS–STING signaling in aging and neurodegeneration: Neuroinflammation emerges as a significant hallmark in numerous neurological disorders. Given the pivotal role of the cGAS–STING pathway in inflammatory processes, there is a compelling rationale to thoroughly investigate this pathway in the context of neurological disorders (Paul et al., 2021). Notably, the cGAS–STING pathway has been implicated in diverse neurological conditions such as brain injury, aging, and neurodegenerative disorders. In particular, brain aging and Alzheimer’s disease (AD) are highlighted in the following discussion. Aging is the predominant risk factor for the majority of neurodegenerative diseases, often accompanied by the accumulation of senescent cells and inflammation, commonly referred to as inflammaging (Paul et al., 2021). Senescent cells exhibit significant secretory activity known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype. The dysregulated activity of cGAS–STING is consistently observed among various types of senescent cells, playing a crucial role in the secretion of several senescence-associated secretory phenotype components. Mechanistically, the cGAS–STING pathway triggers the senescence-associated secretory phenotype secretion through the accumulation of cytoplasmic DNA, which is released into the cytosol from the nucleus and mitochondria in senescent cells (Paul et al., 2021). Research has demonstrated that aging-related inflammation is driven by cGAS–STING activation (Gulen et al., 2023). Notably, inhibiting the cGAS-STING pathway in aged mice has been shown to prevent aging-related inflammation and enhance cognitive and motor performance (Gulen et al., 2023). Upon reflection of these findings, it is possible to speculate that the aberrant signaling of cGAS–STING contributes to age-related dysfunction through its pro-inflammatory properties. AD is the most common neurodegenerative disease. Within AD, the aggregation of amyloid-beta and hyperphosphorylated tau induces cellular stress, resulting in mitochondrial dysfunction and the release of mtDNA, which is subsequently recognized by cGAS (Xie et al., 2023). This process triggers heightened expression of type I IFN, provoking neuroinflammation characterized by astrogliosis and microglial activation. Notably, in AD, the STING–IRF3 pathway seems to predominantly activate microglia, exacerbating neuronal damage (Xie et al., 2023). Consequently, the inhibition or deficiency of cGAS in AD models reduces AD pathology, neuroinflammation, and cognitive impairment (Xie et al., 2023). In summary, it has been consistently revealed that the cGAS-STING pathway undergoes activation during both brain aging and injury, as well as in the progression of neurodegenerative diseases. Across various studies, the manipulation of this pathway through genetic knockout of associated genes or inhibition via chemical interventions has largely demonstrated a reduction in neuronal injury and an improvement in disease outcomes. These compelling results strongly indicate a primarily adverse impact of the cGAS–STING pathway in these conditions, underscoring its significance as a potential target for therapeutic interventions. Furthermore, it highlights the importance of understanding the potential contribution of each cell type in this context. cGAS–STING signaling in brain endothelial cells: Currently, the cell type-specific role of cGAS–STING signaling in the brain is poorly understood. The cGAS–STING pathway has been shown to be activated predominantly in microglia (Gulen et al., 2023; Xie et al., 2023), but it is also present in astrocytes and neurons. While there is little research on the importance of cGAS–STING activity specifically in BECs in neurodegenerative diseases, its significance has been explored in the context of aging (Yu et al., 2022) and various diseases, such as diabetic retinopathy (Liu et al., 2023), COVID-19 (Domizio et al., 2022), and cerebral malaria (Pais et al., 2022). The common activators of the cGAS–STING pathway mentioned above, such as viral, bacterial, and self-DNA, have been shown to activate this pathway in BECs. During aging, mitochondrial dysfunction in blood vessels leads to the release of mtDNA into the cytoplasm. Simultaneously, nuclear DNA damage increases the amount of cytoplasmic chromatin fragments. These processes activate the cGAS–STING pathway in endothelial cells, contributing to aging-related endothelial dysfunction. Evidence of the activation of the cGAS-STING pathway is shown by the increased expression of cGAS, STING, and p-IRF3 in older aortic endothelial cells compared with younger ones, both in aged mice and humans (Yu et al., 2022). Consequently, inhibiting cGAS or STING in aging models improves endothelial function, reduces senescence, and decreases the levels of aging markers (Yu et al., 2022). Diabetic retinopathy is a common microvascular complication in diabetes mellitus, characterized by damage to the retinal blood vessels, which can lead to vision impairment or even blindness. cGAS-STING was found to be crucial to retinal endothelial cell senescence, inflammation, and the consequent capillary degeneration (Liu et al., 2023). Interestingly, by measuring free-floating DNA in the diabetic eyes, significantly higher levels of extracellular DNA are observed in diabetic patients compared with nondiabetic controls, suggesting a key role for increased free-floating extracellular DNA in the activation of the cGAS–STING pathway (Liu et al., 2023). In COVID-19, infection with SARS-CoV-2 causes mitochondrial dysfunction and mtDNA release in endothelial cells in the skin, lungs, and brain, which activates cGAS–STING signaling, leading to cell death and type I IFN production. This process is a key driver of the overall inflammatory response, significantly contributing to the pathogenesis of COVID-19 (Domizio et al., 2022). Remarkably, pharmacological inhibition of STING reduces severe lung inflammation induced by SARS-CoV-2 and improves disease outcomes in mice. In further support of the role of BEC cGAS-STING signaling in brain disease, a recent study showed that BECs are the main cell drivers of the STING1-IFN axis in the brain during cerebral malaria, a fatal neurological complication of malaria infection (Pais et al., 2022). The study identified extracellular particles released from Plasmodium (the parasite responsible for malaria)-infected erythrocytes bind STING1 and activate the STING1-dependent type I IFN response in BECs (Pais et al., 2022). Furthermore, it pinpointed heme, a product of hemoglobin degradation within these extracellular particles, as a potential STING1 ligand. In addition, a recent study has shown that cGAS-STING signaling can also be activated in ECs independently of the DNA sensing pathway, for example, by vascular endothelial growth factor (Luo et al., 2023). Vascular endothelial growth factor activates the pathway by stimulating cGAS nuclear translocation via an importin-β pathway. Activation of cGAS–STING signaling in BECs results in increased production of type I IFNs and other cytokines (Figure 1). Type I IFNs from BECs, together with those from microglia, astrocytes, and neurons, elicit the interferon response, exacerbating or possibly even initiating neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration. They signal through the heterodimeric receptor (IFNAR) and Janus kinase/signal transducer and activator of transcription signaling cascade, activating IFN signaling and stimulating the transcription of interferon-stimulated genes (Paul et al., 2021). These interferon-stimulated genes include proinflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-1β, interleukin-6, and tumor necrosis factor-alpha. In addition to their role in natural immunity, interferon-stimulated genes are essential in the pathogenesis of CNS disorders including neuroinflammatory and neurodegenerative diseases (Paul et al., 2021). Type I IFNs produced by other cell types or by the endothelium itself can activate the IFNAR on BECs, i.e., binding to IFNARs on BECs in an autocrine and paracrine fashion. Activation of the IFN signaling pathway in BECs can result in neurovascular inflammation and BBB leakiness through multiple mechanisms: (1) Promoting endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, senescence, or death (Domizio et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023); (2) Impairing BBB integrity by downregulation of adherens junction protein VE-cadherin and tight junction proteins such as occludin and claudin-5 (Jana et al., 2022); (3) Enhancing leukocyte recruitment and infiltration (Pais et al., 2022). These findings prompt us to propose the significance of cGAS–STING signaling in BECs in aging and neurodegenerative diseases. Indeed, elevated STING expression is observed primarily in BECs in various neurodegenerative diseases including AD, PD, ALS, and multiple sclerosis (Ferecsko et al., 2023). Consistent with this, recent single-cell/nucleus RNA sequencing of BECs from aged mice and human AD brains (Yang et al., 2022) has revealed heightened IFN inflammatory responses and IFN expression, hinting a possible role of the cGAS-STING signaling in neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration in the context of aging and AD. We therefore propose that the abnormal activation of the cGAS–STING pathway in BECs not only triggers BEC inflammation and dysfunction, but also exacerbates or even initiates a cascade of events culminating in the unrestrained and prolonged synthesis of inflammatory genes. Concurrently, the BBB’s integrity is compromised, marked by increased permeability and leakage. BBB disruption then facilitates the infiltration of harmful peripheral substances into the brain parenchyma, fueling the escalation of neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration (Figure 1). BBB dysfunction is a pathological hallmark shared by both aging and AD and is believed to play a pivotal role in driving downstream neuroinflammation, neurodegeneration, and cognitive decline (Sweeney et al., 2019). However, while appreciation of the pathological significance of BBB dysfunction has been growing, the direct cause-and-effect link between BBB dysfunction and disease progression, as well as the molecular mechanisms underlying BBB dysfunction, is still not fully understood. Activation of cGAS–STING signaling in BECs may offer a potential molecular mechanism in understanding this connection and BBB dysfunction. Conclusions and perspectives: Excessive cGAS–STING activity in microglia, astrocytes, and neurons occupy an important role in the inflammation and pathogenesis of brain aging and neurodegenerative diseases, but BECs also have high cGAS–STING activity under these conditions (Ferecsko et al., 2023). The significance of cGAS–STING activation in peripheral ECs across various diseases prompts us to contemplate the potential importance of cGAS–STING in BECs in the context of aging and neurodegeneration. We hypothesize that aberrant activation of cGAS–STING signaling in BECs may trigger neurovascular inflammation and play a pivotal role in aging and neurodegeneration. Therefore, targeting cGAS–STING activation in BECs may attenuate endothelial dysfunction and brain inflammation, and should be an intriguing avenue for future inquiry regarding brain aging and neurodegeneration. Targeting signaling pathways in BECs offers a potential advantage of bypassing the BBB, a significant challenge in drug development. To date, few studies have examined the role of the cGAS–STING pathway in BECs in neurodegenerative disorders. Therefore, further research using BEC-specific approaches is needed to evaluate this hypothesis. BECs in arterial, capillary, and venous locations exhibit differences in transcriptomes in response to circulatory cues related to aging, innate immunity, and oxidative stress, with more significant changes in capillary BECs (Yang et al., 2022). It would be interesting to investigate whether the location of BECs exhibits differences in the activity and response of the cGAS–STING pathway during disease. As discussed above, cGAS–STING signaling can also be activated in ECs independently of the DNA sensing pathway (Luo et al., 2023). This raises an intriguing question: Can the cGAS–STING pathway be triggered in a DNA-independent manner in the context of neurodegeneration, and what roles do DNA-dependent and DNA-independent mechanisms play in this process? Another area of research is to study the interplay between BECs and the component cells of the brain. Could disruptions in the pathway within the brain cells produce secondary alterations in the endothelium? Answers to these questions will provide significant insights into this innate immune system and have therapeutic implications for treating neurodegenerative diseases. title: Complementary roles of glial cells in generating region-specific neuroinflammatory responses and phagocytosis in Parkinson’s disease
abstract: Neuroinflammation is associated with Parkinson’s disease: Reactive gliosis and neuroinflammation are hallmarks of Parkinson’s disease (PD), a multisystem neurodegenerative disorder characterized by a progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons. Neuroinflammation has long been considered a mere consequence of neuronal loss, but whether it promotes PD or is a key player in disease progression remains to be determined. Human leukocyte antigen, also known as major histocompatibility complex class II (MHCII), is expressed on all antigen-presenting cells of the immune system including microglia and central nervous system resident macrophages, and interestingly, its expression is increased in post-mortem PD samples (McGeer, 1988; Imamura, 2003). The strongest evidence for a link between the immune system and PD comes from genome-wide association studies, which have identified several polymorphisms in human leukocyte antigen-DR that are associated with an increased risk of idiopathic PD (Harms, 2023). Neuroinflammation is a complex and dynamic process that requires a cross-talk between glial and peripheral immune cells. Understanding these interactions is crucial for developing immunomodulatory interventions that could delay disease progression. Regional states of activation of microglia and astrocytes in the context of dopaminergic degeneration: Microglia are the resident immune cells of the central nervous system. Their dynamic ramified morphology and their motility allow them to be in a constant state of surveillance. In the adult brain, homeostatic microglia are in contact with neurons, axons, and dendritic spines and participate in synaptic plasticity (Salter and Stevens, 2017). This state can change dramatically when microglial cells are exposed to extracellular stimuli. Brain regions with specific neuronal activity, different neuron:glia ratios, and morphological and transcriptomic microglial heterogeneity would drive a context-dependent switch of these cells (Paolicelli, 2022). The dynamic nature of these states needs to be addressed in the context of neurodegeneration. Subcortical structures such as the ventral midbrain, which contains dopaminergic cell bodies, and the striatum, which contains GABAergic medium spiny neurons receiving dopaminergic afferents, are poorly characterized. Dopamine plays a key role in the control of basal ganglia function, and impairment of the nigrostriatal pathway is implicated in the motor symptomatology of PD. Analysis of glial activity in the midbrain and striatum would provide new clues to understanding the regional heterogeneity of the brain and new opportunities for therapeutic intervention in PD. The transcriptomic profile of midbrain and striatal CD11b+ cells shows that pathways involved in immune function and major histocompatibility complex (MHC) complexes are overexpressed in the midbrain, while those involved in synaptic function are underrepresented (Abellanas, 2019). Compared to the striatal cells, midbrain microglia (CD11b+CD45low) show a high state of immune alert with increased expression of TLR4, major histocompatibility complex class I (MHCI), MHCII, CD80, and CD86 and unique cell subsets, one MHCII+ with antigen-presenting properties and another TLR4+. As a result, higher levels of CD4 and CD8 T cell infiltration are detected in this region (Figure 1A). Systemic administration of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) induced a classical pro-inflammatory response with the production of tumor necrosis factor α (TNFα), interleukin (IL)1β, and IL6 in both regions and a specific increase of IL10 and transforming growth factor β in the midbrain. The production of these anti-inflammatory cytokines was accompanied by a loss of MHCII expression, a decrease in CD4 T cell infiltration in the midbrain, and an increase in regulatory T cells (Figure 1B). Morphological changes in microglia indicated an altered activation state, but did not correlate with their inflammatory profile. We concluded that the high basal immune alert state of the midbrain elicits immunosuppressive responses when exposed to an inflammatory stimulus (Abellanas, 2019).Figure 1: Glial activation states in the ventral midbrain and striatum in response to various stimuli.Schematic representation of the inflammatory and phagocytic phenotype of microglia and astrocytes, and the infiltration of peripheral immune cells in: (A) homeostasis (Abellanas, 2019), (B) systemic LPS administration (Abellanas, 2019), (C) αSyn overexpression (Basurco, 2023), (D) subacute and (E) chronic MPTP injection (Ayerra, 2024). Created with BioRender.com. αSyn: α-Synuclein; cMPTP: chronic MPTP mouse model; IL10: interleukin 10; IL1β: interleukin 1β; IL6: interleukin 6; LPS: lipopolysaccharide; MHCI: major histocompatibility complex class I; MHCII: major histocompatibility complex class II; sMPTP: subacute 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine mouse model; TGFβ: transforming growth factor β; TLR4: toll-like receptor 4; TNFα: tumor necrosis factor α; Treg: regulatory T cells.Neuroinflammatory microglia can induce a neurotoxic polarization of astrocytes by secreting TNFα, IL1α, and the complement factor C1q (Liddelow, 2017). Astrocytes, provide support to neurons by controlling ion and nutrient balance, participate in synaptic transmission, and are part of the blood–brain barrier (Han, 2021). The loss of homeostatic functions of glial cells and the acquisition of new activities may have an impact on disease pathogenesis. Therefore, we investigated about the functional state of microglia and astrocytes during the active phase of nigrostriatal pathway degeneration using experimental models of PD. In the α-synuclein (αSyn) overexpression mouse model, an adeno-associated virus was injected into the substantia nigra pars compacta to overexpress αSyn or the control protein mCherry. In these mice, we distinguished between an early stage with mild motor symptoms (2 weeks) and a late stage with severe motor impairment, neurodegeneration, and weight loss (4 weeks). To understand the early neuroinflammatory events that occur during dopaminergic dysfunction, we focused on the activation state of microglia and astrocytes at 2 weeks, hypothesizing that their functionality would differ between the striatum and the midbrain (Basurco, 2023). CD11b+ cells in the midbrain showed a phagocytic and an anti-inflammatory profile that was distinct from microglial signatures described in other neurodegenerative diseases (Keren-Shaul, 2017). In this region, astrocytes were the main pro-inflammatory players with a neurotoxic phenotype (Liddelow, 2017) and increased expression of transcripts associated with TNF, interferon γ and IL6 pathways. At the same time, a pro-inflammatory phenotype close to that of disease-associated microglia (Keren-Shaul, 2017) was detected in striatal CD11b+, which was not accompanied by morphological changes or by variation in the activation state of astrocytes. Iba1+ cells were actively involved in the clearance of cellular debris in the substantia nigra pars compacta. The relative increase in CD11b+CD45high cells detected by flow cytometry and in Iba1+ cells not expressing Tmem119, suggests that monocyte/macrophage infiltration in this area may play a relevant role in the early stages of neurodegeneration or when microglial cells are overwhelmed by the extent of neuronal damage. The mild loss of striatal dopaminergic terminals did not attract CD11b+CD45high and did not allow the detection of phagocytic activity (Figure 1C; Basurco, 2023). To determine whether glial activation states are generated by αSyn overexpression or by nigrostriatal degeneration, we used the 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP) mouse model. Dopaminergic neuronal death was induced by two intoxication regimens, subacute (sMPTP) and chronic (cMPTP) (Ayerra, 2024). The sMPTP induced an inflammatory response with a different contribution from each cell type. In the striatum, the pro-inflammatory phenotype of CD11b+ cells was counteracted by the anti-inflammatory astrocytic profile. In the midbrain, the roles were reversed, with CD11b+ cells exhibiting an anti-inflammatory profile and astrocytes being pro-inflammatory. The balance of the inflammatory responses resulted in reduced CD4 and CD8 T cell infiltration in both regions (Figure 1D). In contrast, cMPTP exposure resulted in a mild and prolonged neuronal loss that induced a pro-inflammatory response and increased CD4 T cell infiltration in the midbrain (Figure 1E). The phagocytic activity of glial cells was different in the two MPTP administration regimens. In addition, to eliminate the “time of analysis” factor, a new set of mice with the cMPTP administration regimen was generated and termed early cMPTP (ecMPTP). These animals were processed at the same time as the sMPTP mice and showed a milder motor impairment, but no nigrostriatal degeneration. At the onset of the neurodegenerative process (sMPTP and ecMPTP), microglia and astrocytes cooperated in removing striatal dopaminergic terminals. Over time (cMPTP), only microglia maintained the phagocytic activity. In the ventral midbrain, the lack of activation of a phagocytic program in microglia at the early stages of neurodegeneration (sMPTP and ecMPTP) was compensated by astrocytes, which were the main phagocytic mediators in this region. An increased number of infiltrating CD11b+CD45high and CD4 T cells was detected exclusively in ecMPTP mice suggesting that these cells may play a relevant role in the prodromal stages of the disease. As the dopaminergic lesion becomes chronic (cMPTP), only phagocytic microglia were detected in the midbrain. Overall, these results suggest that the inflammatory status and phagocytic activity of glial cells depend on the region, the intensity of neuronal damage, and the stage of degeneration. Morphological changes do not reflect the inflammatory state of glial cells. In the short term, midbrain CD11b+ cells generate an anti-inflammatory response in the presence of an intense stimulus such as LPS, αSyn, or MPTP, which becomes pro-inflammatory after chronicity of the lesion. In contrast, striatal CD11b+ cells always display a pro-inflammatory profile. The phagocytic activity of CD11b+ cells depends on the region and the stage of the degenerative process. Concluding remarks: Neuroinflammation is at the intersection of the major risk factors for PD, genes, environment, and aging. To target neuroinflammation as an intervention strategy, it is necessary to understand the dynamics of this response in the striatum and the midbrain and its impact on neuronal viability. The midbrain has unique properties in the generation of neuroinflammatory responses, with a high basal immune alert state generating a short-term anti-inflammatory response, in contrast to the classical pro-inflammatory response generated in the striatum. The anti-inflammatory microglial profile in the midbrain may represent an early event in neurodegeneration, and whether it protects or exacerbates neuronal death remains to be investigated. Interestingly, the activation state of microglia correlates with T cell infiltration, suggesting that these cells, rather than astrocytes, would drive immune extravasation in this region. Dopaminergic degeneration in PD is progressive, whereas in the experimental models is triggered simultaneously. Comparison of human and mouse glial cell phenotypes shows that the cMPTP mice better recapitulate the pro-inflammatory and phagocytic state of midbrain microglia sequenced from PD patients with advanced disease (Smajic, 2022; Ayerra, 2024). Early events in this model (ecMPTP) may help to understand prodromal glial activation states and their relationship to degeneration. Considering that glial cells stablish dynamic inflammatory and phagocytic phenotypes in the time course of the neurodegenerative process, it would be necessary to define therapeutic windows. The cooperativity between microglia and astrocytes suggests that therapeutic strategies should target specific glial activation states rather than a cell population. title: Shuttle and stabilize: H1.2-FUS complex in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis pathogenesis
abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal, late-onset neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the progressive degeneration of motor neurons in the motor cortex, brainstem, and spinal cord (Feldman et al., 2022). ALS affects approximately 1.68 per 100,000 individuals worldwide, although its incidence varies across different populations (Feldman et al., 2022). The initial clinical manifestations typically include muscle twitching and weakness, which progressively lead to impairments in speech, swallowing, and respiration. Additionally, approximately half of ALS patients experience cognitive decline or behavioral changes, underscoring the broad spectrum of disease symptoms. The intricate interplay between genetic predisposition, environmental factors, and aging contributes to ALS pathogenesis, posing significant challenges for the development of effective therapies. Thus, a deeper understanding of the molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying ALS is essential for identifying targeted therapeutic strategies. The etiology of sporadic ALS, which accounts for over 85% of cases, remains largely unknown, suggesting the involvement of multiple genetic variants in combination with additional risk factors (Feldman et al., 2022). The remaining cases follow a Mendelian pattern of inheritance. These familial ALS cases are associated with mutations in one of over 30 different genes, including several that encode RNA-binding proteins (Feldman et al., 2022). Among these, mutations in the fused in sarcoma (FUS) gene are among the most common causes of familial ALS (Feldman et al., 2022). FUS is predominantly a nuclear protein involved in DNA repair and RNA processing. However, non-synonymous mutations in its C-terminal nuclear localization signal, such as the aggressive P525L mutation, disrupt FUS nuclear transport, leading to its sequestration and aggregation in the cytoplasm (Vance et al., 2013; Feldman et al., 2022). Notably, mutant FUS accumulates in stress granules (SGs), which are dynamic cytoplasmic RNA-protein assemblies that form in response to cellular stress when translation is stalled, thereby protecting RNA molecules from degradation (Vance et al., 2013; Alirzayeva et al., 2024). While SG assembly initially serves as a protective mechanism, their prolonged persistence can contribute to protein aggregation and cell death, which are hallmark features of many neurodegenerative diseases, including ALS (Wolozin and Ivanov, 2019; Gutierrez-Garcia et al., 2023). These findings suggest that FUS-ALS pathology is driven not only by a loss of nuclear FUS function but also by a toxic gain-of-function in the cytoplasm. Indeed, the incorporation of mutant FUS disrupts the dynamic properties of SGs, altering their assembly and clearance (Wolozin and Ivanov, 2019; Alirzayeva et al., 2024). In a recent study, we used motor neurons derived from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) and Caenorhabditis elegans models to uncover molecular mechanisms underlying FUSP525L-driven pathology (Alirzayeva et al., 2024). Our findings provide deeper insight into the altered dynamics of the FUSP525L interactome and its post-translational modifications (PTMs), while also identifying a previously unknown role of histone H1.2 in ALS pathogenesis. iPSC-derived motor neurons expressing endogenous levels of FUSP525L provided a more physiologically relevant model for studying ALS-related changes in its interactome to previous approaches that relied on ectopic overexpression of mutant FUS. Moreover, the results were validated in motor neurons derived from patient iPSCs carrying other ALS-causing FUS mutations (R514S and R521C), reinforcing the broader implications of these pathogenic mechanisms. The FUSP525L interactome differs significantly from that of wild-type FUS, resulting in both loss and gain of protein interactors. Remarkably, mutant FUS exhibits increased interaction with histone H1.2, the only histone variant known to shuttle between the nucleus and cytoplasm (Lai et al., 2021). This gain of interaction influences FUSP525L intracellular localization and aggregation, SG dynamics, and motoneuronal survival (Alirzayeva et al., 2024). The elevated interaction between H1.2 and FUSP525L was observed exclusively in motor neurons, but not in their parental iPSCs, suggesting a reduced cellular capacity to maintain proteostasis following differentiation. Knockdown of H1.2 was sufficient to alleviate disease-related phenotypes in motor neurons, leading to predominantly nuclear localization of mutant FUSP525L, reduced cytoplasmic FUS aggregates, and restored SG dynamics. Conversely, H1.2 overexpression exacerbated ALS-related phenotypes (Alirzayeva et al., 2024). PTMs, such as phosphorylation, ubiquitination, and poly(ADP-ribosyl)ation (PARylation), regulate protein-protein interactions and SG dynamics. For instance, ubiquitination and ubiquitin-like modifications modulate SG clearance via autophagy (Wolozin and Ivanov, 2019). PARylation, catalyzed by ADP-ribosyl transferase enzymes (PARPs), involves the transfer of poly(ADP-ribose) (PAR) to target proteins, playing roles in chromatin remodeling, DNA repair, and cell survival. The dysregulation of PARP enzymes, accompanied by elevated nuclear PARylation levels has been associated with ALS, suggesting a potential role in disease progression (McGurk et al., 2018). Furthermore, transient interactions between PAR and FUS — through an unknown mechanism — induce FUS condensation, leading to protein accumulation that mimics the ALS phenotype (Rhine et al., 2022). Through a combination of approaches, we demonstrated that mutant FUSP525L-H1.2 interaction is regulated by PARylation and promotes FUSP525L accumulation in the cytoplasm (Alirzayeva et al., 2024). Importantly, pharmacological inhibition of PARylation via olaparib weakened the FUSP525L-H1.2 interaction and reduced motoneuronal degeneration, while PDD0017273, an inhibitor of poly(ADP-ribose) glycohydrolase, exacerbated FUSP525L aggregation and apoptosis. These findings highlight a critical role of PARylation in FUSP525L accumulation mediated by H1.2. The relevance of the FUSP525L-H1.2 interaction in ALS pathology was further validated in vivo using Caenorhabditis elegans models. Expression of human FUSP525L in the Caenorhabditis elegans nervous system leads to age-dependent FUS aggregation, reduced motility, and shortened lifespan, replicating disease-related phenotypes. Notably, these pathological phenotypes were rescued by downregulation of H1.2 and PARP1 orthologs. Conversely, neuron-specific overexpression of H1.2 worsened ALS-related phenotypes in ALS worm models (Alirzayeva et al., 2024). Together, our study identifies a role for histone H1.2 in FUS-ALS pathology, demonstrating its involvement in cytoplasmic FUS mislocalization and aggregation through a PARylation-dependent mechanism (Figure 1). These findings provide new insights into ALS pathogenesis and suggest potential therapeutic strategies targeting histone dynamics and PARylation to mitigate disease progression, while also raising new questions for future investigation.Figure 1: Proposed model of H1.2 and PARylation-driven FUS P525L toxicity in motor neurons.The increased interaction between mutant FUSP525L and H1.2, stabilized by PARylation, promotes the cytoplasmic accumulation of FUS, its enhanced incorporation into SGs, and altered SG dynamics, ultimately leading to neuronal cell death. Targeting PARylation through PARP1 inhibition or reducing H1.2 levels mitigates disease-related phenotypes by decreasing FUSP525L toxicity. This schematic was generated based on data from Alirzayeva et al. (2024). Neuronal morphology elements were adapted from Servier Medical Art (https://smart.servier.com/citation-sharing/) and all other components were created in Adobe Illustrator. FUS: Fused in sarcoma; H1.2: histone H1.2; PAR: poly(ADP-ribose); PARP1: poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase 1; SG: stress granule.For instance, further research is needed to elucidate the factors that modulate FUS-H1.2 interaction in the context of ALS. FUS oligomerization is primarily driven by its N-terminal low-complexity domains and is enhanced by nucleating molecules such as RNA or PAR (Rhine et al., 2022). Similarly, histone H1.2 possesses disordered N-terminal and C-terminal domains, which we found to be required for FUSP525L-H1.2 interaction (Alirzayeva et al., 2024). However, it remains unclear which FUS domains mediate interactions with H1.2 and how ALS-related mutations influence FUS conformation and its affinity for H1.2. Both FUS and H1.2 undergo extensive PTMs. PARylation, a key mechanism in PARP1-dependent FUS condensation at DNA damage sites, is typically reversible and does not normally lead to insoluble nuclear FUS aggregates (Singatulina et al., 2019). While in vitro studies suggest that PAR is a more potent nucleator of FUS compared to RNA, the interplay between low intracellular PARylation levels, its rapid and reversible nature, and competition with RNA molecules may be involved in fine regulation of FUS interactome and cellular functions (Rhine et al., 2022). Based on our findings, we speculate that elevated total PARylation levels, along with the increased affinity of mutant FUS for PAR, may drive its aberrant aggregation and promote FUS binding to H1.2 through the acquisition of additional interactions or the stabilization of transient interactions typical of wild-type FUS. Further in vitro studies using recombinant proteins could help clarify the molecular mechanisms and specific regions involved in FUS-H1.2 interactions. For instance, experiments incorporating FUS mutations that affect cellular localization or putative interacting domains, combined with different nucleators such as PAR and RNA, may provide deeper insights into the dynamics of FUS-H1.2 interactions under various cellular conditions. Moreover, beyond PARylation, other PTMs (e.g., H1.2 phosphorylation and the previously characterized arginine methylation of FUS) could modulate FUS-H1.2 interactions, further contributing to the complex pathological mechanisms underlying ALS. Notably, most pathological features observed in our study were either more pronounced (e.g., alterations in SG dynamics) or exclusively detectable in motor neurons (e.g., the gain of interaction of mutant FUS with H1.2), but not in their parental iPSCs (Alirzayeva et al., 2024). This suggests a potential explanation for the higher sensitivity to FUS-induced toxicity in motor neurons. While motor neurons remain the primary focus of ALS research, a study indicates that microglial dysfunction can also contribute to disease progression and neuronal pathology (Clarke and Patani, 2020). Therefore, it would be valuable to investigate whether PARylation-mediated FUS-H1.2 complexes are specific to neurons or if they represent broader ALS-associated hallmarks across different cell types. Beyond familial cases linked to FUS mutations, cytoplasmic inclusions of wild-type FUS are frequently observed in sporadic ALS cases. This suggests that while FUS mislocalization and aggregation may not always be the primary trigger of disease onset, they likely play a role in disease progression. Based on our data, it would be of interest to investigate whether FUS-positive cytoplasmic foci in sporadic ALS result from PTM-driven alterations in the FUS interactome. To address this, proteomic analysis of the interactome of wild-type FUS and its PTMs in iPSC-derived motor neurons from sporadic ALS patients could provide valuable insights. If wild-type FUS has aberrant PARylation and enhanced interaction with histone H1.2 similar to mutant FUS, the next step would be to determine whether these alterations contribute to sporadic ALS pathology, including FUS aggregation and neurodegeneration. In addition to ALS, we speculate that the interaction between FUS and histone H1.2 may also play a role in frontotemporal dementia (FTD). FTD largely overlaps with ALS at the genetic level and shares key pathological and molecular features, including alterations in SG dynamics (Feldman et al., 2022). Approximately 50% of ALS patients develop cognitive and behavioral symptoms associated with FTD, while 30% of FTD patients present with motor symptoms characteristic of ALS. Thus, FTD and ALS are considered to represent two ends of a spectrum disorder (Feldman et al., 2022). Given that FUS mutations and dysregulation are implicated in both disorders, it is plausible that increased FUS PARylation and interaction with H1.2 may contribute to SG dysregulation and neurodegeneration in FTD as well. As with sporadic ALS, iPSC-derived neurons from FTD patients could provide a valuable model to investigate this hypothesis. title: Chromatin remodeling, BRCA1, SAHF and cellular senescence
abstract: Cellular senescence is a state of stable cell growth arrest. Activation of oncogenes in primary mammalian cells typically triggers cellular senescence. Oncogene-induced senescence is an important tumor suppression mechanism, driving stable growth arrest of cancer progenitor cells harboring the initial oncogenic hit. Chromatin in the nuclei of senescent human cells is often reorganized to form specialized domains of facultative heterochromatin, known as senescence-associated heterochromatin foci (SAHF).1 SAHF contribute to senescence-associated cell growth arrest by sequestering and silencing proliferation-promoting genes such as the E2F target gene cyclin A.1 Notably, SAHF are different from constitutive heterochromatin, such as pericentromeres, which are largely excluded from SAHF.1 BRCA1 has been implicated in regulating chromatin structure. For example, oncogene-induced BRCA1 chromatin dissociation is known to regulate SAHF formation during senescence.2 Consistently, it has been demonstrated that BRCA1 causes large-scale chromatin de-condensation.3 In contrast, BRCA1 is implicated in regulating pericentromeric heterochromatin by silencing the repetitive satellite transcripts through ubiquitination of histone H2A.4 This suggests that BRCA1 may function to antagonize or promote heterochromatin formation in a genomic locus-specific manner. BRCA1 interacts with BRG1 in transformed cells. BRG1 is the catalytic subunit of the SWI/SNF chromatin-remodeling complex. BRG1 is known to regulate heterochromatin structure. For example, similar to the effects of BRCA1 loss on pericentromeres, it has been previously demonstrated that BRG1 deletion results in dissolution of pericentromeric heterochromatin.5 These findings support the notion that the BRCA1 and BRG1 complex is critical for constitutive heterochromatin structure at pericentromeres. It will be interesting to investigate whether the BRCA1 and BRG1 complex remains at pericentromeres to maintain the silencing of the satellite repeats in senescent cells. Activation of oncogenes such as RAS dissociates BRCA1 from chromatin.2 Interestingly, the interaction between BRCA1 and BRG1 is disrupted in cells undergoing senescence.6 This correlates with an increase in the level of BRG1 in the chromatin fraction.6 Indeed, ectopic BRG1 is sufficient to drive SAHF formation. Further, BRCA1 chromatin dissociation and the disruption of the interaction between BRCA1 and BRG1 correlate with SAHF formation during senescence.6 This suggests that BRCA1 antagonizes SAHF formation in the euchromatic genomic loci that encode for proliferation-promoting genes by sequestering BRG1 away from chromatin. Consequently, dissociation of BRCA1 from chromatin silences the expression of these genes through SAHF formation by BRG1. In addition, we discovered that the association of BRG1 with the promoters of the p21- and p16- encoding genes are enhanced during senescence.6 However, there is no detectable change in BRCA1’s association with the promoters of these genes.6 These findings suggest that BRG1 promotes or silences the expression of its target genes in a context-dependent manner during senescence. Further studies using global profiling of the changes in the distribution of BRG1 and BRCA1 by chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by next generation sequencing (ChIP-seq) in young and senescent cells will ultimately test these possibilities. As discussed above, BRG1’s association with the promoters of the p16- and p21- encoding genes are enhanced in senescent cells.6 Upregulation of p16 and p21 by BRG1 depends upon its chromatin remodeling activity.6 For example, a mutant BRG1 that is defective in its chromatin remodeling activity fails to upregulate p16 and p21 and is also impaired in SAHF formation.6 This suggests that BRG1 may drive SAHF formation directly via its chromatin remodeling activity and/or indirectly through upregulating p16 and p21 expression. BRG1 has been shown to interact with pRB,7 a key regulator of SAHF formation.1 Interestingly, the interaction between BRG1 and pRB is enhanced during senescence.6 This correlates with an increased level of BRG1 in the chromatin fraction of senescent cells.6 A similar increase in BRG1 in the chromatin fraction of senescent cells was also observed using non-biased proteomic analysis of young and senescent cells.8 Consistent with the idea that the enhanced BRG1 and pRB complex drives SAHF formation, BRG1 overexpression drives SAHF formation, and its knockdown suppresses SAHF formation induced by oncogenic RAS or BRCA1 knockdown.6 Significantly, BRG1’s interaction with pRB is necessary for its ability to drive SAHF formation. For example, a mutant BRG1 that can no longer bind to pRB also fails to induce SAHF formation.6 Interestingly, the mutant BRG1 remains capable of upregulating p16 and p21.6 This finding suggests that the interaction between BRG1 and pRB is necessary for SAHF formation and likely for silencing proliferation-promoting genes through SAHF formation. However, this interaction is dispensable for upregulating p16 and p21 by BRG1, which depends upon its chromatin remodeling activity.6 Oncogene-induced BRCA1 chromatin dissociation contributes to the accumulation of DNA damage in senescent cells due to impaired BRCA1-mediated DNA repair.2 Interestingly, senescence and SAHF formation induced by ectopic BRG1 is independent of the DDR.6 These findings suggest that BRG1 and the DDR function independently of each other downstream of BRCA1 chromatin dissociation to promote SAHF formation and senescence. In summary, BRCA1 chromatin dissociation increases the level of BRG1 in the chromatin fraction of senescent cells. This correlates with an enhanced BRG1 and pRB interaction that drives SAHF formation by silencing proliferation-promoting genes, while upregulating p16 and p21 senescence-promoting factors via BRG1’s chromatin remodeling activity in a pRB-independent manner.

title: Unpicking neurodegeneration in a dish with human pluripotent stem cells
abstract: Neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and Parkinson disease are characterized by the selective loss of specific neuronal subtypes. While the precise mechanisms underlying neuronal dysfunction and subtype specificity remain the subject of intense study, the cellular environment in which degenerating neurons reside has been shown to be an integral part of the disease. Converging lines of evidence highlight the crucial role of glia in setting the pace of, and perhaps in some instances initiating, neurodegeneration. ALS disease models, especially hSOD1G93A transgenic mice, have been particularly influential in establishing the conceptual framework of cellular autonomy and neurodegeneration. Astrocytes, microglia, and oligodendrocytes all play different roles in neuronal death; selective lineage-specific downregulation of mutant SOD1 transgene in ALS mouse models results in altered disease onset and/or progression. The development of embryonic stem cell (ESC)-derived neural cell co-culture systems has further enabled an exploration of the role of glia on neuronal survival at the molecular level. Several groups have independently established that both rodent hSOD1G93A astroglia1,2 and astrocytes derived at postmortem from human mutant SOD1 and sporadic ALS cases are toxic to mouse ESC-derived motor neurons (MNs). Even though mutant SOD1 cases constitute a relatively small fraction of ALS pathobiology, reactive glia are a defining feature of all neurodegenerative disorders. Astrocytes are in constant signaling exchange with the surrounding cells, acquiring a number of dynamic phenotypic changes in response to different stress stimuli broadly defined as “reactive astroglia”. Against this background, several key questions emerge. These include: are there disease or mutation specific reactive properties of astrocytes?; are there aspects of reactive gliosis common to all neurodegenerative conditions?; and which, if any, of these properties are glia-intrinsic, or are they secondary to neuronal degeneration? Dissection of these pathways requires a better understanding of glial diversity and function, a field that has been mostly left in the shadow of a neuro-centric focus on neurodegeneration. The advent of induced human pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) now provides the opportunity to build human cellular platforms that will allow us to directly address these questions. Directed-differentiation protocols permit the generation of near-homogenous populations of functional human neurones and glia, where the effect of particular mutations and/or stressors can be studied both in isolation and in co-culture. Using patient-derived iPSCs, we and others have recently shown that a mutation in TARDBP encoding TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) associated with familial ALS underlies a cell-autonomous vulnerability both in isolated motor neurones3,4 and astrocytes.5 Importantly, these iPSC-derived models recapitulate key cellular and biochemical aspects of the TDP-43 proteinopathies that account for 95% of ALS and 55% of frontotemporal dementia (FTD) cases. Is there a contribution of mutant TDP-43 astrocytes to human ALS pathology? Our in vitro co-culture experiments with real-time single-cell longitudinal survival analysis did not reveal an adverse survival effect of mutant TDP-43 astrocytes on either WT or MT human MNs, whereas hSOD1G93A transgenic mouse glia were toxic to both, as predicted.5 These contrasting findings may point to a mechanistic divergence of TDP-43 and SOD1 associated toxicity, or may simply reflect that in vitro differentiation of astrocytes from human PSCs in the absence of degenerating neurons does not capture the full spectrum of in vivo reactive properties. Indirect support of such an idea is provided by a recent study using transgenic rat models with selective neuronal lineage expression of mutant TDP-43 or fused in sarcoma (FUS), another RNA-binding protein linked to ALS and FTD, that identified lipocalin 2 as a neurotoxic factor induced in reactive astrocytes in response to neurodegeneration. This event is independent of the expression of the mutant proteins in the glial lineage.6 Improved understanding of the role of astrocytes in neurodegeneration requires multiple experimental—in vitro and in vivo—approaches. First, enriched in vitro astrocyte differentiation platforms from human PSCs should not only achieve the expression of specific lineage markers, both for glial restricted progenitors and differentiated progeny, but also include detailed functional characterization, such as glutamate uptake, induction of synaptogenesis, and propagation of calcium waves.5 The relevance of regional heterogeneity is uncertain, as is the perennial question of whether one can ever truly replicate the complexity inherent in an aged brain in an essentially developmental in vitro system. Consequently, in vivo transplantation and/or slice culture explant studies are necessary to extend the in vitro observations of function. Second, comparative transcriptomic and proteomic approaches—ideally with reference to pathological disease samples—are necessary to delineate reactive properties of glia under different disease settings. The interplay between neuronal degeneration and glial response has recently been addressed in a genome-wide study uncovering distinct as well as shared pathways in reactive gliosis caused by inflammation, stroke, and hSOD1G93A trangenic astroglial-mediated toxicity.7 It is now clear that glia can substantially affect the survival of neurons in disease states both by acquisition of reactive properties that are toxic and also through impairment of their normal physiological roles. Therefore, modulating astrocyte behavior by promotion of their neuroprotective functions8 and/or limiting their neurotoxic properties offers a new therapeutic strategy for neuroprotection in neurodegenerative disorders.

title: Proactive Healthcare - Fighting the affects of aging (Closed-Loop Biological Restoration & Multi-Omics Optimization Platform)
abstract: The Guardian System v7.0Ultimate Closed-Loop Biological Restoration & Multi-Omics Optimization PlatformFebruary 2026 Authors: Morgan Elliott Smart¹ and Jasper Kiron Smart¹Independent Research CollectiveCorresponding Author: Morgan Elliott Smart AbstractWe present The Guardian System v7.0, a comprehensive theoretical framework, computational architecture, and open-source simulation platform for closed-loop biological age reversal and multi-omics optimization. Aging remains the primary driver of chronic disease, disability, and mortality. Traditional medicine is overwhelmingly reactive, intervening only after clinical symptoms appear. The Guardian System represents a fundamental paradigm shift toward continuous, predictive, and restorative biology. It integrates real-time daily monitoring, yearly high-resolution calibration, environmental optimization, reversible RNA-based reprogramming, and (in future phases) AI-programmed nanotechnology into a single, self-improving closed-loop platform that treats aging as correctable software drift in a complex biological system.The core innovation is a rapid, iterative “Detect → Design → Deliver → Verify” feedback loop that uses temporary RNA AI machine learning editing to provide safe, reversible, and learnable gene expression modulation. This approach directly addresses the longstanding “confidence gap” in biological AI interventions by allowing the system to test, verify, and refine edits in real time without permanent genomic changes. Early simulations project 4–8 years of biological age reversal in targeted tissues over a 5–10 year period when all layers are integrated, with the system becoming progressively more accurate and effective through longitudinal data accumulation.Accompanying this vision paper is a fully runnable Python orchestrator (v7.0) that simulates 730–3650 days of multi-omics dynamics across a spatially-mapped 3D digital twin of 17 body regions. The simulator incorporates daily biological drift, nanobot anomaly detection, scheduled interventions (HBOT, rapamycin, senolytics, plasma dilution), microbiome and endocrine tracking, and restoration factor scaling. It produces publication-quality plots and detailed reports, making the framework immediately testable and extensible by the community.Executive SummaryThe Guardian System is a five-layer, closed-feedback platform designed to detect, localize, and correct biological deviations associated with aging in real time: Daily Monitoring Layer — Guardian Bracelet (multi-wavelength PPG, Raman spectroscopy, bio-impedance) Yearly Calibration Layer — Guardian Smart Suit + multi-site blood sampling for full multi-omics baselines Environmental Optimization Layer — Mild hyperbaric oxygen therapy (1.5–2.0 ATA) paired with AI-tuned frequency stimulation (PEMF, near-infrared, focused ultrasound) Active Reprogramming Layer — RNA AI machine learning editing for precise, reversible gene expression correction Future Active Repair Layer — AI-programmed Nano-Guardian Swarm for localized delivery Central Intelligence Layer — Quantum-hybrid Guardian AI maintaining a living, evolving digital twin The system is explicitly designed as a scalable roadmap: consumer-grade wearables in 2026–2028 → full in-vivo restoration capabilities by 2035–2045. It includes explicit integration pathways for long-duration space missions aboard the SCG-HMH Starship.Detailed System ArchitectureThe platform maintains a high-fidelity, spatially-mapped digital twin calibrated to a previously saved younger baseline (typically 10 years prior). Real-time data from the bracelet is continuously compared against the yearly suit-derived ground truth. When deviations are detected, the AI orchestrates personalized interventions across all layers, with RNA edits delivered during optimized HBOT windows to maximize cellular responsiveness.Key Components in Depth• Guardian Bracelet: Skin-like, <15 g wearable using multi-modal sensing for continuous blood flow, inflammation proxies, oxygenation, and indirect epigenetic markers. Data transmitted every 5–30 seconds.• Guardian Smart Suit: Full-body clinical garment for 45–90 minute yearly sessions providing spatial multi-omics mapping and painless micro-sampling.• Hyperbaric + Frequency Layer: 60–90 minute sessions 2–4× weekly, AI-tuned to the user’s DNA signature for amplified DNA repair and stem cell mobilization.• RNA AI Editing: Transformer-based models trained on the user’s longitudinal multi-omics data design custom RNA editors (CRISPR-Cas13, base editors, ASOs) in real time. Temporary nature enables safe iteration.• Nanobot Swarm (2035+): 200+ AI-programmed units for real-time anomaly scanning and localized repair delivery.• Digital Twin & AI: 17 anatomically mapped regions with epigenetic age, inflammation, and senescence tracking. Neuralink-style interface for brain-specific modulation.The GuardianAI Python Simulator (v7.0)Included as a core deliverable is a complete, runnable Python implementation that models: Daily stochastic biological drift across 10+ biomarkers Nanobot patrol and anomaly detection (epigenetic drift, senescence, mtDNA damage, etc.) Scheduled interventions with realistic effect sizes (rapamycin every 120 days, senolytics every 45 days, HBOT every 5 days, plasma every 365 days, RNA edits every 10 days) Microbiome, endocrine axis, sleep, and fitness trackers Restoration factor accumulation (up to 3.5×) 4-panel publication-quality matplotlib outputs (deviation, epigenetic age, microbiome, hormones) The simulator is deliberately minimal yet extensible, allowing researchers to fork, modify drift/repair parameters, or integrate real clinical datasets.Projected Outcomes and RoadmapsUnder optimistic synergies, the integrated system is projected to achieve 4–8 years of targeted tissue rejuvenation over 5–10 years of use. Conservative scenarios (based on current 2025–2026 trial data) still predict meaningful healthspan extension through reduced inflammaging, improved immune function, and delayed onset of age-related diseases.Implementation Roadmap (2026–2045) 2026–2028: Bracelet + basic AI deviation alerts + existing interventions (HBOT, rapamycin, senolytics) 2029–2032: RNA editing integration and first human safety trials 2033–2037: Full digital twin + Smart Suit commercialization 2038–2045: Nano-Guardian deployment and space-qualified versions Ethical, Regulatory, and Societal ConsiderationsThe document includes detailed sections on data privacy (digital twin as highly sensitive personal information), equity of access, risk assessment of repeated RNA interventions, informed consent for iterative learning systems, and regulatory pathways (starting with wellness-device classification and progressing to combination biologic-device approvals). Societal impact analysis covers potential compression of morbidity, workforce implications, and ethical frameworks for human enhancement.Cost Estimates (rough order of magnitude): Phase 1 (2026–2028 consumer MVP): $8,000–15,000 initial + $2,000/year Full clinical-grade system (2030s): $45,000–120,000 initial + $12,000/year Space Mission Integration: The platform is explicitly designed for integration with the SCG-HMH Starship, providing autonomous health maintenance for multi-year deep-space missions where real-time ground support is impossible.Call for CollaborationThis work is published as an open-source vision paper under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC-BY 4.0) to stimulate interdisciplinary collaboration across longevity science, AI, regenerative medicine, bioinformatics, bioengineering, and space medicine. We invite developers to fork the simulator, researchers to validate components, clinicians to propose trial designs, and ethicists to stress-test the governance model.Keywords: biological age reversal, closed-loop health systems, RNA AI editing, digital twin, epigenetic reprogramming, hyperbaric oxygen therapy, nanotechnology, multi-omics, personalized longevity, space medicine License: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 InternationalAccess: Open Access
